Hyperscaler capex is surging ~77% YoY to ~$725B in 2026 vs revenue growth lagging (e.g., Microsoft AI at $37B run rate vs ~$190B capex), keeping the gap wide; however, Q1 2026 earnings showed strong cloud/AI revenue acceleration (Google Cloud +63% YoY, AWS +28%, Microsoft Azure demand exceeding supply) and analysts noted 'the AI economy is healthy,' indicating the gap is wide but stabilizing rather than widening uncontrollably or closing.

Consumer survey data shows BNPL late payments rising steadily — a LendingTree March 2026 survey put 47% of users reporting a late payment (up from 41% in 2025 and 34% prior), and the Richmond Fed's February 2026 brief noted 'indicative evidence from consumer surveys that late payment and delinquency behavior among BNPL users has increased since 2023.' However, Affirm's 30+ day delinquency rate was flat YoY at 2.8% in Q1 2026, charge-off rates remain below credit card benchmarks, and the Richmond Fed found 'no clear evidence of elevated or accelerating consumer financial stress,' ruling out a score of 2.

As of mid-2026, Red Sea and Hormuz submarine cables face elevated and credible threats — repair vessels cannot safely operate, Meta paused new cable work, and Houthi/IRGC activity keeps both corridors effectively closed — but no confirmed new major outage-causing cut in 2026 is documented; the last confirmed major multi-cable outage was September 2025.

Q1 2026 global insured catastrophe losses totaled $20B, 26% below the 10-year average (Gallagher Re), with no single event exceeding $10B; the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season forecast (CSU/NOAA) calls for below-average activity due to El Niño, and reinsurance rates continued softening at April renewals — no evidence of an elevated or severe loss season underway.

China's NDRC suspended phosphate fertilizer exports through August 2026, and urea exports are managed under a tightly controlled June–August quota (~1.5–1.6M tonnes) with strict price floors ($660–670/t FOB), meaning curbs remain firmly in place even as a partial managed reopening for urea occurred in late May 2026. Between half and three-quarters of China's fertilizer export volume remains restricted.

China's National Bureau of Statistics (stats.gov.cn) officially reported that PPI increased by 3.9% year-on-year in May 2026, confirmed by TradingEconomics. This is the most recently published figure as of 2026-06-29.

The SEC formally extended compliance dates by one year in February 2025 (cash to Dec 31, 2026; repo to Jun 30, 2027), and as of April–May 2026 open exemptive relief requests from SIFMA (inter-affiliate) and IIB (extraterritorial) remain unresolved, with the Treasury TBAC noting 'still open issues' on scoping—constituting phased/partial relief and notable industry pushback, but not a full pause or rescission of the mandate.

Trepp data reported by ConnectCRE and Wolf Street shows the CMBS office delinquency rate spiked 103 bps to an all-time high of 12.34% in January 2026; a May 2026 Trepp LinkedIn post references an overall CMBS rate of 7.55% but does not surface an office-specific figure, so January 2026 remains the latest confirmed office sector data point.

The ICSG's April 2026 Copper Market Forecast 2026/2027 revised its 2026 outlook to a surplus of ~96,000 metric tons, reversing the October 2025 deficit forecast of 150,000 mt; the shift is attributed to lower-than-anticipated copper usage (demand growth cut from 2.1% to 1.6%) and higher secondary refined production.

As of early June 2026, the New York State Legislature passed a one-year statewide moratorium on AI data centers (S10642) awaiting the governor's signature, at least 12 states have introduced moratorium bills, dozens of municipalities have enacted local pauses (Minneapolis, Denver, Baltimore, Seattle, Reno, etc.), Florida and Oklahoma have signed major ratepayer-protection/cost-allocation laws, and over 300 data center-related bills have been filed in 30+ states — constituting widespread legislative bans and major project-level disruption well beyond 'several states weighing moratoria.'

Proskauer's Private Credit Default Index — tracking 697 senior-secured/unitranche US loans ($189.2B in original principal) — reported a Q1 2026 default rate of 2.73%, up from 2.46% in Q4 2025 and 1.84% in Q3 2025 (published April 27, 2026). Moody's (April 2026) corroborates with a 2025 range of ~1.6%–4.7%, and KBRA projected ~2% for 2026, consistent with the Proskauer reading.

Multiple major escalations are active simultaneously: the bipartisan MATCH Act (introduced April 2026) proposes banning even DUV lithography tool exports to China threatening ASML's remaining China business; the U.S. Commerce Secretary raised a formal EUV component-shipment allegation against ASML in June 2026 with BIS enforcement looming; and China enacted June 11, 2026 regulations granting explicit prospective retaliation authority against nations restricting Chinese technology access, described by CSIS as a 'qualitative shift' in China's control framework.

Meaningful diversification efforts are actively underway — TSMC's Arizona Fab 1 began mass production in 2025, a second Arizona fab is on track for 2H 2027, and Japan's Kumamoto Fab 2 is being upgraded to 3nm for 2028 — yet Taiwan still accounts for over 90% of leading-edge chip production and the Southern Taiwan Science Park facilities handle the majority of current 3nm output, leaving concentration high even as the multi-year buildout progresses.

The FAO Food Price Index averaged 130.8 points in May 2026, essentially flat from April's multi-year high of ~131 points, which itself marked a third consecutive monthly increase and the highest reading since early 2023. The index is elevated and on a broadly rising trend (up from ~125 in February 2026), though the May dip of 0.2% does not constitute a sharp spike.

Equable Institute's State of Pensions 2025 Year-End Update (published January 8, 2026) reported the aggregate funded ratio for U.S. state and local retirement systems at 82.5% as of December 31, 2025, up from 78.0% in 2024. Milliman's Public Pension Funding Index separately tracked the 100 largest public plans at 87.6% as of April 30, 2026, reflecting April's strong market rebound.

The GENIUS Act was signed into law on July 18, 2025, and regulators (OCC, FDIC, Treasury/FinCEN) have issued multiple notices of proposed rulemaking through April 2026, but all implementing rules remain in proposed—not final—form as of late June 2026, with the statutory deadline for final regulations falling on July 18, 2026 and the Act itself not taking effect until January 18, 2027 at the latest. This rulemaking-in-progress state, combined with noted inter-agency divergences (e.g., OCC vs. FDIC on reserve-breach consequences) and unresolved issues such as the stablecoin yield/rewards standoff and state 'substantial similarity' certification framework, constitutes implementation gaps and compliance friction (rubric level 1), but there is no evidence of a major non-compliant failure (level 2).

France's Lecornu minority government survived multiple no-confidence votes in January–February 2026 and passed the 2026 budget via Article 49.3, but remains a fragile minority government facing ongoing parliamentary fragmentation and budget deficit pressures. No snap election has been called and no government collapse has occurred as of late June 2026.

Multiple sources from early-mid 2026 identify early but not acute stress: CoreWeave faces a $4.2B refinancing wall in 2026 on GPU-collateralized debt whose collateral value has declined sharply, and repayments on an 11%-rate facility began in January 2026 just as GPU collateral values fell — consistent with 'early signs of strain.' However, CoreWeave has continued to access capital markets (tapping high-yield for $3.75B at ~9% and securing an $8.5B investment-grade GPU-backed deal), and no confirmed broad default or acute refinancing failure has been documented, so level 2 is not warranted.

The Strait of Hormuz has been effectively closed since late February 2026, severely disrupting fertilizer (ammonia, sulfur, urea) shipping that normally accounts for ~30% of global trade; a US-Iran MOU signed June 17 triggered a partial reopening, but as of June 29 only ~5 vessels/day transit vs. ~93/day pre-crisis, the IMO evacuation program is paused after a new vessel attack, and war-risk insurance remains at 8x pre-crisis levels — firmly disrupted/elevated risk, not yet restored to normal.

The Strait of Hormuz, effectively closed since late February 2026 following US-Israeli strikes on Iran, is now in a fragile reopening phase: a US-Iran MOU signed June 17 lifted both blockades, commercial traffic has begun to recover (IMO paused its evacuation plan on June 23), but Iran declared the strait 'closed' again on June 20 citing Lebanon ceasefire violations, the JMIC widened a naval transit corridor only on June 27, transit volumes remain far below normal (5% of pre-crisis on June 21 per IMF PortWatch), and war-risk insurance remains ~8x pre-crisis levels. The Red Sea is also contested, with Houthis having resumed attacks on Israeli-linked vessels and threatening broader escalation, while the Bab el-Mandeb remains disrupted below pre-war capacity.

Benchmark Minerals (March 2026) reported dysprosium oxide CIF North America at 4.4x EXW China prices in 2025, with the multiple rising into 2026; Ucore's Feb 2026 press release cited ex-China dysprosium at >5x China domestic (~$1,000/kg vs ~$200/kg), and The Oregon Group (June 2026, citing Argus/Reuters data) confirmed HREEs climbed 4–5x outside China. A central estimate of ~4.5x reflects the current mid-2026 range across key HREEs (dysprosium, terbium), noting significant element-by-element variation.

Non-renewals remain elevated and are spreading across 13+ states (CA, FL, TX, NC, OK, MN, NE, GA, CO, etc.) with insurers using ZIP-code-level AI underwriting to drop policies, and nonrenewal notices surged ~30% between 2018–2022 with the trend continuing into 2026; however, some offsetting stabilization signals exist — AM Best revised the US homeowners outlook from negative to stable, reinsurance costs are softening, Florida's market is improving, and a mid-2026 consumer survey found only 10% of homeowners had a policy canceled or non-renewed, down from 11% the prior year — pointing to a 'rising but not yet accelerating across the board' picture.

LBNL's 'Queued Up: 2025 Edition' (published December 2025, analyzing data through end of 2024) reports that the typical project reaching commercial operation in 2024 spent 55 months (4.5 years) in the queue, with the median duration from interconnection request to COD having doubled to over 4 years for projects built in 2018–2024. The LBNL summary states 'over 4 years' but a secondary source citing the same report gives the specific figure of 55 months.

TradingEconomics reported the Japan 30-year JGB yield at 3.88% on June 24, 2026, up 0.03 percentage points from the prior session and 0.97 points higher year-over-year. No same-day (June 29) 30-year figure was retrievable, though the 10-year yield was confirmed declining modestly through June 29.

China's rare earth magnet export licensing regime is active but selectively restrictive: a 'general license' system was introduced in December 2025 for approved major producers (e.g., JL Mag, Ningbo Yunsheng), yet approvals remain slow, documentation-intensive, and unpredictable for most applicants, with European firm approval rates reported below 25% and prices surging sixfold since January 2026. Grasberg (world's 2nd-largest copper mine) has been operating at ~35% reduced capacity since a September 2025 mudslide forced force majeure, with full restart now pushed to 2028; combined with Kamoa-Kakula seismic disruptions and El Teniente's collapse, major institutions (Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan, ICSG) forecast a 150,000–600,000-tonne 2026 refined copper deficit — a clear cluster of major outages materially tightening supply.

Multiple new IMF programs appeared in 2026 (Pakistan $7B bailout tranche in March, Ukraine new $8.1B EFF in February, further Ukraine review in June), and the IMF warned in mid-April that at least a dozen more countries are expected to seek programs due to Middle East conflict-driven energy shocks. Japan's 10-year JGB yield is elevated at ~2.61–2.65% as of late June 2026, with the 30-year yield at ~3.88%, reflecting persistent yield pressure tied to Takaichi's expansionary fiscal stance and BOJ rate-hike expectations; while Takaichi pledged no extra net borrowing in the May supplementary budget to assuage markets, financing concerns remain active (potential consumption tax cuts, rising debt-servicing costs) without evidence of disorderly auction failures.

Multiple large managers — including Apollo, Blue Owl, BlackRock (HPS), Morgan Stanley, Ares, and Cliffwater — have all activated 5% quarterly redemption caps in Q1–Q2 2026 following redemption requests ranging from 9% to 40%+ of NAV, with a CRS report noting the wave generated 'widespread concerns and congressional attention.' The FDIC reports only 2 bank failures in 2026 (Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust in January and Community Bank & Trust – West Georgia in May), both small, firm-specific collapses with no evidence of systemic deposit flight or a cluster of CRE-driven failures. Broader analysis confirms that while CRE stress on regional banks is elevated—with office loan delinquencies near 12% and ~$875B in maturing CRE debt in 2026—the pattern remains one of 'individual institution events rather than systemic episodes,' consistent with isolated regional-bank stress (level 1) rather than a cluster of failures (level 2).

As of late June 2026, Lake Mead sits at approximately 1,045 feet — just 10 feet above the critical 1,035-foot threshold where Hoover Dam loses 70% of its power-generating capacity — and is only 29% full, at 47% of average for the date per USBR data. The USBR's June 2026 24-Month Study projects continued decline toward a record-low 1,015 feet by July 2027, federal shortage conditions are in effect, and the entire Colorado River system is at ~33% capacity with inflows at 15% of the 30-year average.

The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026) projects OASI trust fund depletion in Q4 2032—one year earlier than prior estimates—with only 78% of benefits payable at that point, triggering active reform debate; however, no concrete benefit cuts or emergency legislative measures have been enacted, with CRFB and Brookings both noting that Congress has yet to act on any reform plan.

fact: Fitch Ratings (via Auto Remarketing, May 21 2026): subprime auto ABS 60+ day delinquency rate declined to 6.11% in March 2026, aided by seasonal tax-refund cures, down from 6.80% in February and a record 6.90% in January 2026. 'This improvement is expected to be short lived,' Fitch said, projecting renewed deterioration through 2026.
rationale: The rubric asks for the latest reported subprime auto 60+ day delinquency rate as a percent; the most recent hard Fitch index reading published (May 21, 2026 report covering March data) is 6.11%, which maps directly to the rubric's request for a single percentage figure. Confidence is medium rather than high because Fitch's April and May 2026 index prints had not yet been publicly released as of the available search results.

dissent.view: Some analysts (Stimson Center's Yun Sun, Taipei Times, Jan 2026) argue the structural trend — normalized drills, eroded median line, contiguous zone incursions — represents a slow-motion crisis that could tip quickly in 2026, implying the rubric's Level 1 understates cumulative risk.

fact: As of June 26, 2026, the ISW/AEI China & Taiwan Update reports ongoing CCG incursions (4 near Kinmen, 1 near Pratas in May) and ADIZ incursions at rates 'markedly decreased from previous averages exceeding 300 per month,' with no new named large-scale PLA drill in 2026 H1. The most recent significant military event was the PLA carrier Fujian transiting the Taiwan Strait (~June 24, 2026, SCMP) amid Taiwan's Immediate Combat Readiness Exercise — characterized by PLA Eastern Theater Command as 'routine training.' The last named blockade-rehearsal drill was Justice Mission 2025 (Dec 29–30, 2025). No kinetic clash, actual blockade, or full mobilization has been reported. Source: ISW/AEI China & Taiwan Update, June 26, 2026 (https://www.aei.org/articles/china-taiwan-update-june-26-2026/); SCMP, ~June 24, 2026 (https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3358227).
rationale: Activity is assertive — persistent CCG incursions, carrier transits, and grey-zone coercion — but ADIZ incursion rates are declining from prior peaks and no new named large-scale blockade drill has occurred in 2026 H1, ruling out Level 0 (calm/routine). The absence of any kinetic clash, actual blockade, or full mobilization rules out Level 2 (crisis), placing the indicator squarely at Level 1 (elevated).

No deadline extension has been announced and the SEC reaffirmed the Dec 31, 2026 / Jun 30, 2027 deadlines in March 2026, precluding a score of 2; but the unresolved scope issues and bespoke legal negotiation burden preclude a clean score of 0.

dissent.view: IEA April 2026 'Key Questions on Energy and AI' frames the dominant dynamic as developers bypassing slow queues via onsite gas generation rather than forced curtailment of operating facilities — consistent with TIGHT (1) rather than ACUTE (2) as a systemic characterization

LBL Queued Up 2025 edition notes a 12% decrease in total active queue volume year-over-year through end-2024, suggesting queues may be beginning to self-correct via withdrawals, which would point toward TIGHT rather than ACUTE

fact: On May 18, 2026, the U.S. DOE issued a Section 202(c) emergency order authorizing PJM Interconnection to curtail data centers and other large loads with backup generation; PJM simultaneously activated pre-emergency demand response in the Dominion, BGE, and PEPCO areas due to <5,800 MW reserve margins during a heat/maintenance crunch (Utility Dive, May 19 2026). Separately, on June 9 2026 Seattle City Council enacted an emergency moratorium on new data center siting citing grid capacity constraints (Seattle City Council, June 9 2026). LBL 'Queued Up' (May 2026 update, emp.lbl.gov) reports 2,060+ GW in U.S. interconnection queues as of end-2025, with median queue duration doubled to >4 years. IEA Electricity 2026 (iea.org, ~June 2026) confirms 2,500+ GW stalled in global queues and 'many power systems already experiencing rising congestion-related curtailment.'
rationale: The DOE 202(c) emergency order authorizing PJM curtailment of data-center-class load, combined with actual demand-response activation across Mid-Atlantic zones on May 18-19 2026, constitutes a confirmed grid-emergency curtailment of data-center load — the rubric-2 threshold. The Seattle power-scarcity-driven moratorium (June 9 2026) is an additional rubric-2 indicator; together these push the reading firmly to ACUTE.

fact: Q1 2026 earnings (per Financial Times/Statista aggregation, April 29-30 2026): combined hyperscaler capex guidance for 2026 rose to ~$725B (+77% YoY from ~$410B in 2025); individual quarterly capex: Alphabet $35.67B (>+100% YoY), Amazon $44.2B (~+77% YoY), Microsoft $30.88B (+84% YoY), Meta $20B (+54% YoY, full-year guide raised to $125-145B). AI-attributable revenue: AWS +28% YoY ($37.6B), Google Cloud +63% YoY ($20B), Microsoft AI run-rate $37B annualized (+123% YoY). Allianz Research characterizes the capex-vs-revenue divergence at ~46% (Forbes, June 2, 2026). Sequoia Cahn estimates a $600B annual revenue gap, widening in 2026.
rationale: Capex growth (~77-84% YoY) clearly exceeds AI-revenue growth for AWS (+28%) and is comparable-to-lower than Google Cloud (+63%) and Microsoft AI (+123%), placing the aggregate gap firmly in WIDE territory. AI revenue is still accelerating strongly YoY with no confirmed QoQ deceleration in Q1 2026, ruling out score=2; Meta raised capex without proportional revenue proof but did not cut its AI-revenue outlook, so the score=2 trigger is not cleanly met.

dissent.view: Richmond Fed (Feb 2026 EB-26-05) characterises BNPL financial-stability impact as 'limited at present' with 'no clear evidence of elevated stress,' suggesting a more benign reading closer to level 0 on systemic grounds.

CFPB Dec 2025 market spotlight found charge-off rates and late-fee frequency declined through 2023, which if extrapolated would support level 0; however Affirm's own 2026 SEC filings show delinquency has since risen YoY.

fact: Affirm FQ3'26 SEC filing (affirmfq326shareholderle.htm, filed ~May 2026): 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans ex-Peloton/Pay-in-X rose 29 bps YoY to 2.8% (vs. 2.5% in FQ3'25); allowance for credit losses at 6.0% of loans held for investment; cumulative net charge-offs on recent cohorts tracking ~3.5% of cohort GMV, in-line with expectations.
rationale: 30+ DPD is up 29 bps YoY — rising but well below the 100 bps threshold for level 2. Charge-offs (~1.83% per CFPB 2023 data; ~3.5% cumulative cohort GMV per Affirm) remain contained below the 5% spike threshold and the 3% containment ceiling, firmly placing this in rubric level 1.

dissent.view: Australian Defence Minister Marles (AUKUS, May 2026) stated cables are being cut 'at an unprecedented rate' over the past 18 months, implying ongoing active incidents, though no specific currently-unrepaired cable is named.

Better World Campaign (Mar 2026) states '2024 and 2025 disruptions rippled across Middle East and South Asia after cables were severed by Iranian-backed Houthi forces', and Meta paused 2Africa Pearls in the Gulf — suggesting continued active disruption environment.

fact: No confirmed currently-severed and unrepaired major submarine cable identified in Red Sea, Hormuz, or Baltic as of late June 2026. The most recent confirmed mass-cut event was ~6 Sep 2025 (Bab el-Mandeb: SEA-ME-WE-4, IMEWE, EIG, FALCON/GCX, ~15 cables total per Marine Technology News, Dec 2025), which has since been rerouted/repaired. TeleGeography (May 4, 2026) and AGBI (Mar 2026) assess Hormuz cables as at elevated risk but intact. Forbes (Jun 26, 2026) flags ongoing Baltic shadow-fleet threat but names no new 2026 cut. AUKUS communique (May 31, 2026) cites 'unprecedented' pace of cuts over 18 months without naming a current active break.
rationale: Rubric level 1 (THREATENED) applies: multiple credible, active threat vectors exist — shadow fleet in Baltic, Iran conflict risk at Hormuz, residual Houthi activity near Bab el-Mandeb — but no primary source confirms a major cable currently severed and unrepaired as of 2026-06-30, so level 2 (CUT) is not warranted.

dissent.view: Aon characterizes the same $20 billion Q1 figure as '6% above the 21st-century average,' implying a slightly above-average reading on a longer historical baseline rather than the 10-year window used in the rubric.

fact: Global insured catastrophe losses in Q1 2026 totaled $20 billion — 26% below the 10-year Q1 decadal average of $26 billion — with no single event exceeding $10 billion insured; Aon independently confirms ~$20 billion. Source: Gallagher Re Q1 2026 Natural Catastrophe and Climate Report (ajg.com/gallagherre, April 21 2026) and Aon Q1 2026 Global Catastrophe Recap.
rationale: YTD insured losses of $20 billion are below — not above — the 10-year average, and no individual event breached the $10 billion threshold, satisfying every condition of the NORMAL (0) tier. The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season (peak: Aug–Oct) had not yet produced any named-storm insured losses as of the report date.

dissent.view: The Philippines reported China indicated fertilizer exports would not be restricted, though Chinese officials never publicly confirmed this (Reuters, Mar 2026)

fact: NDRC suspended phosphate fertilizer exports through August 2026 (directed Dec 2025; confirmed by S&P Global Platts, Exiger, SunSirs). In mid-March 2026, Beijing added a NEW ban on nitrogen-potassium (NK) blends and additional phosphate varieties (Reuters/Bloomberg, ~18 Mar 2026). For urea, export quotas were suspended Jan-May 2026 (only 461,500 t shipped Jan-Mar); on ~26 May 2026, NDRC issued a fresh 1.5-1.6 mt quota for Jun-Aug with a mandatory price floor of $660/t FOB prilled and $670/t FOB granular - still a tightly controlled quota regime, not unrestricted exports (Profercy, 26 May 2026; Keyuan Fertilizer, 29 May 2026). Phosphate ban remains intact. Between half and three-quarters of China's fertilizer exports are restricted (Exiger/Reuters, Apr 2026).
rationale: The mid-March 2026 addition of NK-blend and further phosphate bans on top of existing urea quotas and the Dec-2025 NDRC phosphate suspension constitutes a NEW/BROADENED restriction within the trailing 3 months, satisfying rubric level 2; the May 2026 urea quota reopen is itself a controlled quota (not a lifting), and the phosphate ban remains in place through August 2026.

fact: NBS official press release (https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202606/t20260611_1963929.html, released 2026-06-11): 'In May 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 3.9% year on year and 0.5% month on month.'
rationale: The rubric requires the signed YoY figure exactly as published by NBS; +3.9% is the most recent official NBS print (May 2026, released 2026-06-11), confirmed by CNBC and TradingEconomics. A +3.9% reading is a large positive move — the highest since July 2022 — signalling a meaningful cost-push input-price shock that could export inflationary pressure to trading partners.

dissent.view: Commissioner Uyeda stated Sep 30, 2025 that 'the Commission does not intend to consider further extensions,' suggesting the SEC views the current dates as firm and the trajectory as on-track relative to the extended schedule.

fact: On Feb 25, 2025, the SEC formally extended the original compliance dates by one year to Dec 31, 2026 (cash) and Jun 30, 2027 (repo) via Exchange Act Release No. 34-102487 (SEC.gov press release, Feb 25, 2025). As of Apr 20, 2026, Commissioner Uyeda confirmed the current dates stand, but the SEC simultaneously published two pending exemptive-relief requests (SIFMA inter-affiliate relief and IIB extraterritorial relief, both published Apr 17, 2026, comment deadline May 29, 2026) that are unresolved as of today. Sep 30, 2025 Uyeda statement noted 'the Commission does not intend to consider further extensions.' No second extension order has been announced.
rationale: The rubric scores 1 ('SLIPPING') when 'an official extension [has been] granted, OR exemptive-relief requests pending.' One formal one-year extension was granted (Feb 2025), and two exemptive-relief requests remain pending and unresolved as of Jun 30, 2026 - both prongs of the rubric-1 trigger are satisfied. No second extension has been announced, so rubric-2 is not met.

dissent.view: January 2026 office CMBS delinquency was 12.34%, an all-time high per Trepp — 114 bps above the February reading used as the primary value.

fact: Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate fell 114 basis points to 11.20 percent in February 2026, pulling back from January's all-time high of 12.34 percent, driven by modifications and extensions of five large matured office loans. Source: multihousingnews.com / Trepp, reported ~June 2026.
rationale: The last explicitly cited office-sector CMBS delinquency rate from Trepp is 11.20% for February 2026; the May 2026 overall report notes three property types moved lower but does not publish a specific office rate in available excerpts, so 11.20% remains the most recent hard figure. At ~11%, office CMBS delinquency is sharply elevated versus historical norms and near all-time highs, reflecting deep structural stress rather than idiosyncratic single-loan events.

dissent.view: J.P. Morgan projects a 330,000 mt refined copper deficit for 2026, driven by hyperscale AI data-center demand
ICSG October 2025 forecast (now superseded) projected a 150,000 t deficit for 2026

fact: ICSG 'Copper Market Forecast 2026-2027' (April 2026): global refined copper market forecast at a SURPLUS of ~96,000 metric tons in 2026, reversing the prior October 2025 forecast of a 150,000 t deficit; driven by lower-than-expected demand growth (usage now +1.6% vs prior +2.1%) and higher secondary refined production. Source: ICSG.org April 2026 press release, corroborated by Recycling Today (Apr 28 2026) and ADMIS (Apr 24 2026).
rationale: The latest ICSG forecast (April 2026) places 2026 refined copper balance at +96,000 t surplus, well above the +100kt surplus threshold in the rubric. This unambiguously maps to score 0 (SURPLUS) under the stated rubric.

dissent.view: datacenterbans.com characterized (June 1, 2026) 'the path to broad statewide data center moratoriums remained closed,' implying no statewide enactment — consistent with our reading, but suggesting a more cautious overall assessment of the movement's success.

theaiconsultingnetwork.com stated (April 2026) 'Maine is the only state to pass a statewide data center moratorium into law' — but this is now outdated/inaccurate; Maine's bill was subsequently vetoed April 24, 2026.

fact: As of mid-June 2026, no statewide moratorium has been signed into law (NY S10642 passed the legislature June 4 but awaits Gov. Hochul's signature; Maine LD 307 was vetoed April 24). However, enacted local construction pauses exceed 10 jurisdictions: Michigan alone has 20+ local moratoriums, plus Smithfield RI (outright ban), Reno NV (May 14 pause), Lysander NY (May 7), Town of Perth NY, Groton CT, Peculiar MO, Bangor ME, Seattle WA (in committee/emergency moratorium cleared May 20), and Indianapolis IN (non-binding pause-resolution June 3), among others. Source: datacenterbans.com (June 1, 2026); Rockefeller Institute of Government (June 2026); MultiState (June 2026).
rationale: The rubric's level-2 threshold of '>10 jurisdictions with enacted pauses/cancellations' is clearly met by the 20+ enacted local moratoriums in Michigan alone, plus confirmed enacted pauses in RI, NV, NY towns, CT, MO, and ME localities. A statewide enacted moratorium has not yet been confirmed, but the >10 local enacted threshold independently qualifies as WIDESPREAD.

dissent.view: Fitch Ratings reported the US private credit default rate hit a record 6.0% in April 2026 (broader/adjusted definition including distressed exchanges), per Forbes May 25 2026
With Intelligence estimates the 'true' default rate including selective defaults and liability management exercises approaches 5%, versus the sub-2% headline figure
CAIA/Morgan Stanley cite direct lending defaults 'currently running at around 5.6%' (Apr 2026), with Morgan Stanley forecasting a rise to 8%
FS KKR Capital (individual-investor BDC) reported its own portfolio default rate jumped to 8.1% in Q1 2026 from 5.5% in Dec 2025 — a fund-specific reading, not market-wide

fact: Proskauer's Private Credit Default Index, tracking 697 senior-secured and unitranche US loans totalling $189.2 billion in original principal, recorded a default rate of 2.73% for Q1 2026 — up from 2.46% in Q4 2025 and 1.84% in Q3 2025. Released April 27 2026. Source: https://www.proskauer.com/report/proskauers-private-credit-default-index-reveals-rate-of-273-for-q1-2026
rationale: Proskauer's index is the most granular, loan-level, primary-source dataset for US direct lending defaults and is the standard benchmark cited by the Fed, Forbes, and the broader leveraged-finance community; 2.73% is the single most recent authoritative print. The rising trend (1.76% → 1.84% → 2.46% → 2.73% over four consecutive quarters) is corroborated by higher PIK income at BDCs and BDC equity discounts, consistent with mounting but not yet systemic funding stress. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (2.73 vs 0.0); held for review]

fact: IMF COFER Data Brief (published 2026-03-27, data.imf.org/en/news/imf%20data%20brief%20march%2027): 'The share of US dollar holdings decreased to 56.77 percent in 2025Q4, from 56.93 percent in 2025Q3.' Total FX reserves stood at $13.14 trillion. This is the most recent official COFER release as of 2026-06-30; Q1 2026 data is not yet published (COFER runs with ~3-month lag, next release expected late June/early July 2026).
rationale: The rubric asks for the latest IMF COFER USD share of allocated global FX reserves as a percent. The most recent published figure is 56.77% for 2025Q4, released by the IMF on 2026-03-27, which maps directly and mechanically to the indicator. No Q1 2026 COFER release has been detected as of the search date.

dissent.view: US Southwest drought has been improving: USDM West page notes snowpack 'returned to near-normal' with D1-D4 improvements in NM/SW Colorado, suggesting conditions may be easing from peak severity

fact: Taiwan's Water Resources Agency imposed water rationing after the driest winter in 75 years, explicitly affecting chipmaking hub Hsinchu County; emergency measures authorised through July 2026 (Taipei Times, 2026-03-27, https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/front/archives/2026/03/27/2003854549). TSMC CEO C.C. Wei warned of mounting water-supply constraints in June 2026 (Reuters/Astute Group, 2026-06). Separately, US Southwest (New Mexico) shows D2=55% and D3=30% area coverage per USDM ~2026-06-24 (droughtmonitor.unl.edu/Data/pdf/current/current_NM_cat.pdf).
rationale: A confirmed government water-rationing order at Taiwan's Hsinchu fab hub satisfies the rubric's ACUTE (2) criterion of a confirmed water-rationing order at a fab region, independent of whether D3/D4 thresholds are met. The US Southwest additionally shows D3 coverage (~30% of NM) corroborating regional severity.

dissent.view: East Asia Forum (Mar 11 2026) characterises the Trump White House as 'cooling' chip controls and prioritising trade-talk stability, suggesting the executive branch posture is more TIGHTENING than full RETALIATION escalation; congressional proposals (MATCH Act) remain unenacted.

fact: Within the trailing 3 months (Apr–Jun 2026), both sides enacted documented measures. US/allied: (1) MATCH Act introduced ~Apr 2, 2026 proposing blanket DUV ban on ASML/Japan tools to China (CNBC, Apr 7 2026); (2) BIS guidance ~Jun 1, 2026 affirming Blackwell chip restrictions apply to overseas subsidiaries of China-HQ companies (Al Jazeera, Jun 1 2026). China retaliation: (3) MOFCOM Jun 22, 2026 added 10 US firms—including MP Materials and USA Rare Earth—to its export control list, explicitly as retaliation for Pentagon military-company designations (Al Jazeera/Yahoo Finance, Jun 22 2026); (4) China enacted Jun 11, 2026 tech-transfer regulations granting statutory retaliation authority against nations restricting Chinese tech investments (abhs.in citing FT, Jun 2026); (5) MOFCOM Announcement No. 26, Jun 24, 2026, formalised a whistleblower/reporting mechanism for strategic-mineral dual-use export-control violations, effective Jul 1 2026 (geopolitechs.org, Jun 2026). ASML China revenue share fell from 36% (Q4 2025) to 19% (Q1 2026), corroborating demand compression from cumulative controls.
rationale: Rubric level 2 (RETALIATION) is met: China enacted affirmative countermeasures—entity-list additions explicitly framed as retaliation plus new statutory retaliation authority—within the trailing 3-month window, alongside concurrent US/allied TIGHTENING actions; volume signal (ASML China share 36%→19%) anchors the disruption read.

dissent.view: Analysts project overseas capacity (all nodes) hitting ~20% of TSMC total by 2028, and sub-2nm mix could reach 30% US / 70% Taiwan by 2030, suggesting trajectory toward rubric level 1 within 4 years - but these are forward projections, not current operational reality.

fact: As of Q2 2026, all TSMC leading-edge (<=3nm and 2nm) production capacity is located exclusively in Taiwan (Fab 20 Hsinchu and Fab 22 Kaohsiung, ~180,000-200,000 wafers/month at 3nm by end-2026; 2nm ramping to ~100,000 WPM). TSMC Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 operates at 4nm only; Phase 2 (3nm) begins tool installation Q3 2026 with mass production targeted 2H 2027. JASM Kumamoto Fab 2 (3nm-upgraded) targets equipment install and production in 2028. Taiwan Ministry of Economic Affairs estimates sub-5nm production remains ~85% Taiwan-based through 2030. Sources: TSMC 2025 Annual Report (investor.tsmc.com); TSMC 6-K Q1 2026 (SEC, April 2026); TrendForce April 27 2026; Taiwan Ministry of Economic Affairs via TrendForce Feb 6 2026; Taipei Times April 1 2026.
rationale: Zero operational ≤3nm capacity exists outside Taiwan as of June 2026 - Arizona is at 4nm and Japan is at 12-28nm; overseas ≤3nm fabs are under construction with earliest production in 2H 2027 (Arizona) and 2028 (Japan), placing this squarely in the EXTREME (<10% outside Taiwan AND no operational overseas leading-edge fab) category.

fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 130.8 points in May 2026, down 0.2 points (-0.2% MoM) from a revised April level of 131.0 (highest since Jan 2023), but still above year-ago levels; June 2026 release is scheduled 3 July 2026. Source: fao.org/worldfoodsituation/foodpricesindex, released 5 June 2026.
rationale: MoM change is -0.2%, so not spiking (rubric 2 threshold not met), but the index remains at a multi-year high and is positive YoY, ruling out rubric 0 (which requires both MoM and YoY declines); rubric 1 (ELEVATED, MoM change <3%) applies.

dissent.view: Equable Institute (State of Pensions 2025, Jan 8 2026) reports 82.5% aggregate funded ratio for US state and local retirement systems as of December 31, 2025 — a broader universe and an older valuation date, but a formal annual study figure.

fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI): 'The PPFI funded ratio stood at 87.6% as of April 30' (Milliman, public-pension-funding-index-may-2026, released June 3, 2026), covering the 100 largest US public DB plans with $6.009T in assets vs. $6.860T in total pension liability.
rationale: The Milliman PPFI is the preferred primary source per the rubric and its April 30, 2026 reading of 87.6% is the most recent published monthly estimate for large US public pensions; the rubric asks for a representative funded ratio as a percent, which maps directly to 87.6.

dissent.view: Paradigm's rulemaking tracker notes that implementation timelines are 'largely suggestive' and agencies face no formal penalties for missing the deadline, implying the gap may be procedurally tolerated rather than constituting a hard failure — softening the severity of the gap reading.

The American Prospect (2026-06-24) characterizes the Federal Reserve's absence from solo rulemaking as creating a risk that OCC/FDIC will finalize rules without Fed alignment, which some analysts read as trending toward a score-2 (deadline miss) outcome rather than a score-1 gap.

fact: As of 2026-06-30, all GENIUS Act rules across OCC, FDIC, NCUA, Treasury, FinCEN, and OFAC remain in proposed/NPRM stage — zero final rules have been issued — with 18 days until the statutory July 18, 2026 deadline. The Federal Reserve, a mandated primary federal payment stablecoin regulator, had not published any standalone proposed rule as of June 9, 2026 (only co-signed a joint CIP NPRM on June 18/22 with comment deadline August 21, 2026 — after the finalization deadline). Sources: OCC NPRM Federal Register (2026-03-02, OCC-2025-0372); FDIC NPRM Federal Register (2026-04-10, RIN 3064-AG19); FinCEN/OFAC joint NPRM Federal Register (2026-04-10); CIP joint NPRM Sullivan & Cromwell (2026-06-22); American Prospect (2026-06-24); Chapman & Cutler GENIUS Act Rulemaking Tracker.
rationale: All six agencies' rules are still in proposed/comment stage with 18 days to the July 18 deadline, and the Federal Reserve has not issued a standalone prudential proposed rule at all — a documented inter-agency gap confirmed by multiple primary sources. This maps cleanly to rubric score 1 (GAPS: rules still in proposed/comment stage near the deadline, OR documented inter-agency divergence).

fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu's minority government is still in office, having survived multiple no-confidence votes (most recently Jan 23, 2026, when LFI's motion drew 269 votes vs. 288 needed, and Feb 2, 2026, when the budget passed after two further failed motions). Lecornu invoked Article 49.3 in Jan 2026 to force through the 2026 budget. The National Assembly remains a hung parliament with no party holding an absolute majority. Source: Euronews Jan 23 2026; Al Jazeera Feb 2 2026; Wikipedia (Sébastien Lecornu, updated ~Jun 2026).
rationale: The government is governing but relies on Article 49.3 to pass legislation and survives only because Socialists and Republicans refuse to join no-confidence majorities — a textbook Rubric-1 (FRAGILE) configuration. No dissolution or PM resignation has occurred since Lecornu's reappointment in Oct 2025.

fact: CoreWeave (CRWV) carried a ~$4.2B 2026 refinancing wall on GPU-collateralized debt (DDTL 2.0, originated at ~11% avg rate, repayments beginning Jan 2026) against GPU collateral whose rental rates have fallen 50-70%. CoreWeave partially addressed this by closing an $8.5B investment-grade DDTL 4.0 (A3/Moody's, March 31 2026), a $3.1B DDTL 5.0 (Ba2/Moody's, May 18 2026), and $2.75B in 9.75% senior notes (April 2026) partly earmarked for debt repayment -- but no confirmed default or failed refinancing has occurred. Sources: CoreWeave IR (investors.coreweave.com, March 31 and May 18 2026); Quinn Emanuel client alert (quinnemanuel.com, March 16 2026); Level-Headed Investing / Quartz (qz.com, May 8 2026); BIS Annual Economic Report 2026 (June 28 2026).
rationale: CoreWeave is a named borrower with a publicly disclosed 2026 GPU-backed refinancing wall and GPU collateral whose rental rates have declined 50-70%, satisfying the rubric-1 criterion of 'a named borrower facing a refinancing wall.' No default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing has been confirmed, so rubric-2 is not met.

dissent.view: Straits.live rates the strait 'effectively closed to commercial shipping' as of June 30, reporting only 5 transits vs ~93/day normal, implying a near-total shutdown still in effect.

WTO Trade Tracker reports fertilizer-related cargoes outbound still ~94% below pre-war levels through early June, suggesting the partial reopening had not yet translated into meaningful cargo flows at the time of its last update.

fact: Windward MIOC (June 28, 2026): 42 total Hormuz transits recorded (28 inbound, 14 outbound); 'Strait remains open with no disruption to freedom of navigation.' Fertilizer flows: Kpler/Bloomberg (week ending June 21) show at least 16 fertilizer vessels exited carrying ~530,000 tonnes, nearing pre-war weekly levels for that window — but WTO Trade Tracker records fertilizer cargoes still ~94% below pre-war by early June. No confirmed deliberate full flow cut-off physically carried out in 2026 is evidenced — India's 'stop all water' statement is prospective, not confirmed as executed — so rubric level 2 is not met.

dissent.view: Some secondary sources (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) claim BRICS Pay is already 'operationally launched' in 2026 and has reduced USD intra-bloc trade by two-thirds, which if true could approach band 2 threshold for a major economy moving off USD settlement
Wikipedia (May 2026) notes Moscow Arbitration Court granted Russia's $229bn claim against Euroclear on 15 May 2026, a legal counter-move, not a Western seizure

fact: As of June 2026, no new sovereign reserve freeze or outright confiscation has been executed beyond the original 2022 G7/EU freeze of ~$280bn in Russian CBR assets (still frozen, not seized). On non-dollar settlement, BRICS Pay is described as entering an 'operational phase' in 2026 with pilot links between national systems (CIPS, UPI, SPFS, Pix), but authoritative sources (EBC Financial Group, 13 Apr 2026; bricspayment.ru citing Russian FM Lavrov at Rio summit) confirm full deployment is targeted for the New Delhi BRICS summit (late 2026) and a working prototype is not expected until 2027-2028; no major economy has operationally moved reserve settlement off USD. Sources: Brookings Jun 2026, CFR Jun 2026, IAI Apr 2026, EBC Apr 2026, bricspayment.ru.
rationale: No new sovereign reserve seizure/freeze qualifies for band 2; the original Russian freeze predates 2026 and no confiscation of principal has been executed. BRICS Pay expansion and the 'Unit' gold-backed token are active rhetoric and pilot-stage infrastructure, meeting band 1 (new non-dollar settlement launches/rhetoric without operational major-economy reserve shift).

dissent.view: SemiAnalysis (June 2026) argues that projects with signed interconnection agreements and site control continue to progress on schedule, and that moratoriums land overwhelmingly in markets with negligible real capacity; they characterise broad 'crisis' framing as exaggerated. The curtailment event was a one-off emergency window, not sustained forced curtailment.

fact: On May 18 2026, the U.S. DOE issued a Federal Power Act Section 202(c) emergency order authorising PJM Interconnection to curtail data centres and other large loads with backup generation during a grid-stress event driven by hot weather plus 40+ GW of planned plant outages (Utility Dive, 19 May 2026). Separately, Seattle City Council unanimously passed an emergency moratorium on new data-centre siting (>20 MVA) on 9 June 2026 citing grid-capacity and utility-rate impacts (Seattle City Council, 9 June 2026). The IEA 'Electricity 2026' report (late-June 2026) independently documents >2,500 GW of projects stalled in global grid queues and notes that 'many power systems are already experiencing rising congestion-related curtailment' (iea.org/reports/electricity-2026). LBNL 'Queued Up 2026 Edition' records ~8,200 U.S. projects (1,312 GW) in queue as of end-2025, with average wait times exceeding five years (emp.lbl.gov).
rationale: The DOE Section 202(c) emergency order on 18 May 2026 authorising forced curtailment of data-centre loads in the PJM footprint is a confirmed, grid-operator-level curtailment action — the precise trigger for band 2 under the rubric. Seattle's power-scarcity-driven moratorium on new data-centre connections is a corroborating confirmed physical-policy impact, not merely a forecast.

fact: Q1 2026 earnings (April 29, 2026): combined hyperscaler 2026 capex ~$725B, up 77% YoY per Financial Times; Microsoft Q3 FY26 capex $30.88B +84% YoY vs AI revenue run rate >$37B +123% YoY; Alphabet capex $35.67B >2x YoY vs Google Cloud +63% YoY to $20B; Amazon capex $44.2B vs AWS +28% YoY to $37.6B. Allianz Research (March 2026, allianz.com PDF) quantifies the capex-to-revenue growth divergence at ~46%, exceeding the 32% seen in the 2001 telecom excess cycle. AI revenue is still strongly accelerating YoY across all three cloud hyperscalers; no hyperscaler cut its AI-revenue outlook.
rationale: Capex growth (77-84%+ YoY) materially outpaces AI-attributable revenue growth (28-63% YoY), confirming the gap is WIDE (rubric 1). However, AI cloud revenues are still accelerating strongly on a YoY basis with no QoQ deceleration reported, and no hyperscaler raised capex while simultaneously cutting AI-revenue guidance, so rubric 2 is not triggered.

dissent.view: LendingTree/Benzinga (March 2026 survey): 47% of BNPL users reported a late payment in the past year, up from 41% in 2025 — suggesting broader consumer stress than Affirm's 30+ DPD series captures; however, this is a self-reported survey metric, not a formal delinquency rate, and does not override hard loan-level data.

Richmond Fed (Feb 2026, EB 26-05): 'There is indicative evidence from consumer surveys that late payment and delinquency behavior among BNPL users has increased since 2023,' but concludes no clear evidence of elevated stress through 2025 in broader consumer credit markets.

fact: Affirm FQ3'26 Shareholder Letter (SEC 8-K, filed ~May 2026): '30+ day delinquencies excluding Peloton and Pay in X loans increased 29 basis points year over year and increased 7 basis points quarter over quarter to 2.8%.' Allowance for credit losses was 6.0% of loans held for investment; recent cohort cumulative net charge-offs tracking ~3.5% of cohort GMV — well below the 5% charge-off spike threshold.
rationale: The 29 bps YoY rise in Affirm 30+ DPD confirms delinquency is rising, satisfying the rubric's Level 1 condition. The rise does not clear the >100 bps YoY threshold for Level 2, and cohort charge-offs (~3.5%) are contained below the 5% spike threshold, so Level 2 is not warranted.

dissent.view: Australian Deputy PM Marles (May 31 2026) said cables are being cut 'at an unprecedented rate' over 18 months, which some outlets frame as an ongoing crisis rather than a threat posture -- but no specific currently-severed named cable is cited.

fact: No confirmed major submarine cable currently severed and unrepaired as of July 2026. The most recent confirmed multi-cable cut event was Red Sea on Sept 6 2025 (SEA-ME-WE-4, IMEWE, FALCON GCX, EIG near Jeddah), since rerouted. 2026 sources (TeleGeography May 2026, AGBI Mar 2026, CNN May 2026, Forbes Jun 2026) document elevated threat at Hormuz and Red Sea -- including Meta pausing 2Africa Pearls Gulf work and Iranian sovereign-toll threats -- but no named cable confirmed severed and unrepaired. Australian Defence Minister stated cables are 'being cut at an unprecedented rate' (CNN, May 31 2026) without specifying a current unrepaired cut.
rationale: The rubric requires >=1 major cable currently severed and unrepaired for level 2; no such confirmed active cut is found in sources as of July 2026. Multiple credible threat signals (shadow fleet activity, Hormuz shipping congestion, Iran threats, AUKUS protection pact, paused cable projects) satisfy rubric level 1 (THREATENED).

dissent.view: Aon describes Q1 2026 insured losses as 6% ABOVE the 21st-century average (vs. Gallagher Re's 26% below 10-year average); the divergence reflects different baseline periods, not different dollar totals — both cite ~$20bn.

fact: Global insured catastrophe losses totaled $20 billion in Q1 2026, 26% below the 10-year decadal average of $26 billion, with no single event exceeding $10 billion (Gallagher Re, Q1 2026 Natural Catastrophe and Climate Report, April 2026). Aon independently confirmed at least $20 billion for Q1 2026 (Aon Global Catastrophe Recap Q1 2026, April 2026).
rationale: YTD insured losses of ~$20bn are below — not above — the 10-year Q1 average, and no single event breached the $10bn threshold, satisfying the NORMAL (0) criteria on both the aggregate and single-event tests. The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season (peak Aug-Oct) has not yet produced any major events as of the assessment date.

dissent.view: Philippines reported China indicated fertilizer exports would not be restricted, though Chinese authorities never formally confirmed this position
Some read the late-May urea quota issuance as a 'liberalization' or return to export, potentially arguing for rubric level 1 rather than 2

fact: NDRC convened a special meeting on Dec 11 2025 suspending phosphate fertilizer exports through August 2026 (S&P Global/Platts, Dec 11 2025; SunSirs/China Chemical News). In mid-March 2026 Beijing extended restrictions to nitrogen-potassium blends and additional phosphate varieties (Reuters/Bloomberg via Taipei Times Mar 21 2026; Exiger Apr 16 2026). In late May 2026 a tightly managed urea quota of ~1.5-1.6M tonnes for June-August was issued with a mandatory $660/t FOB price floor -- a controlled reopening, not a lift. Phosphate suspension to August 2026 remains in force. Between half and three-quarters of China fertilizer exports are now restricted (Exiger/Reuters customs data analysis).
rationale: The mid-March 2026 expansion of bans to NK blends and additional phosphate categories is a NEW broadened restriction added within the trailing 3 months, satisfying rubric level 2; the May urea quota is a heavily gated, price-floored allocation -- not a lifting -- while the NDRC phosphate suspension continues through August 2026, confirming tightening remains in effect.

fact: NBS official press release (stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202606/t20260611_1963929.html, released 2026-06-11): 'In May 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 3.9% year on year and 0.5% month on month.' Corroborated by CNBC (2026-06-10) and TradingEconomics citing same NBS release.
rationale: The rubric requires the signed YoY figure as published by NBS; +3.9% for May 2026 is that figure. Per the rubric, the engine scores on the SIZE of the move — +3.9% is the fastest pace since July 2022, a sharp cost-push inflation print that flags input-cost pressure spillover risk.

fact: The SEC granted a first one-year extension on Feb 25, 2025 (SEC Release 34-102487), shifting cash clearing to Dec 31, 2026 and repo to June 30, 2027. No second extension has been announced. However, the SEC published SIFMA's inter-affiliate exemptive-relief request on Apr 17, 2026 (comment deadline May 29, 2026), and on Jun 23, 2026 the Federal Register (2026-12613) shows the SEC issued a conditional exemptive order related to the inter-affiliate exclusion from the Trade Submission Requirement. The core compliance dates remain unchanged as of today. Source: sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-43; federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/23/2026-12613; SEC Commissioner Uyeda statement Apr 20, 2026.
rationale: A first formal extension was already granted (Feb 2025), which by itself maps to rubric level 1. Additionally, exemptive-relief requests were pending and one has now been conditionally granted (Jun 23, 2026), further confirming level 1. There is no evidence of a second deadline extension or a passed deadline, so level 2 is not warranted.

dissent.view: January 2026 CMBS office delinquency rate was 12.34% — the all-time high per Trepp, per multihousingnews.com

fact: Per multihousingnews.com citing Trepp data (updated ~June 2026 page): 'Office posted the largest decline, falling 114 basis points to 11.20 percent, pulling back from January's all-time high of 12.34 percent' — February 2026 office CMBS delinquency rate = 11.20%; January 2026 all-time high = 12.34%. No more recent explicit office sub-rate figure was recoverable from available excerpts.
rationale: The rubric requires the latest CMBS office delinquency rate as a percent; 11.20% is the most recently quoted office-sector figure from Trepp/multihousingnews (Feb 2026), down from Jan's record 12.34% driven by large office loan modifications/extensions. Confidence is medium because the May 2026 report excerpt does not explicitly state the current office sub-rate, leaving a 3-month gap in office-specific data.

dissent.view: ICSG October 2025 forecast: refined copper deficit of -150,000 mt for 2026 - superseded by April 2026 update
J.P. Morgan projects a steeper deficit of -330,000 mt for 2026 driven by AI data-centre demand
Goldman Sachs base case: 2026 surplus of ~160,000 mt

fact: ICSG Copper Market Forecast 2026-2027 (April 2026 press release, icsg.org): global refined copper surplus of ~96,000 metric tons in 2026, reversing its prior October 2025 deficit forecast of -150,000 mt; attributed to lower-than-anticipated copper usage (demand growth revised down to 1.6% from 2.1%) and higher secondary refined production.
rationale: A forecast surplus of +96,000 mt exceeds the +100kt threshold marginally - it sits just inside the BALANCED band, but ICSG characterises it as a surplus and the April 2026 figure is the authoritative current reading; mapped to rubric band 0 (SURPLUS). Note: at 96kt this is within ~4kt of the +/-100kt balanced boundary, but ICSG language is unambiguously 'surplus' so band 0 is the correct call.

dissent.view: As of April 2026, Maine was described as 'the only state to pass a statewide data center moratorium into law' — but this predates the April 24 veto and is now superseded; no statewide moratorium is in force as of July 3 2026.

Encino Environmental (April 2026) states '12 states have taken up data center moratoriums and 11 have been unsuccessful,' suggesting most state-level bills have failed; only local-level pauses are broadly enacted.

fact: As of July 3 2026, no statewide moratorium is enacted and in force (Maine's LD 307 was vetoed by Gov. Mills on April 24 2026; New York's S10642 passed both chambers June 4 2026 but remains unsigned by Gov. Hochul). However, Sanders/AOC's March 25 2026 press release (datacenterdynamics.com) states 'more than 100 local communities around the country have enacted moratoriums on data centers,' corroborated by Multistate (July 2026) reporting 'dozens of municipalities have moved ahead with local construction pauses' and the Rockefeller Institute (June 2026) confirming 14 states have considered statewide moratoriums. Primary source: datacenterdynamics.com, March 25 2026; rockinst.org, June 2026; multistate.us, July 2026.
rationale: Rubric level 2 requires a statewide moratorium enacted OR >10 jurisdictions with enacted pauses/cancellations. No statewide moratorium is currently in force, but 100+ local communities have enacted local moratoriums — far exceeding the 10-jurisdiction threshold for the second prong of level 2. Jurisdictions with enacted local pauses include municipalities across NY (e.g. Lysander/Onondaga County), VA, GA, TX, PA, NJ, MI, OH, and many others per the cited sources.

dissent.view: Fitch Ratings reported US private credit default rate hit a record 6.0% in April 2026, with private-credit-backed corporates at 9.2% for full-year 2025 — methodology includes distressed exchanges.
With Intelligence estimates 'true' default rate approaches 5% once selective defaults and liability-management exercises are included, vs. headline below 2% (2026 outlook).
Moody's Analytics estimates 2025 private credit default rate in the range of ~1.6%–4.7% depending on treatment of distressed restructurings (April 28 2026).
Morgan Stanley warned direct lending defaults could surge to 8% driven by AI disruption of software sector (March 16 2026).

fact: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index: 2.73% for Q1 2026 (Jan 1 – Mar 31 2026), tracking 697 senior-secured/unitranche US loans totalling $189.2bn in original principal; up from 2.46% in Q4 2025 and 1.84% in Q3 2025. Source: https://www.proskauer.com/report/proskauers-private-credit-default-index-reveals-rate-of-273-for-q1-2026, published April 27 2026.
rationale: The rubric calls for the latest direct-lending default rate as a percent; the Proskauer Index is the most granular, loan-level US direct-lending series available and reports 2.73% for the most recent complete quarter (Q1 2026). Dissenting readings from Fitch (6.0%, April 2026) and With Intelligence (~5% 'true' rate) are materially higher because they include distressed exchanges and liability-management exercises that Proskauer counts separately, so 2.73% is the most conservative loan-count-based anchor.

fact: IMF COFER Data Brief (March 27, 2026): 'The share of US dollar holdings decreased to 56.77 percent in 2025Q4, from 56.93 percent in 2025Q3.' Total FX reserves = $13.14 trillion. Source: https://data.imf.org/en/news/imf%20data%20brief%20march%2027
rationale: The rubric requires the latest published USD share of allocated global FX reserves as a percent; the IMF COFER brief dated March 27, 2026 reports 56.77% for Q4 2025, which is the most recent official release. Note that from 2025Q3 onward IMF eliminated the allocated/unallocated distinction so this figure now covers 100% of world FX reserves, making it directly comparable to the prior 'allocated' series.

dissent.view: Taiwan government said it aimed to prevent 'zoned domestic rationing before end of June' and that emergency pipeline transfers had 'bought time' — implying no full production curtailment confirmed at fabs themselves as of late March 2026
US Southwest monsoon forecast leans above-average, suggesting short-term drought may improve in July 2026, potentially moderating the D3 reading

fact: Taiwan's Water Resources Agency imposed formal water rationing affecting chipmaking hub Hsinchu County after the driest winter in 75 years; Baoshan Reservoirs inflow at only 77% of 2021 century-drought levels; emergency diversion measures active through July 2026 and agricultural irrigation postponed in southern Taiwan (Taipei Times, 2026-03-27; Taiwan News, 2026-06-02). Simultaneously, the US Drought Monitor (2026-06-30) shows extreme drought D3 expanding across the Four Corners states (NM, UT, CO, AZ) with record-low April snowpack across 8 western states (droughtmonitor.unl.edu; drought.gov).
rationale: Taiwan's WRA rationing order at Hsinchu — the world's leading chip-fab hub — is a confirmed water-rationing order at a fab region, satisfying the rubric's level-2 threshold directly. The US Southwest concurrently registers D3 (extreme) drought on the USDM, also independently meeting level 2.

dissent.view: East Asia Forum (Mar 2026) argues the White House has 'cooled down' chip controls in 2026, prioritising trade talks over new BIS rules, suggesting the executive branch posture is more TIGHTENING (level 1) than full RETALIATION — China's countermeasures are framed as defensive/symbolic rather than a hard equipment ban on ASML specifically.

fact: Within the trailing 3 months (Apr–Jul 2026): US side — MATCH Act introduced Apr 2 2026 to ban DUV tools to China (CNBC/Reuters, Apr 7 2026); BIS June 1 2026 guidance tightening Blackwell chip controls on China-HQ firms globally (Al Jazeera, Jun 1 2026). China side — State Council enacted tech transfer controls Jun 11 2026 with explicit statutory retaliation authority (MOFCOM/FT via abhs.in, Jun 11 2026); MOFCOM added 10 US firms to export control entity list Jun 22 2026, described by experts as retaliation (Al Jazeera, Jun 22 2026); MOFCOM Announcement No. 26 (Jun 24 2026) tightened strategic mineral export enforcement, effective Jul 1 2026 (geopolitechs.org); 50% domestic equipment procurement mandate for Chinese chipmakers threatening ~$18B in US equipment sales (thenextweb.com, May 2026). ASML China share fell from 36% (Q4 2025) to 19% (Q1 2026), corroborating volume signal.
rationale: Both the US/allied side (MATCH Act, BIS Blackwell guidance, VEU revocations) and the Chinese side (June 11 tech-transfer retaliation law, June 22 US-firm entity-list additions, mineral enforcement tightening) have enacted or formally proposed new measures in the trailing 3 months; China's June 2026 actions constitute documented statutory countermeasures explicitly framed as retaliation against Western controls, satisfying rubric level 2. The ASML China revenue volume drop from 36% to 19% in one quarter corroborates material disruption rather than mere headline noise.

dissent.view: TSMC CEO C.C. Wei projected (July 2025) that the completed Arizona gigafab cluster will account for ~30% of 2nm-and-more-advanced capacity — but this is a long-run build-out target (2029+), not current capacity, and does not contradict the current 0% reading.

fact: As of Q1-Q2 2026, all five of TSMC's volume-producing 2nm fabs are in Taiwan (Hsinchu x2, Kaohsiung x3); TSMC Arizona Fab 21 produces 4nm only; Arizona Fab 2 (3nm) is equipment-installation phase with commercial production targeted H2 2027; Kumamoto Japan Fab 2 (3nm) targets 2028. SemiAnalysis (Jan 2026) states 'over 90% of TSMC total capacity is in Taiwan... over 90% of global advanced-node capacity.' TSMC 2025 Annual Report (investor.tsmc.com, 2026) confirms overseas fabs are Nanjing (mature), Arizona (4nm only), JASM Kumamoto (22/28/12/16nm). No operational <=3nm fab exists outside Taiwan. Source: TSMC 2025 Annual Report (investor.tsmc.com); TSMC Q1 2026 6-K (SEC, Apr 2026); Focus Taiwan Apr 16 2026; SemiAnalysis Jan 2026.
rationale: Zero operational <=3nm capacity exists outside Taiwan as of mid-2026; Arizona's only running fab is 4nm and overseas 3nm fabs are 12-18 months from production. This places outside-Taiwan share of leading-edge (<=3nm) capacity well below 10% (effectively ~0%), satisfying the EXTREME rubric condition of '<10% outside Taiwan AND no operational overseas leading-edge fab.'

fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 130.3 points in June 2026, down 0.3% MoM from May 2026 (130.8) but 2.2% higher than a year earlier. Source: FAO via bizcommunity.com, July 3, 2026 (FAO June 2026 release).
rationale: The index is falling MoM (-0.3%) but still elevated YoY (+2.2%), failing the rubric's requirement that BOTH MoM and YoY be negative for a score of 0; MoM change is far below the 5% threshold and the 3-month gain (~+1.4%) is far below 10%, so SPIKING does not apply either.

dissent.view: Equable Institute estimates the aggregate funded ratio for all U.S. state and local retirement systems improved from 78.0% in 2024 to 82.5% for fiscal year 2025 (as of December 31, 2025), covering a broader universe of 245+ plans including weaker-funded smaller systems.

fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI): funded ratio of the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans rebounded to 87.6% as of April 30, 2026, up from 83.7% at end of March 2026, driven by estimated aggregate investment returns of 4.7% in April. Source: Milliman PPFI release via Business Wire, published June 3, 2026 (https://lasvegassun.com/news/2026/jun/03/milliman-analysis-public-pension-funded-ratio-rebo/).
rationale: The Milliman 100 PPFI is the preferred primary-source index for the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans; the April 30, 2026 reading of 87.6% is the most current published figure and maps directly to the rubric's request for a representative large-plan funded ratio expressed as a percent. Equable Institute's broader-universe estimate of 82.5% (end-2025) is consistent in order of magnitude but covers a wider, lower-funded universe and is less current.

dissent.view: Chapman & Cutler tracker characterizes all comment periods as closed by June 9, 2026, implying agencies are in active final-rule drafting and could theoretically meet the deadline; some sources treat the deadline as achievable if agencies act in the final weeks.

fact: As of July 3, 2026 — 15 days before the statutory July 18, 2026 deadline — all major agency rulemakings remain at the NPRM (proposed rule) stage, not final rules. OCC published its NPRM on March 2, 2026 (comment period closed May 1); FDIC approved its NPRM on April 7, 2026 (comments closed June 9); FinCEN/OFAC issued a joint NPRM in April 2026 (comments closed June 9); Treasury issued its state-comparability NPRM in April 2026. Critically, the Federal Reserve had not published any substantive proposed rule for applications or prudential frameworks as of the last confirmed tracker update (KPMG, May 4, 2026: 'No proposals have yet been released by the FRB regarding applications or prudential frameworks under the GENIUS Act'). Six agencies must finalize simultaneously with comment periods closing only weeks before the deadline (vaasblock.com, ~June 24, 2026; angelinvestorsnetwork.com, ~June 19, 2026). Sources: occ.gov bulletin-2026-3; fdic.gov FIL April 7 2026; federalregister.gov 2026-06974; treasury.gov SB0435; kpmg.com GENIUS Act alert May 2026.
rationale: All primary agency rules are still in proposed/comment stage within 15 days of the July 18, 2026 statutory finalization deadline, with no final rules published by any agency and the Federal Reserve having issued no prudential-framework NPRM at all — a documented gap among the primary regulators. This maps squarely to rubric level 1 (GAPS: rules still in proposed/comment stage near the deadline, with documented inter-agency divergence in readiness).

fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu's minority government faces a new no-confidence motion filed by Green lawmakers on July 2, 2026 (Reuters, France24), scheduled for a National Assembly vote on July 6; the motion has only ~58 backers vs. 289 needed and is widely expected to fail, as RN has declined to support it. The government previously survived no-confidence votes in January and February 2026 and passed the 2026 budget under Article 49.3-linked pressure.
rationale: France has a hung parliament since the 2024 snap election; Lecornu leads a minority government that has survived multiple confidence challenges by assembling ad hoc support, without a working majority — squarely Rubric 1 (FRAGILE). No dissolution has been called and the government has not fallen, ruling out Rubric 2.

dissent.view: CoreWeave's DDTL 4.0 closed at investment-grade (A3/Moody's, March 31 2026), CDS tightened sharply, and Applied Digital bonds priced at 7% vs prior 10%, suggesting conditions are normalizing rather than stressed.

fact: Banks including JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and SMBC were actively trying to offload AI data-center debt at a discount via SRT structures and direct loan sales as exposure approached internal limits (FT, reported via resultsense.com, May 6 2026). CoreWeave, the largest GPU-backed borrower, carried a $4.2B refinancing wall due in 2026 on pre-IPO GPU-collateralized facilities with underlying H100 collateral having depreciated 50-70% (davefriedman.substack.com, April 19 2026; levelheadedinvesting.com). CoreWeave's 5yr CDS peaked at 881bps in December 2025 before falling to ~452bps (Bloomberg/Yahoo Finance, ~June 2026). The $4.2B wall was partially addressed via the March 31 2026 DDTL 4.0 ($8.5B, rated A3 by Moody's) but no confirmed default or failed refinancing has been reported.
rationale: Two rubric-1 triggers are confirmed: banks offloading AI/data-center debt at a discount (FT, May 2026) and CoreWeave as a named borrower with a documented $4.2B 2026 refinancing wall on GPU-backed paper. No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing (rubric-2) has been reported as of July 3 2026.

dissent.view: straits.live labels the strait 'effectively closed' (day 124), which could argue for band 2 on physical grounds alone

hormuzstraitmonitor.com crisis timeline notes VP Vance claimed on ~June 21 that 'the straits really are open' after a record 16-20 million barrels transited in a single day, suggesting a brief band-0 window that did not sustain

fact: Per IMF PortWatch (via straits.live, updated 03 Jul 2026 1222Z), 27 vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on June 28 — 32% of the pre-crisis ~84/day norm; war-risk insurance at 8.0x pre-crisis; ~820 ships stranded; June 17 Islamabad MOU signed but failed to hold durably; Brent crude at ~$72/bbl, near pre-war levels ($71.32 on Feb 27). Fertilizer/ammonia ships explicitly deprioritized behind oil/LNG in any partial reopening (Aawsat/Kpler, ~June 18 2026).
rationale: The strait is physically contested and fertilizer/sulfur/ammonia flows are severely reduced (vessels at 32% of normal, ammonia under special scrutiny), satisfying rubric band 1 disruption. Band 2 is capped out by the rubric itself because a signed MOU exists and Brent at ~$72 is NOT elevated at crisis levels, so the oil price signal does not corroborate a full closure rating.

dissent.view: straits.live labels the strait 'effectively closed' as of July 3, citing June 28 AIS data at 32% of normal and 508 vessels anchored; characterises pressure index at 84 (extreme)

fact: IMF PortWatch recorded 27 vessel transits on June 28 (32% of ~84/day normal); by July 1 Windward logged 43 transits in one day; a US official confirmed crude flows exceeded 10 million bpd under US military oversight; Brent crude fell to ~$71/bbl on July 2-3, its lowest since pre-war Feb 27, as indirect US-Iran talks progressed in Doha. (Sources: IMF PortWatch June 28; Windward Daily Intelligence July 1 2026; TradingEconomics/Reuters July 2-3 2026)
rationale: Hormuz transit is severely below normal but recovering under US naval oversight with active peace talks underway — fitting CONTESTED (1) on both the physical and diplomatic dimensions. Brent at ~$71, near pre-war lows and falling, is explicitly inconsistent with a closure scenario and caps the rating at 1 per rubric.

dissent.view: CREIA domestic price (June 29 2026) of ~US$120/kg Dy vs Argus ex-China ~US$1,450/kg implies ~12x on illiquid spot offers - likely reflects thin market and distressed procurement rather than a clearing price multiple
IEA reports European prices 'up to six times' Chinese prices, and InvestingNews analysts cite '4-6x'; the upper end of 6x is supported by European bilateral contract data
Benchmark Minerals forecasts premium doubling to 8.3x by 2027 from 4.4x in 2025, implying mid-2026 is transitionally above 4.4x but well below 8x

fact: Argus data cited by Reuters (Oregon Group, ~June 2026): ex-China dysprosium oxide ~US$1,450/kg vs China domestic ~US$119-123/kg (CREIA, June 29 2026), a ratio of ~11x on spot; but Argus/Reuters characterises the overall HREE ex-China premium as 'x4 to x5' for dysprosium and terbium since April 2025 controls. Benchmark Minerals (March 24 2026) independently pegs the 2025 dysprosium CIF North America at 4.4x EXW China, forecasting 8.3x by 2027.
rationale: The rubric asks for the ex-China HREE price premium as a multiple of the China price. The most-cited authoritative figures from Argus (via Reuters) and Benchmark Minerals bracket the mid-2026 multiple at 4-5x for dysprosium, with IEA and industry analysts extending the range to 6x in European markets; 4.5 is the defensible central estimate for the current period.

dissent.view: Some markets show partial stabilization: Florida Citizens hit a record-low 385K policies and received an 8.7% rate decrease approval, and reinsurance rates fell 10-25% at June 1 2026 renewals, suggesting the non-renewal wave may be peaking rather than spreading, supporting a STABLE = 0 reading in select markets.

fact: A June 2026 industry aggregation (climatecosmos.com) identifies 13 US states with active non-renewal waves in 2026 — CA, FL, TX, LA, NC, GA, OK, NE, MN, CO, and others — corroborated by state-specific disclosures: CA DOI moratorium expired Jan 7 2026 enabling new non-renewals; TX and LA enacted transparency laws effective Jan 1 2026 in response to ongoing non-renewals; NC saw Nationwide drop 10K policies; CO enacted wildfire-model disclosure law July 2026. NAIC issued a nationwide data call (deadline June 15 2026) covering cancellations and non-renewals across all states. AM Best revised US homeowners outlook from Negative to Stable in December 2025 (AM Best Market Segment Report, accessed Jan 2026 per NAIC filing commentary).
rationale: The state count of ~13 active non-renewal markets falls squarely within the 5–15 range (RISING = 1); no top-10 insurer has fully exited a major state in 2026 (State Farm remains in CA under a rate settlement), and AM Best's Stable outlook plus falling reinsurance rates rule out the ACCELERATING = 2 threshold.

dissent.view: LBNL 2025 Edition (data through 2024) reported median IR-to-COD of 'over 4 years' (~48-55 months) for 2018-2024 COD projects; Loopback Systems commentary on same report cites 55 months average for 2024 COD projects.
Environment+Energy Leader (July 2026) states 'national median wait time for interconnection studies alone exceeded 40 months in 2024' -- a studies-only metric, narrower than full IR-to-COD.

fact: LBNL Queued Up: 2026 Edition (data through end of 2025), emp.lbl.gov/queues: 'For the regions with available data, the median duration from IR to COD was over 5 years for projects built in 2025.' Over 5 years = >60 months.
rationale: LBNL reports the median IR-to-COD duration crossed the 5-year (60-month) threshold for 2025 COD projects, up from 'over 4 years' in the prior edition; 60 is the minimum integer consistent with 'over 5 years' since the full-precision figure is not broken out in the public summary.

dissent.view: Duramag (Dec 2025) characterises HREE magnet licensing as near-frozen for heavy-REE products like SmCo and Dy/Tb-bearing NdFeB, with approvals 'rare, documentation-intensive, and unpredictable' and timelines often exceeding 3 months — suggesting a reading closer to rubric 2 for HREE-specific magnets

fact: China's MOFCOM April 2025 Announcement No. 18 controls on 7 HREEs and derivative magnets remain fully in force; the October 2025 expansions are suspended until Nov 10 2026 (MOFCOM Ann. No. 70). As of Dec 2025, only three producers (JL Mag, Ningbo Yunsheng, Zhong Ke San Huan) received 'general licences' covering specific client lists; all other exporters remain on case-by-case review with opaque timelines exceeding 45-60 days. Jan 2026 MOFCOM Announcement No. 1 [2026] added new controls on samarium/gadolinium/lutetium compounds. Merics (Apr 2026) confirms approvals remain 'slow and targeted'. Sources: Reuters/Mining.com Dec 2 2025; MOFCOM Ann. 70 Nov 7 2025; Merics Apr 2026; Andersen Institute Apr 29 2026.
rationale: Licenses are being issued but only to a small whitelist of large producers covering specific approved customer lists, with all other applicants facing non-automatic case-by-case review far exceeding 30 days — a textbook rubric-1 condition. No evidence of categorical halt (rubric 2), and no evidence of normal timelines for most applicants (rubric 0). [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]

dissent.view: Freeport's Jan 2026 guidance had projected ~1.0 billion lb for full-year 2026, implying a less severe cut than the May 2026 revision to ~700 million lb; some analysts (Goldman Sachs late-2025) initially modelled only ~270,000 t lost at Grasberg in 2026, a lower deficit figure than BMI's 400,000 t.

fact: Two major top-20 copper mines have confirmed, ongoing production cuts as of early July 2026: (1) Grasberg (world's 2nd-largest copper mine, Indonesia/Freeport-McMoRan) — Grasberg Block Cave still in phased ramp-up after Sep 2025 mudslide; Freeport's May 2026 earnings update (mining.com, 2026-05-08) cut 2026 copper output target to ~700 million lb from 1 billion lb, aiming only 65% capacity in H2 2026 and full restart delayed to early 2028; (2) Kamoa-Kakula (DRC/Ivanhoe Mines, world's 3rd-largest) — seismic flooding from May 2025 forced guidance cut to 290,000–330,000 t in 2026 vs. original ~600,000 t target, with Q1 2026 output at 71,417 t (annualising to ~286,000 t), per Ivanhoe Q1 2026 release (ivanhoemines.com, 2026-04-13) and Metalnomist (2026-05-30). Multiple institutions (Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, Goldman Sachs, Citi) forecast a copper market deficit of 400,000+ t in 2026, corroborated by price near record highs. TFM/CMOC (DRC) strike (June 1–5, 2026) resolved quickly with minimal production impact and is NOT counted as an active outage.
rationale: Two top-20 mines — Grasberg and Kamoa-Kakula — have confirmed, physically measured production cuts active right now (sub-65% and sub-55% of normal rates respectively), and multiple institutions have formally forecast a 2026 market deficit as a direct consequence; this satisfies the rubric's CLUSTER threshold of >=3 mines OR lost output large enough that institutions forecast a market deficit.

dissent.view: The Burkina Faso RSF could be classified as a supplemental climate facility rather than a sovereign-distress program, which would push the distress-event count toward 0 (CALM).

fact: In the trailing 6 months (Jan–Jul 2026), the IMF approved a new RSF arrangement for Burkina Faso on Feb 18 2026 (SDR 90.3 mn, alongside a pre-existing ECF augmented in May 2026 by 50% of quota); Sri Lanka completed combined 5th+6th EFF reviews; Argentina completed its 2nd EFF review (EFF approved Apr 2025). No confirmed sovereign missed coupon or selective-default rating action in this window was found. IMF DSA list as of Mar 31 2026 shows 9 countries 'in debt distress' (pre-existing stock).
