Allowance for credit losses = 6.0% of loans held for investment; recent cohort NCOs tracking ~3.5% of cohort GMV. Klarna Q1 2026 (SEC 6-K): delinquency rates 'continue to trend down,' realized losses ~0.44% of GMV.
rationale: Affirm 30+ DPD rose +29 bps YoY to 2.8% — above zero but well below the >100 bps spiking threshold — satisfying the RISING condition; provider charge-offs (~3.5% cohort NCO for Affirm, <1% for Klarna) remain below the >5% SPIKING threshold, confirming level 1.

dissent.view: Australian Defence Minister Marles (May 31 2026) stated undersea cables 'are being cut at an unprecedented rate' and cited 'attacks against subsea critical infrastructure at a scale and frequency that is historically unprecedented over the past 18 months,' implying ongoing active cutting beyond what is individually confirmed.

fact: As of late April–July 2026, no major intercontinental submarine cable in the Red Sea, Hormuz, or Baltic is confirmed currently severed and unrepaired. Iran's IRGC-linked Tasnim News Agency issued veiled threats against Hormuz cables (Apr 23 2026); TeleGeography (Apr 2026) and Modern Diplomacy (Apr 28 2026) confirm 'subsea cables have not yet suffered damage' from the Iran conflict. The most recent actual confirmed cut is Taiwan's minor Matsu No. 3 cable (Beigan-Dongyin, ~1,500 residents affected, late Apr 2026). The last major Red Sea cuts (SEA-ME-WE-4, IMEWE, FALCON GCX, EIG) were Sep 6 2025 and are in repair/rerouting status. TeleGeography Submarine Cable Map last updated Jul 3 2026 shows no new emergency outage notices. Sources: Modern Diplomacy Apr 28 2026 (moderndiplomacy.eu); AGBI Apr 15 2026 (agbi.com); The Diplomat May 21 2026 (thediplomat.com); TeleGeography submarinecablemap.com Jul 3 2026.
rationale: No major cable is currently severed and unrepaired in the queried corridors (Red Sea, Hormuz, Baltic), ruling out level 2. However, Iran's documented, credible threats against Hormuz cables via state-linked IRGC media and heightened operational risk from military activity in the Gulf constitute a credible threat condition, matching level 1 (THREATENED).

dissent.view: Aon calculates Q1 2026 global insured losses of $20bn as 6% above the 21st-century average (rather than 26% below the decadal average used by Gallagher Re), reflecting different baseline periods — still well within NORMAL bounds

fact: Global insured losses from natural disasters totaled $20 billion in Q1 2026 — 26% below the 10-year average of ~$27 billion — with no single event exceeding $10 billion; Q2 2026 SCS activity added only mid-single-digit billions cumulatively and no major hurricane landfall has occurred through July 13, 2026 (Gallagher Re Q1 2026 Natural Catastrophe and Climate Report, April 2026; Goldman Sachs/Gallagher Re Q2 estimates, July 2026).
rationale: YTD 2026 insured catastrophe losses are running well below the 10-year average with no single event breaching the $10bn threshold, satisfying both conditions for NORMAL (score 0) under the rubric. The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is below-forecast and has produced no material US landfall losses through the assessment date.

dissent.view: Philippines reported China indicated fertilizer exports would not be restricted, though Chinese authorities never publicly confirmed this position (Reuters, March 2026)
Urea quota re-opening (May 26, ~1.5-1.6M t, $660/t floor) could be read as partial easing for urea specifically, though restrictions on phosphate and NK blends remain

fact: In mid-March 2026, Beijing banned exports of nitrogen-potassium fertilizer blends and additional phosphate varieties (Reuters/Bloomberg, March 19-21 2026), extending beyond the NDRC-directed December 2025 phosphate suspension through August 2026. Urea was partially reopened on May 26 via a tightly controlled quota of ~1.5-1.6M tonnes with a $660/t FOB price floor (Profercy/Keyuan, May 26-29 2026), but phosphate and NK blend bans remain active. International urea prices +~40% vs pre-war levels confirmed by multiple sources.
rationale: The mid-March 2026 addition of NK-blend and broader phosphate bans constitutes a NEW/BROADENED restriction within the trailing 3 months from July 2026, meeting rubric level 2 (TIGHTENED). The partial urea quota reopening under a strict price floor does not constitute a lifting; phosphate suspension through August 2026 remains confirmed by NDRC-directed industry action.

fact: NBS official press release (stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202607/t20260710_1964093.html, released 2026-07-10): 'In June 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 4.1% year on year and decreased by 0.3% month on month.'
rationale: The signed YoY figure is +4.1%, the highest since July 2022, driven by energy and materials cost-push from Middle East supply disruptions; rubric treats this as a large positive move signaling input-cost pressure export to global supply chains. All major secondary sources (Xinhua, CNBC, Reuters pool) confirm +4.1% with zero dissent.

dissent.view: Commissioner Uyeda stated Sep 30, 2025 that 'the Commission does not intend to consider further extensions,' and the TBAC May 2026 report notes industry 'is resolved to meeting the central clearing deadlines' — suggesting implementation may remain on the current (extended) track without further slippage toward level 2.

Commissioner Uyeda stated Sep 30, 2025 that 'the Commission does not intend to consider further extensions.' The SEC implementation page (updated ~Jul 6, 2026) shows deadlines unchanged at Dec 31, 2026 / Jun 30, 2027. No second extension has been announced. Sources: sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-43; sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/uyeda-093025; sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/uyeda-update-sec-work-toward-treasury-clearing-implementation-042026; home.treasury.gov/system/files/221/TBACCharge1Q22026.pdf (May 2026).
rationale: One official extension has been granted (Feb 2025), placing the indicator squarely at rubric level 1 ('an official extension granted'). Additionally, exemptive-relief requests from SIFMA and IIB are pending as of the comment deadline (May 29, 2026), satisfying a second independent rubric-1 criterion; no second formal deadline extension has been announced, precluding level 2.

fact: Trepp June 2026 CMBS report: 'office edged up four basis points to 11.57%' — MBA Newslink / Trepp, July 2026
rationale: The latest Trepp property-type breakdown for June 2026 shows the CMBS office delinquency rate at 11.57%, up 4 bps month-over-month; this is the most recent hard data point and maps directly to the rubric's request for the latest percent figure.

dissent.view: ICSG October 2025 forecast projected a 150,000t refined copper DEFICIT for 2026 — superseded by the April 2026 update
J.P. Morgan projected a 330,000t deficit for 2026, driven by AI/hyperscale data center copper demand

fact: ICSG 'Copper Market Forecast 2026-2027' (April 2026 Lisbon meeting): global refined copper surplus of ~96,000 metric tons forecast for 2026, reversing the prior October 2025 deficit forecast of 150,000t, driven by lower-than-expected demand growth (usage now +1.6% vs prior +2.1%) and higher secondary/scrap refined output. Source: icsg.org (April 2026 press release), corroborated by Recycling Today (Apr 28 2026), ADMIS (Apr 24 2026), Metalnomist (Jul 2026).
rationale: The latest (April 2026) ICSG official forecast is a refined copper surplus of +96,000t for 2026, which exceeds the +100kt surplus threshold in the rubric. Under the rubric, a forecast surplus maps directly to score 0.

dissent.view: datacenterbans.com (as of June 1 2026) characterised the statewide path as 'closed' and emphasised no broad statewide moratorium had passed, highlighting that local pace was the primary front - a reading that slightly underweights the sheer number of enacted local pauses in assigning systemic severity.

fact: DLA Piper (July 2026, dlapiper.com) reports 'more than 100 local moratoria have been adopted nationwide' and 'at least 12 states have considered moratorium legislation'; NY legislature passed statewide moratorium bill S10642 on June 4 2026 (Senate 44-16, Assembly 102-39) but it remains unsigned by Gov. Hochul as of early July 2026; Maine's statewide moratorium was vetoed April 24 2026; no statewide moratorium is currently in force, but enacted local pauses include: Minneapolis MN, Denver CO, Baltimore City MD, Dubuque County IA, Bloomington IL, Normal IL, Iron County UT, Manitowoc County WI, Reno NV, Smithfield RI, Oneonta NY, East Fishkill NY, Lysander NY, 20+ Michigan localities, multiple Georgia counties - well exceeding 10 enacted jurisdictions.
rationale: The rubric awards Band 2 for either a statewide moratorium enacted OR >10 jurisdictions with enacted pauses; the confirmed count of enacted local moratoria (100+, per DLA Piper July 2026) overwhelmingly exceeds the 10-jurisdiction threshold, anchoring a Band 2 rating even without a signed statewide law.

Moody's: excluding distressed restructurings yields headline rates of 1.6%-4.7%; including them shows materially worse picture — no single point estimate published

fact: As of July 2026, TSMC has zero operational <=3nm capacity outside Taiwan. Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 produces 4nm (N4) at ~20,000-30,000 wpm but no <=3nm. Arizona Phase 2 (3nm) construction completed April 2026 with tool installation beginning Q3 2026 and volume production targeted H2 2027. Kumamoto Japan 3nm targeted 2028. Sources: TrendForce 2026-04-16, Focus Taiwan CNA 2026-04-16, Taipei Times 2026-04-29, tech-insider.org 2026-06-04, Wikipedia TSMC Arizona.
rationale: The rubric's EXTREME threshold requires <10% outside Taiwan AND no operational overseas leading-edge fab; all <=3nm TSMC capacity is currently 100% Taiwan-based with no overseas <=3nm fab yet in production, satisfying the EXTREME condition unambiguously. Arizona's sole overseas operational fab runs 4nm, which is above the <=3nm threshold, and no <=3nm overseas fab reaches volume production until H2 2027 at the earliest.

fact: As of July 13, 2026 — five days before the statutory July 18, 2026 rulemaking deadline — zero final rules have been issued by any of the six required agencies. OCC published its NPRM on March 2, 2026 (comment period closed May 1); FDIC published its prudential NPRM on April 10, 2026 (comments closed June 9); FinCEN/OFAC published a joint AML NPRM on April 9, 2026 (comments closed June 9); NCUA published a supplemental NPRM (comments closing July 17, 2026 — the day before the deadline). The Federal Reserve Board, a named primary federal payment stablecoin regulator, had not published any proposed rule for applications or prudential frameworks as of the most recent reporting (KPMG reg alert, May 2026; CryptoTimes, May 18, 2026). The FDIC's comment period on one of its rules closes August 4, 2026 — two weeks after the statutory finalization deadline — making timely FDIC finalization procedurally impossible without bypassing its own comment process. Sources: OCC Bulletin 2026-3 (occ.gov); Federal Register 2026-04089 (Mar 2, 2026); FDIC.gov press release (Apr 7, 2026); Treasury/FinCEN press release sb0435 (Apr 9, 2026); VaaSBlock analysis citing Fed non-participation (Jun 9, 2026); Chapman & Cutler rulemaking tracker (updated Jun 1, 2026).
rationale: All rules remain at NPRM/comment stage within five days of the July 18, 2026 statutory deadline, with the Federal Reserve (a primary regulator) having issued no proposed rule at all — fitting the rubric's 'GAPS' definition of rules still in proposed/comment stage near the deadline with documented inter-agency divergence in participation. No court stay or compliance-failure event has been identified, so score 2 is not warranted.

fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu leads a weak minority government. The most recent government-threatening event was on 2 February 2026, when two no-confidence motions (LFI: 260 votes; RN: 135 votes) failed to reach the 289-vote threshold needed to topple the government, allowing the 2026 budget to pass. fact: IMF PortWatch (July 5): commercial transit at 39% of pre-crisis volume (34 vs ~88 vessels/day); Windward data July 10-11 shows only 6 vessel crossings in a 12-hour window vs 18-22/day earlier in July; Iran declared strait 'closed until further notice' after IRGC missile attacks on tankers July 7-12; JMIC (July 12) says Omani southern lane 'still available' but threat level 'severe' with mine danger; Brent crude +4% to $78.82/barrel on July 13 (Al Jazeera, July 13 2026), corroborating supply-disruption premium. Fertilizer/sulfur/ammonia flows have been near-halted since Feb 28 conflict onset per FAO/NDSU/World Bank (3-4M tonnes/month restrained; fertilizer price index at Oct-2022 highs).
rationale: The rubric requires rating 2 only if the strait is 'CLOSED' AND a market signal corroborates it, and stipulates that a signed truce or convoys moving cap the rating at 1. However, the June 17 MOU has effectively collapsed under renewed July 7-12 hostilities; transit has dropped to near-zero (6 crossings in 12 hours); Brent is +4% and elevated to ~$79, providing a corroborating price signal; and Iran's formal 'closed until further notice' declaration is the operative sovereign statement, with the Omani lane practically inaccessible to large commercial vessels (no vessel >10,000 DWT has transited the Southern Highway with AIS on since July 7 per Lloyd's List). On balance the strait has re-approached a functional closure state with a corroborating oil move, but residual dark-ship transits and JMIC's claim the Omani lane is 'available' introduce sufficient ambiguity to hold medium confidence rather than high.

fact: IMF PortWatch (Jul 5, primary source) recorded 34 Hormuz transits vs ~88/day normal (~39% of pre-crisis volume); Windward recorded just 6 crossings in a 12-hour window Jul 10-11; Lloyd's List Intelligence reported no large vessels (>10,000 dwt) on the US-coordinated Southern Highway with AIS on since Jul 7. ESMA's residual caveat about 'a subset of funds' facing potential challenges is a forward-looking stress-test flag, not an observed margin event, insufficient to elevate to band 1.

fact: China MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026, issued 22 June 2026, added 10 named US entities to its export control list under the Export Control Law and Dual-Use Items Regulations, effective immediately. The two US rare-earth producers explicitly named are MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc. The action is entity-specific: it bars Chinese exporters from supplying dual-use items to those firms and prohibits any party worldwide from transferring China-origin dual-use goods to them, but does not impose a categorical ban on the US rare-earth sector as a class. Market signal: share-price reaction on announcement day was muted (MP Materials roughly flat, USA Rare Earth modestly higher), consistent with an entity-level rather than sector-wide restriction. Source: MOFCOM announcement No. 23/2026 (https://www.mofcom.gov.cn/zwgk/zcfb/art/2026/art_dfa9cc5c1e004d7fbb86f83d249e7986.html), corroborated by Al Jazeera, Benchmark Minerals, Arnold & Porter advisory, SMM, and Reuters market data, all dated 22 June 2026.
rationale: Two named US domestic rare-earth producers (MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc.) are on China's MOFCOM export-control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying rubric level 1. The restriction is firm-specific (10 named entities across multiple sectors), not a sector-wide or categorical ban on US rare-earth producers as a class, so level 2 does not apply.

dissent.view: Some analysts frame CoreWeave's successive new facilities as evidence that GPU-backed debt is now normalizing and attracting IG institutional capital at scale, arguing the market has moved beyond stress to routine execution -- consistent with a score of 0.

fact: CoreWeave carried a '$4.2 billion refinancing wall due in 2026' on GPU-collateralized debt with collateral values (H100 GPU rental rates) down ~70-90% since 2023 (Quinn Emanuel client alert, March 2026; Wedbush/Finterra, Feb 23 2026). CoreWeave successfully navigated the wall: it closed the $8.5B DDTL 4.0 (rated A3/Moody's -- first IG GPU-backed facility) on March 31 2026 (SEC filing / CoreWeave IR), and the $3.1B DDTL 5.0 (Ba2/Moody's, oversubscribed, priced 50bps tighter) on May 18 2026 (CoreWeave IR). No default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing was confirmed at any named issuer as of the research date.
rationale: A named borrower (CoreWeave) faced an identified 2026 refinancing wall on GPU-backed debt against sharply depreciated collateral -- a textbook rubric-1 stress signal. The wall was resolved via new facilities, not a default or distressed exchange, so rubric-2 is not warranted; the idiosyncratic refinancing pressure and flagged structural risks (QTS bullet-structure spread widening per Citi/Forbes June 2026, GPU depreciation warnings across sector) keep the score at 1.

dissent.view: straits.live rates strait 'effectively closed to commercial shipping as of July 20' (Day 141), which could support a 2 if crude were also at crisis levels
iranwarlive.com (July 5) reported ~35 transits/day via temporary corridors, characterizing the strait as 'operationally open' at reduced volume -- more consistent with a contested-1 than closed-2

fact: IMF PortWatch (July 12, 2026, most recent published): 10 vessel transits vs ~88/day pre-crisis (~11% of normal). WTO Trade Tracker confirms fertilizer/ammonia/sulfur outbound AIS flows 'absent or effectively at zero' post-MoU. War-risk insurance at 8x pre-crisis; Iran re-declared closure after July 8 ceasefire collapse; US reinstated naval blockade July 14 (CENTCOM). Brent crude ~$88-90/bbl (straits.live, July 19-20) -- elevated but well below the $126 March peak. Sources: IMF PortWatch; WTO DataLab Hormuz Trade Tracker; straits.live; Windward MIOC (July 19); AgBull (July 14); Wikipedia 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis (updated July 20).
rationale: Fertilizer/ammonia/sulfur input flows through Hormuz are severely reduced (near-zero on AIS, ~11% of normal transits), insurance is extreme, and Iran has re-declared closure -- firmly exceeding the threshold for rating 1 (DISRUPTED). However, the rubric caps at 1 unless the strait is rated CLOSED (2) AND crude oil corroborates; Brent at $88-90 is elevated but not at crisis-peak levels, the US disputes full closure, and some dark transits continue, so the rubric ceiling of 1 applies.

fact: IMF PortWatch recorded 10 vessel transits on July 12 vs. ~88/day baseline (~11% of normal); Kpler counted 14 crossings on July 9; the June 17-18 US-Iran MOU ceasefire has effectively collapsed per Iran (July 19), the US reinstated its naval blockade on July 14, and the IRGC declared all maritime traffic banned and stopped 4 vessels on July 18; Brent crude trading ~$80-90/bbl, up ~30% from July lows (TradingEconomics, 2026-07-20; IMF PortWatch via straits.live, 2026-07-12; EIA STEO, 2026-07-07; UN News, 2026-07-10).
rationale: Transit volume is at ~11% of pre-crisis normal (well under 25%), the ceasefire has collapsed with active IRGC attacks on vessels and no functioning convoy workaround per AIS data, and Brent crude up ~30% is fully consistent with a near-closure market signal — all three rubric conditions for a 2 are met. The only mitigating factor is active diplomatic mediation reported July 20 and a US claim that some vessels are still transiting dark, but the volume collapse and corroborating oil price signal dominate.

dissent.view: FOB terbium $1,483/kg vs domestic $1,179.54/kg (July 2026 SMM) implies only ~1.26x FOB/domestic spread — a much lower multiple if FOB China rather than CIF Western is used as the ex-China price

Project Blue/Discovery Alert (May 2026): ex-China monazite concentrate premium only ~2.6x Chinese benchmark — but this is a concentrate-level blended figure diluted by low-value light REEs, not a pure HREE oxide multiple
Benchmark Minerals (March 2026) forecasts the multiple rising to 8.3x by 2027, suggesting the current 4.4-4.5x reading may be conservative if export licence tightening accelerates
Physical/retail terbium ex-China at $4,028.50/kg (Jul 10 2026) vs ~$1,179/kg domestic implies ~3.4x — retail market, not industrial contract price

fact: Argus data cited by Reuters (Oregon Group, June 10 2026): dysprosium and terbium oxide prices outside China 'climbed x4 to x5' since China's April 2025 export controls took effect, with dysprosium ex-China ~$1,450/kg vs ~$209-262/kg domestic China. Benchmark Minerals (March 2026) pegged CIF North America dysprosium at 4.4x EXW China in 2025, rising. Multiple industry sources for mid-2026 converge on 4-5x for CIF/landed Western price vs domestic China benchmark.
rationale: The load-bearing Argus/Reuters figure of x4-to-x5 for ex-China heavy rare earth oxide prices vs Chinese domestic, corroborated by Benchmark's 4.4x CIF North America reading and analyst consensus of 4-6x, maps directly to the rubric's request for the premium multiple; midpoint 4.5 is the best single reading. FOB China spreads (~1.3-1.5x) are narrower but do not reflect landed Western cost, so the CIF/North America multiple is the appropriate anchor.

dissent.view: insurance.com survey (May 2026) reports only 10% of homeowners nationally had policies canceled or non-renewed, with carrier exits cited by only 3% of respondents, suggesting the consumer-level impact may be more limited than state-count metrics imply

AM Best (Dec 2025) and HousingWire/Openly (mid-2026) characterize the national homeowners market as stabilizing, which could argue for a STABLE rating if state-count non-renewals are viewed as contained and trending toward resolution

fact: A June 2026 analysis (climatecosmos.com, citing NAIC MCAS data via Weiss Ratings) identifies 13 US states with active insurer non-renewal waves in 2026, including FL (3.35% non-renewal rate, highest in nation), CA (3.18%, 3.9x its 2018 rate), TX, CO, NE, OK, NC, MN, GA, KS, LA, and others. NAIC issued a nationwide data call in March 2026 covering cancellations/non-renewals across all 50 states. AM Best revised the US homeowners segment outlook from negative to stable (December 2025), and reinsurance rates fell ~10-25% at June 1, 2026 renewals (Openly mid-year 2026 outlook). No top-10 insurer has fully exited a major state market in 2026; State Farm remains present in CA (~72K non-renewals but not a full exit); Florida added ~20 new approved carriers (Insurance Journal, May 2026).
rationale: Thirteen states with documented non-renewal waves places the indicator firmly in the RISING band (5-15 states); however, AM Best stability upgrade, softening reinsurance, and new carrier entrants in FL preclude classification as ACCELERATING, and the rubric threshold for level 2 (>15 states or full top-10 exit) is not met.

dissent.view: LBNL 2025 Edition (data through end of 2024) reported median IR-to-COD of 'over 4 years' (~55 months) for projects built in 2018-2024; Loopback Systems interpreted this as exactly 55 months average for 2024 COD projects.
Secondary source cites 'national median wait time for interconnection studies alone exceeded 40 months in 2024' — a narrower metric covering study phase only, not full IR-to-COD.

fact: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition (emp.lbl.gov/queues, July 2026, data through end of 2025): 'the median duration from IR to COD was over 5 years for projects built in 2025' — i.e. >60 months.
rationale: Over 5 years converts to >60 months; value is set at 60 as the floor of the stated range. The 2025 Edition (projects built through 2024) reported a median of ~55 months, confirming the upward trend now exceeding 60 months.

dissent.view: Some reporting (White House statements, Technori April 2026) frames MOFCOM's general licences to three Chinese magnet makers as a meaningful easing of approvals and a 'de facto removal' of controls for US civilian buyers, implying conditions closer to FLOWING for commercial end-users.
Rare Earth Exchanges cites licensing approval rates below 25% for European firms in some sectors (2025-2026 data), which could support a reading closer to FROZEN for those buyer segments.

fact: China's April 2025 MOFCOM Announcement No. 18 licensing regime on seven heavy rare earth elements (dysprosium, terbium, yttrium, scandium, samarium, gadolinium, lutetium) and derived magnets remains fully in force and was never suspended. MOFCOM's statutory review target is 45 working days (~9 weeks), but industry reporting (Duramag, gettransport.com, ~July 2026) confirms heavy-REE approvals 'routinely run past 60 to 120 days.' General licences were issued only to three named Chinese magnet makers (JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng) in December 2025 and are 'not broadly available.' In June 2026 MOFCOM added 10 US entities—including MP Materials and USA Rare Earth—to its export control list, denying them dual-use exports. January 2026 catalogue expansion added samarium, gadolinium and lutetium compounds. CSIS (May 2026) confirms yttrium exports to the US were only ~20 tons in February 2026 vs. 66+ tons in January 2025. Sources: gettransport.com (July 2026); CSIS analysis (May 2026); Morgan Lewis LawFlash (July 2026); Duramag market update; TechTimes (May 2026).
rationale: The regime is strictly case-by-case (general licences cover only three named producers, not broad volume); statutory review is 45 working days but real approvals run 60–120 days, far exceeding the rubric's 30-day threshold; and new categories (samarium/gadolinium/lutetium compounds) were added to the control list in January 2026—all of which satisfy the rubric's SLOWING criteria. A score of 2 (FROZEN) is not warranted because licences continue to be issued for legitimate civilian commercial flows and no blanket categorical denial to an entire country or sector has been announced (the US-entity blacklisting targets named firms, not a country-wide freeze).

fact: Three top-20 copper mines have confirmed, currently active production cuts: (1) Grasberg Block Cave (Indonesia, ~3% of world supply) remains on phased restart at ~65% capacity in H2 2026 after Sept 2025 mudslide; FCX Q1-2026 10-Q reports only 95M lb produced in Q1 vs. 425M lb normal, and full-year PTFI 2026 guidance cut to 0.7B lb from normal 1.7B lb (SEC filing, 2026); (2) Kamoa-Kakula (DRC, world's 3rd-largest) produced only 64,328t in Q2 2026 on 290,000–330,000t annual guidance vs. initial 600,000t target, after May 2025 seismic flooding (Ivanhoe Q2 press release, July 8 2026); (3) Cobre Panama (FQM, formerly top-10) remains closed since Nov 2023 with no restart as of July 2026, president's mid-year deadline slipped (Rio Times/riotimesonline.com, ~July 5 2026). Goldman Sachs and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence both project a 2026 copper supply deficit driven by these disruptions alone (525,000–600,000+ tonnes lost).
rationale: Three named top-20 mines have confirmed, physical production cuts active simultaneously in mid-2026—Grasberg (~59% below normal), Kamoa-Kakula (~50% below guidance), and Cobre Panama (full closure)—and major institutions (Goldman Sachs, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence) have issued deficit forecasts attributable to these outages, satisfying the CLUSTER criterion unambiguously.

dissent.view: Republic of Congo classified as 'debt in distress' with newly accumulated arrears per IMF Mar 2026 Post-Financing Assessment; Senegal's IMF program remained suspended into early 2026 with external payment pressures — these are stress indicators that could shade toward RISING if reclassified as new distress events.

fact: In the trailing 6 months (Jan 20 – Jul 20, 2026), IMF.org news shows only review completions for pre-existing arrangements (Argentina EFF 2nd review May 2026, Ecuador EFF 5th review Apr 2026, Ethiopia ECF 5th review Jul 2026, Ukraine EFF 1st review staff-level agreement Jun 2026). No new IMF lending arrangements approved from scratch and no sovereign missed coupon or standstill event were found in this window. Source: imf.org/en/news, multiple press releases Apr–Jul 2026.
rationale: Rubric requires >=1 new IMF program OR a missed coupon for RISING (1); none found in the window — all IMF actions are reviews of programs approved before Jan 2026. No missed-coupon event identified. Count = 0 → CALM.

fact: TPR market oversight report (Sept 2025, data to 31 Mar 2025): 'LDI managers have maintained higher buffer thresholds, reducing leverage and improved collateral management... Interest rate volatility has returned at various moments in 2025 and the experience has been that LDI related operations have been normal.' Rate buffers raised to ~300bps (vs ~150bps pre-2022); LDI market size halved from ~GBP1.5tn to ~GBP0.7tn. ESMA TRV article (June 2026, data end-2024): 'the ability of funds to meet liquidity demands has improved compared to September 2022 after leverage-related measures under Article 25 of AIFMD were implemented.' Sources: https://www.thepensionsregulator.gov.uk/en/document-library/research-and-analysis/market-oversight-how-well-pension-schemes-are-prepared-for-ldi-risk; https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-06/ESMA50-1949966494-4208_LDI_funds_-_recent_developments_and_methods_for_liquidity_stress_testing_0.pdf
rationale: Both TPR (primary UK regulator) and ESMA confirm buffers are adequate, leverage is reduced, and no margin-call episode or forced selling occurred in 2025-2026; this maps unambiguously to Rubric 0 (NONE). No regulator has flagged active LDI liquidity stress in 2026, and no central-bank intervention has been reported.

dissent.view: Oxford Economics (June 12) frames the yield rise (2.1% to 2.7%) as a mix of global repricing and fiscal concern, with a 'recent slight retreat' after a smaller-than-expected supplementary budget — suggesting the fiscal shock is partially priced and partially stabilising

Lazard (mid-year 2026) notes Takaichi 'tempered expectations for sizable fiscal stimulus, in part to reassure jittery bond markets' — suggesting the fiscal impulse is being managed downward, consistent with a borderline 0/1 reading

fact: 10y JGB yield was ~2.781% as of July 14 2026 (peak 2.901%), up over 70bps YTD partly on Takaichi fiscal concern; most recent JGB auctions clearing strongly (30y July 7 bid-to-cover 4.55x, 20y ~July 14 bid-to-cover 4.52x, tail=0); Takaichi's May 25 ~3 trillion yen supplementary budget claims no extra net issuance but funding path credibility is widely disputed. Sources: CNBC July 14 2026; Business Recorder ~July 14 2026; Dukascopy July 7 2026.
rationale: The cumulative 10y JGB yield rise linked to Takaichi fiscal concerns exceeds 25bps (>70bps YTD, ~60bps since March) and the funding path is credibility-contested (UNCLEAR rubric trigger), but auctions are clearing well above bid-to-cover thresholds with no failed sale, no emergency BOJ op, and no single-event >50bp spike, ruling out DISORDERLY (score 2).

fact: Fitch downgraded France from AA- to A+ on 12 September 2025 (stable outlook); S&P downgraded France from AA-/A-1+ to A+/A-1 on 17 October 2025 (stable outlook); Moody's kept Aa3 but moved outlook to Negative on 24 October 2025. S&P affirmed A+ on 30 May 2026. Sources: S&P Global Ratings (spglobal.com, 2025-10-17), France24/Moody's (2025-10-25), Bloomberg (2026-05-30), ING Think (2025-09), internationalbanker.com (2025-09-25).
rationale: Two of the three major agencies (Fitch on 2025-09-12 and S&P on 2025-10-17) executed actual one-notch rating cuts from AA- to A+ within the trailing 12 months ending 2026-07-20, satisfying rubric band 2 (DOWNGRADE). Moody's negative outlook also independently satisfies band 1, but the higher band (2) takes precedence.

fact: China MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026, issued 22 June 2026, added 10 named US entities to its export control list, including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc. The full list: Aveox, Red Cat Holdings, Teal Drones, IMSAR, Jaia Robotics, Ball Aerospace & Technologies Corp, Oshkosh Defense, L3Harris Maritime Services, MP Materials Corp, and USA Rare Earth. Source: MOFCOM via Global Times / Benchmark Minerals / Al Jazeera / SMM (metal.com), 22 June 2026. Multiple sources and Benchmark Minerals confirm 'the measure is entity-specific rather than a blanket restriction on rare earth exports to the US.'
rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) are explicitly listed on China's MOFCOM export-control entity list as of 22 June 2026, fitting rubric level 1 exactly. The restriction is firm-specific (10 named entities across sectors) and explicitly characterised by Benchmark Minerals and SMM as not a sector-wide or categorical ban, ruling out level 2.

dissent.view: Stanger (May 14 2026) states 'no NAV BDC has gated redemptions' in the strict sense — funds exceeded their 5% caps voluntarily or by fulfilling 100%+ of requests; the gates are contractual caps working as designed, not emergency suspensions. R.A. Stanger press release May 14 2026.

Federal Reserve May 2026 Financial Stability Report characterized Q1 redemption activity as 'limited and manageable', suggesting regulators do not view this as a systemic crisis. Lead Lag Report / LeadLag citing Fed FSR May 2026.

fact: In Q1 and Q2 2026, at least 7 named large private-credit/BDC funds enforced quarterly redemption caps at the contractual 5% ceiling after requests far exceeded that limit: Blackstone BCRED (~$79-82B, 10% Q2 requests gated at 5%, first formal gate in Q2; 7.9% in Q1 fulfilled above cap); Apollo Debt Solutions (~$25B, 16.8% Q2 requests capped at 5%); Ares Strategic Income Fund (~$21.5B, 14.6% Q2 / 11.6% Q1 requests capped at 5%); BlackRock/HPS Corporate Lending (~$26B, 9.3% Q1 requests capped at 5%); Blue Owl OCIC/OTIC (22%/41% Q1 requests capped at 5%; OBDC II permanently closed); Cliffwater Corporate Lending Fund (~$31B, 17% Q2 requests with ~1/3 fulfilled); North Haven Private Income Fund (11.6% Q2 requests, capped at 5%). Congressional Research Service (CRS IN12674, updated April 2 2026), CNBC 2026-06-23, Stanger May 14 2026, Sekond/PitchBook/ZeroHedge June-July 2026 corroborate across primary filings.
rationale: Seven or more named funds — with combined AUM well above $100bn — simultaneously enforced quarterly repurchase caps in the same two-quarter window (Q1-Q2 2026), clearly satisfying the rubric's threshold of >=3 largest funds or combined gated AUM >$100bn, mapping mechanically to score 2 (WIDESPREAD). No corroborating funding-market dislocation (SOFR-EFFR, MOVE, repo) has reached systemic-crisis levels, but the breadth of gating across every major manager is itself the corroborating market signal that structural liquidity stress is real and widespread.

fact: FDIC failed-bank list (last updated July 10, 2026) records 3 US bank failures YTD 2026: Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust ($261M, Jan 30 - FDIC OIG cites C&I asset-quality issues, not CRE); Community Bank & Trust - West Georgia ($288M, May 1 - KBRA cites a Jan 12 2026 FDIC consent order and loan-quality issues; no primary FDIC/OCC document explicitly names CRE concentration as cause); Kentland Federal Savings ($3.7M, Jul 10 - OCC cites unsafe practices/capital depletion, no CRE link). No single failure exceeded $10bn assets. The Jan 12 2026 FDIC consent order against Community Bank & Trust - West Georgia is a confirmed public enforcement action preceding that bank's failure; whether it explicitly cites CRE concentration is unconfirmed in truncated KBRA excerpt. Sources: fdic.gov/resources/resolutions/bank-failures/in-brief/2026 (Jul 10 2026); fdicoig.gov (May 29 2026); kbra.com (May 2026); americanbanker.com (Jul 10 2026).
rationale: At least one public FDIC enforcement/consent action against a subsequently failed community bank (<$10bn) is confirmed within the trailing 6 months, satisfying the ISOLATED rubric threshold of >=1 enforcement action citing bank stress; zero confirmed CRE-concentration language in primary failure documents prevents escalation to CLUSTER, and no failure exceeded $10bn assets or triggered coordinated interagency action. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]

dissent.view: lakeinsights.com reports Lake Mead at -187.06 ft vs full pool (implying ~1,042 ft elevation, consistent with USBR), noting moderate drought in watershed - no material disagreement on level, only drought severity framing.

fact: USBR Lower Colorado Weekly Hydrologic Update (June 29, 2026) reports Lake Mead elevation at 1,042.77 feet and storage at 27% of capacity (usbr.gov/lc/region/g4000/weekly.pdf). Newsweek citing USBR data (~June 14-17, 2026) corroborates at 29% full with 7,487,010 acre-feet in storage.
rationale: At 27-29% of capacity, Lake Mead falls below the rubric's 30% CRITICAL threshold. Elevation ~1,042 ft is also below the ~1,050 ft lower intake threshold at Hoover Dam, and USBR has confirmed reduced hydropower generating capacity as a direct physical consequence - meeting the top band's requirement for a confirmed physical impact.

fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026, SSA.gov/oact/trsum/) projects the OASI Trust Fund depleted in Q4 2032 — one quarter earlier than the 2025 report — with only 78% of scheduled benefits payable at that time; the 75-year actuarial deficit widened to 4.42% of taxable payroll from 3.82% in 2025. No benefit cut has been enacted or automatically triggered. Bipartisan reform bills (PROMISE Act, Senate, July 15 2026; Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act, House, June 2026) are actively debated but none enacted.
rationale: The trustees report worsened the depletion date by one quarter and materially widened the long-run deficit, and reform is actively debated in both chambers — squarely rubric band 1 (DEBATE). No automatic reduction has been triggered (trust fund still solvent until 2032) and no legislation enacting cuts has passed, so band 2 does not apply.

dissent.view: The Diplomat (Jan 3 2026) and AEI/ISW characterize the Dec 2025 Justice Mission 2025 drill as the largest since 2022 and argue PLA activity is structurally escalatory, which some analysts read as approaching crisis-threshold behavior rather than merely 'elevated'.

fact: ISW/AEI China-Taiwan Update (July 17, 2026) and July 2 and July 10 updates report no new named large-scale PLA encirclement drill since 'Justice Mission 2025' (Dec 29-30, 2025). Taiwan's MND recorded 12 days in June 2026 with zero ADIZ median-line crossings and PLA sortie volumes have reverted to ~200/month from the post-Lai peak of 300+. The PLA carrier Fujian transited the Taiwan Strait (late June 2026, characterized by PRC MND as 'normal training'), and PRC-Russia 'Joint Sea-2026' exercises ran July 6-13 near Qingdao. A PLA SSBN conducted a rare SLBM test on July 6 (South Pacific impact). No kinetic clash, no blockade, and no full mobilization reported.
rationale: The absence of a new named encirclement drill and the measurable decline in ADIZ sortie tempo rule out Rubric 2 (crisis) and push against a pure Rubric 0 (calm); the ongoing carrier transits through the Strait, near-weekly joint combat patrols, continuing CCG assertive patrols around Taiwan's outer islands, and the July 6 SLBM test as nuclear signaling collectively maintain an elevated but sub-crisis posture consistent with Rubric 1.

fact: In the trailing 3 months (Apr 20–Jul 20, 2026), confirmed new major-economy trade measures against China include: (1) USTR proposed 12.5% Section 301 tariff on China across broad categories (forced labor), Jun 2, 2026 (china-briefing.com/USTR); (2) EU definitive AD duties on Chinese tyres 4.3–45.3%, Jul 7, 2026 (EC policy.trade.ec.europa.eu); (3) EU definitive AD duties on BDO from China 105.6–113.7%, Jun 24, 2026 (EC policy.trade.ec.europa.eu); (4) EU definitive AD duties on glass fibre materials from China, Reg. EU 2026/1203, Jun 2026 (catts.eu); (5) EU AD investigation opened on polyether polyols from China, Jun 30, 2026 (agenceurope.eu); (6) EU registration/AD investigation on copper pipes from China effective Jun 10, 2026 (catts.eu); (7) US DOC preliminary AD/CVD circumvention findings on Chinese paper plates via Malaysia/Cambodia, Jul 10, 2026 (federalregister.gov); (8) US DOC preliminary CVD/AD on wooden cabinets from China, Jul 13, 2026 (federalregister.gov); (9) China issued Supply Chain Security and Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Regulations, Apr 7–13, 2026 (Mayer Brown July 2026). Total confirmed distinct measures: >=9, including broad tariff rounds >=10% across sectors.
rationale: At least 9 distinct new trade measures (tariffs, AD duties, broad regulatory trade barriers) were imposed or formally proposed against China by major economies in the trailing 3 months, far exceeding the rubric threshold of >=4 new measures; multiple actions constitute broad tariff rounds at sector level (tyres up to 45.3%, BDO up to 113.7%, USTR 12.5% across all China imports), unambiguously meeting the ESCALATING criterion regardless of the managed truce framework.

dissent.view: SEC Chair Atkins (Mar 10 2026) reaffirmed the Dec 2026 deadline and TBAC notes cash clearing is 'relatively better positioned' than repo, suggesting cash-side friction may be manageable; some sell-side majors (JPM, BofA, State Street) are operationally advanced.

fact: TBAC May 2026 presentation (home.treasury.gov/system/files/221/TBACCharge1Q22026.pdf, dated May 2026) states: 'Largest challenge from an implementation standpoint continues to be the amount of legal work and documentation associated with the bilateral agreements between participants'; the SIFMA/ValueExchange pulse survey cited by TBAC found that 'operational readiness and re-papering contracts were cited as the biggest worries for up to 71% of firms' and 'fewer than one in three firms report being very familiar with done-away clearing'; as of April-June 2026, two major exemptive-relief requests (SIFMA inter-affiliate, IIB extraterritorial) remain pending and unresolved before the SEC, with ICMA and SIFMA both flagging outstanding regulatory clarity as a prerequisite for operational builds. SEC Chair Atkins confirmed the Dec 31 2026 cash deadline stands (Bloomberg, Mar 10 2026) and the SEC stated it does not intend further extensions (SEC.gov, Sep 30 2025).
rationale: The rubric's FRICTION criteria are met on multiple counts: a documented documentation backlog in bilateral legal agreements (TBAC May 2026), pending exemptive relief on inter-affiliate and extraterritorial scope (SEC/SIFMA, Apr-Jun 2026), and industry-survey data showing fewer than one-third of firms 'very familiar' with done-away clearing — well below the 60% confidence threshold in the rubric. No deadline extension or confirmed operational failure has occurred, so level 2 is not warranted.

dissent.view: Truce is holding: White House and senior US officials characterise the Oct-2025 suspension as 'still in effect' and frame the April-2025 controls as a separate pre-truce measure outside the agreement's scope, implying no breach of the actual truce terms.
ITI (May-7-2026) notes China 'appears to be upholding its commitments' on the Oct-2025 suspension, but flags license delays/denials as a fraying signal rather than a formal breach.

fact: The Nov-10-2025 MOFCOM suspension of China's Oct-9-2025 rare-earth export controls remains nominally in force through Nov-10-2026 (White House Fact Sheet, Nov-5-2025; confirmed 'still in effect' by senior US official, Reuters/E&E News, May-13-2026). However, China's April-2025 Announcement No.18 controls on heavy REEs (dysprosium, terbium, yttrium, scandium) were never suspended under the truce and remain fully active; Chinese customs data as of May-2026 shows exports of yttrium, dysprosium and terbium still ~50% below pre-April-2025 levels (Reuters/Mining Weekly, May-13-2026; CSIS data via TechTimes, May-27-2026). No formal extension of the Oct-2025 suspension has been announced as of the July-2026 Trump-Xi summit period.
rationale: The rubric classifies '1' for a partial breach; China's April-2025 controls — never lifted — represent exactly that, corroborated by persistent ~50% volume suppression in heavy REE exports. Nominal expiry is ~113 days away (above 90-day threshold) but the unresolved partial breach and absence of a confirmed renewal tip the indicator to EXPIRING/fraying rather than EXTENDED/holding.

dissent.view: Pakistan alleges India already carried out deliberate, abrupt flow manipulations on the Chenab (May 2026: drop from 21,887 to 5,689 cusecs), which could be interpreted as a partial operational flow cut-off approaching Level 2, but India disputes this characterisation and no independent hydrological authority has confirmed deliberate diversion.

fact: INDUS: India has held the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance since April 2025 and India's water minister stated 'not a single drop of water will flow to Pakistan'; Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif declared Pakistan 'would not hesitate to go to war if its water security is breached' (The Diplomat, July 7 2026; CNBC, June 22 2026). India rejected the May 15 2026 Court of Arbitration award on pondage limits, calling the court illegally constituted (Britannica, updated July 2026). GERD/NILE: No binding agreement exists; Egypt contests Ethiopia's filling of GERD as illegal; official threats (Sisi: Egypt 'will not stand idly by'; Egypt deployed military assets near Ethiopia's sea-access routes) have been exchanged but no armed clash or deliberate flow cut-off has occurred (The National, Feb 23 2026; martinplaut.com, Mar 7 2026).
rationale: Both disputes meet Rubric Level 1: a treaty formally suspended/held in abeyance (IWT) and a treaty structurally contested without binding force (GERD/2015 Declaration), with official war-threat language and military posturing exchanged, but no confirmed kinetic action or deliberate physical flow cut-off executed as of July 2026.

dissent.view: Some pro-BRICS sources (watcher.guru, informedclearly.com, Jan-Jun 2026) claim BRICS Pay is already in 'decisive operational phase' in 2026 with 60-67% intra-bloc local-currency trade—implying Band 2 ACTION on settlement shift; however these sources are not authoritative primary sources and conflict with official BRICS/BIS/central bank statements.

fact: As of July 2026, no new sovereign reserve freeze or seizure has been executed beyond the pre-existing Russia CBR freeze (~$280bn, since 2022). On non-dollar settlement, BRICS Pay is in early operational/pilot phase: Russian FM Lavrov (Rio summit, 2025) pegged the pilot launch to end-2026; Russian Deputy FM Ryabkov pegs full operational status to 2030; BRICS Pay tracking site notes 'as of mid-2025 the system remains in the planning and early-pilot stage.' EBC Financial Group (April 13, 2026): 'As of 13 April 2026, there is no official BRICS common currency in circulation and no announced launch date for one.' Sources: bricspayment.ru/en/news; ebc.com; brookings.edu (Jun 2025); reuters.com/cfr.org context.
rationale: No new sovereign reserve freeze or outright seizure has occurred in 2026; the Russia freeze is a continuation, not a new action. BRICS Pay and The Unit represent active official rhetoric and pilot-stage launches—matching Band 1 (TALK/new non-dollar settlement agreements and launches) but not Band 2, which requires an executed new freeze or a major economy operationally off USD in reserves.

dissent.view: FERC June 18, 2026 orders aim to 'significantly shorten the multi-year interconnection queue backlog' - suggesting queues may ease on a 12-24 month horizon, but this is a forward-looking regulatory action, not current relief

IEA Electricity 2026 confirms >2,500 GW stalled in global queues and 'many power systems are already experiencing rising congestion-related curtailment' (iea.org, 2026).
rationale: The rubric's Level 2 threshold requires confirmed curtailment of data-center load, a declared grid emergency, or a power-scarcity-driven moratorium; all three criteria are met simultaneously: DOE/PJM emergency curtailment orders were issued and executed in May and July 2026, a grid emergency was declared under Federal Power Act Section 202(c), and New York enacted a first-in-nation statewide data-center moratorium explicitly citing grid capacity stress.

dissent.view: Sequoia's David Cahn estimated a ~$600B annual gap between AI infrastructure spending and AI ecosystem revenue in 2025, implying the gap may be more severe (closer to Score 2) when measured against total AI ecosystem revenue rather than hyperscaler cloud/AI segment revenue alone

dissent.view: Capacity Media (March 2026) and AGBI (March 2026) characterize the Hormuz cable network as facing a 'credible threat' with 2,500 vessels crowding the strait and 250 untraceable ships — some analysts argue this constitutes a persistent elevated-threat environment closer to a level-2 precursor.

September 2025 Red Sea cuts to SMW4 and IMEWE near Jeddah were confirmed physical severings causing multi-country disruption; if still unrepaired by July 2026, this would be level 2, but historical repair timelines (2–5 months) strongly suggest restoration before July 2026.

Source: Dawn.com / PTA statement, July 2, 2026.
rationale: The SMW5 fault (July 2, 2026) constitutes a single cable incident causing active connectivity degradation but is not confirmed as a complete, unrepaired severing; this maps to rubric level 1 (THREATENED / single incident). No current unrepaired confirmed major cut is documented for July 2026, and the Hormuz threat posture (AGBI, March 2026) remains elevated but without a physical cut materializing.

fact: Global insured catastrophe losses totaled $47bn in H1 2026 per Aon, and at least $46bn per Gallagher Re — 28% below the 10-year H1 average of ~$64bn. The largest single event (U.S. SCS outbreak April 23-29) generated ~$5bn in insured losses, well below the $10bn single-event threshold. Source: Aon Global Catastrophe Recap H1 2026 (Artemis, ~July 22 2026); Gallagher Re Natural Catastrophe and Climate Report H1 2026 (Risk & Insurance, ~July 22 2026).
rationale: YTD insured losses of ~$46-47bn are ~28% BELOW the 10-year average of ~$64bn for H1, and no single event exceeded $5bn — both conditions satisfy the NORMAL rubric (YTD <= 10y average AND no single event >$10bn). The hurricane season is below-average due to El Niño, and H2 has not yet produced a major landfalling storm or large wildfire loss.

dissent.view: The May 26 2026 urea quota release (~1.5-1.6M t, June-August window) could be read as a partial relaxation of urea restrictions, arguably moving back toward level 1 (in place but unchanged) rather than level 2 tightening, since the March broadening is now slightly outside the strict 3-month trailing window (March 19 vs July 27 = ~4 months).

fact: In mid-March 2026 Beijing banned exports of nitrogen-potassium fertilizer blends and certain additional phosphate varieties (per Reuters/Bloomberg, March 19-21 2026), layered on top of (a) the NDRC Dec 11 2025 phosphate suspension through August 2026 and (b) existing urea export quotas. By late May 2026 China issued a limited urea quota of ~1.5-1.6M tonnes for June-August with a $660/t price floor (Profercy, May 26 2026), but the phosphate suspension and NK-blend bans remained in force. Sources: potatopro.com (March 23 2026), exiger.com (April 16 2026), profercy.com (May 26 2026), sunsirs.com (Dec 16 2025).
rationale: The mid-March 2026 addition of NK-blend and expanded phosphate bans constitutes a NEW, broadened restriction beyond prior measures, satisfying rubric level 2 (new or broadened restriction in trailing ~4 months). The partial May urea quota reopening does not lift the phosphate/NK bans nor the overall quota-managed framework, and international urea prices rose ~40% vs pre-war levels confirming physical market impact - corroborating price move is present.

dissent.view: MT Newswires/iTiger headline dated 07-09 claims 'PPI declined 3.6% on year in June' - this is clearly a misdated/recycled item from a prior deflation episode (likely June 2024) and contradicts the NBS official release directly; no current market signal supports ongoing deflation.

fact: NBS official English press release (stats.gov.cn, 2026-07-10): 'In June 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 4.1% year on year and decreased by 0.3% month on month.'
rationale: The rubric requires reporting the signed NBS figure exactly; +4.1% YoY is a sharp positive move representing a cost-push inflation signal that exports input-cost pressure to trading partners. The engine scores on magnitude of move, not sign; +4.1% is the largest reading since mid-2022 per corroborating sources.

dissent.view: DTCC/Risk.net (Mar 2026) characterise infrastructure as ready and compliance path as clear, implying on-track sentiment closer to 0; however the prior formal extension and live exemptive-relief requests objectively satisfy rubric level 1 regardless of readiness optimism.

fact: On Feb 25 2025, the SEC formally extended compliance dates by one year to Dec 31 2026 (cash) and Jun 30 2027 (repo) — a first official extension (SEC Release No. 34-102487; sec.gov, Feb 25 2025). As of Apr 17 2026, the SEC published SIFMA's pending exemptive-relief requests (inter-affiliate exemption expansion and extraterritorial non-U.S. participant exemption), with a May 29 2026 public comment deadline, and open scoping issues for non-U.S. participants remain unresolved per the TBAC Q1-2 2026 charge document (home.treasury.gov, May 29 2026). No second formal deadline extension has been announced.
rationale: The rubric scores 1 for 'an official extension granted OR exemptive-relief requests pending': both conditions are met — the Feb 2025 extension is the first official extension, and SIFMA's inter-affiliate and IIB non-U.S. exemptive-relief requests were formally pending before the SEC as of Apr-May 2026. There is no evidence of a second deadline extension (which would score 2), so the score is capped at 1.

dissent.view: KBRA office CMBS delinquency rate was 13.9% in January 2026 and fell to 12.8% in February 2026 — materially higher than Trepp's figure, reflecting KBRA's rated-universe methodology
S&P Global Ratings noted the office CMBS rate 'surpasses 10.5%' in January 2026, lower than both Trepp and KBRA readings, reflecting S&P's rated-universe scope

fact: Trepp reported office CMBS delinquency at ~11.7% in January 2026 (per Trepp data cited by multiple outlets); Trepp's June 2026 overall CMBS report states office delinquencies 'increased' further in June vs May, but the precise Trepp office sub-rate for June 2026 was not publicly quoted in available sources. KBRA (a competing authoritative source) reported office delinquency at 13.9% in January 2026 and 12.8% in February 2026 (BusinessWire, 2026-02-27). The Trepp June 2026 overall rate was 7.35% (MBA Newslink, 2026-07-08).
rationale: The rubric asks for the latest CMBS office delinquency rate as a percent from Trepp; the most recent Trepp-attributed office-specific figure is ~11.7% (Jan 2026), with Trepp's June 2026 report confirming office delinquencies continued to rise — placing the current Trepp office rate modestly above 11.7%, but no precise June figure was publicly available. KBRA's methodology yields a higher figure (~12.8%), recorded as dissent.

Goldman Sachs base case: 2026 surplus of ~160kt, broadly corroborating ICSG direction but a larger surplus figure

rationale: ICSG officially forecasts a +96,000t surplus for 2026, which exceeds the +100kt surplus threshold in the rubric; this maps mechanically to band 0 (SURPLUS). The surplus figure is above the ±100kt balanced range, so band 1 does not apply.

Jurisdictions with enacted or near-enacted actions include: New York (statewide EO, enacted); Virginia (court-invalidated approvals + 15 enacted bills); Georgia (multiple county moratoria); Maine (legislature passed, governor vetoed); Texas/Hill County (briefly enacted, then rescinded); plus 100+ unnamed local municipalities.

The sustained record-high rate, driven by ~94% distressed-exchange composition, confirms acute private credit stress without a direct funding-market transmission signal in public repo/SOFR data as of this date.

dissent.view: coferdata.com tracker shows USD share at 56.77% for the latest quarter, ~0.15pp below the 56.92% reported by Reuters citing the Dec 22 2025 IMF COFER release, possibly reflecting a minor post-publication revision

No confirmed fab/farm production curtailment found in 2026, but D3-D4 physical conditions alone satisfy the ACUTE threshold under the rubric.

dissent.view: East Asia Forum (Mar 2026) characterises the Trump White House as having 'traded loud escalation for quiet enforcement', approving higher-tier chip exports and suspending further restrictions — implying a partial de-escalation that could support a level-1 rather than level-2 reading on the US side.

fact: Within the trailing 3 months (Apr–Jul 2026): (1) US side — the bipartisan MATCH Act was introduced ~2 Apr 2026 targeting DUV immersion lithography exports to China (CNBC, 7 Apr 2026); US Commerce Secretary Lutnick began private meetings with ASML executives in Apr 2026 over suspected EUV diversion to China (Asia Times, ~14 Jul 2026). (2) China side — Beijing promulgated 'Regulations on Countering Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction by Foreign States' in April 2026, explicitly empowering Chinese authorities to prohibit firms such as ASML from complying with US FDP Rules (JustSecurity/MoFo, ~14 Jul 2026); China's State Council published 'Regulations on Outbound Investment' on 1 Jun 2026, including countermeasures and penalties for foreign restrictions deemed discriminatory against Chinese entities (Morrison Foerster, Jul 2026); Chinese semiconductor firm Wingtech sued Dutch subsidiary Nexperia in a Chinese court in May 2026 for ~US$1.2 bn over Dutch restrictive measures. Primary sources: CNBC reuters.com Apr 7 2026; JustSecurity Jul 14 2026; Morrison Foerster Jul 2026.
rationale: Both sides enacted new measures within the 3-month window: the US introduced major new controls legislation (MATCH Act) targeting DUV lithography and initiated compliance inquiries; China enacted formal countermeasure regulations (April extraterritorial-jurisdiction rules + June outbound-investment regulations with penalty authority) and launched legal retaliation via the Wingtech/Nexperia lawsuit — meeting the rubric definition of level 2 (RETALIATION: target country enacts countermeasures/legal retaliation). Market signal is corroborated by ASML's China revenue share falling from 33% in 2025 to ~19-20% in Q1/full-year 2026 guidance.

dissent.view: Some sources treat Arizona 4nm as 'leading-edge' diversification and note TSMC profits in Arizona/Kumamoto as evidence diversification is underway, potentially warranting a HIGH (1) read if the rubric threshold were relaxed to <=5nm.

fact: As of July 2026, TSMC has zero operational <=3nm capacity outside Taiwan. The sole overseas advanced fab — Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 — runs 4nm at an estimated ~10,000-20,000 wspm. Arizona Phase 2 (3nm) completed construction but begins tool installation Q3 2026 with volume production targeted H2 2027; Kumamoto Fab 2 (3nm) targets 2028. Taiwan hosts all <=3nm volume production: ~180,000 wspm at 3nm and ~90,000-100,000 wspm at 2nm, per TSMC Q1 2026 earnings (April 2026, focustaiwan.tw/trendforce.com) and CNBC/TechTimes Q2 2026 reporting (July 2026).
rationale: The rubric scores EXTREME (2) when <10% of leading-edge (<=3nm) capacity is outside Taiwan AND no operational overseas leading-edge fab exists. As of today, 100% of <=3nm capacity remains in Taiwan; the only overseas advanced node (Arizona 4nm) does not qualify under the rubric's <=3nm threshold, and no <=3nm fab outside Taiwan is in production.

fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 130.3 points in June 2026, down 0.3% MoM from May but 2.2% above its year-earlier level. Source: FAO newsroom (fao.org), released 3 July 2026.
rationale: YoY the index remains elevated (+2.2%), disqualifying a FALLING rating; MoM change is only -0.3% (well inside the ±3% ELEVATED band), and neither the MoM (+5%) nor 3-month (+10%) thresholds for SPIKING are breached.

dissent.view: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index: PPFI funded ratio at 87.6% as of April 30, 2026, for the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans (assets $6.009T vs. liabilities $6.860T)
Equable Institute year-end update to State of Pensions 2025 (Jan 8, 2026): aggregate funded ratio at 82.5% for end of calendar year 2025

(253 statewide and municipal systems, all 50 states + D.C.)

The Milliman PPFI reading of 87.6% (April 30, 2026, top 100 plans only) is directionally consistent, providing corroboration at a slightly higher level due to its focus on the largest plans.

fact: The GENIUS Act's statutory rulemaking deadline of July 18, 2026 was missed: Treasury, OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, and NCUA collectively issued 10 NPRMs but zero final implementing rules by that date; the FinCEN/CIP comment window alone runs through August 21, 2026. Source: multiple corroborating reports (BigGo Finance, CryptoDaily, GNCrypto, CoinTribune) dated July 18-27, 2026; OCC NPRM bulletin occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-3.html; FDIC NPRM fdic.gov FIL dated April 2026.
rationale: The rubric's level-2 criterion is 'deadline missed without final rules' — exactly what occurred on July 18, 2026, with all five mandated agencies still in proposed/comment stage and no final rule published. No court stay was required to satisfy level 2; the plain missed deadline with zero finalized rules is sufficient.

dissent.view: Bloomberg (9 Jan 2026) reported Finance Minister Lescure warning that a further government fall could trigger snap elections/dissolution — indicating the government's hold remains contested, though no dissolution has been executed as of latest data.

The National Assembly remains a three-bloc hung parliament with no party holding an absolute majority, and the government has repeatedly relied on Socialist acquiescence and Article 49.3-type budget manoeuvres to survive.

No dissolution or PM resignation has been recorded after Sep 2025 Bayrou collapse; Lecornu's government is functional but precarious.

dissent.view: CoreWeave's $8.5bn DDTL 4.0 (March 2026) priced at investment-grade (A3/Moody's) and its May $2bn bond was 'heavily oversubscribed', suggesting orderly refinancing rather than stress
Nvidia has stepped in as a backstop guarantor for neocloud GPU offtakes in mid-2026, reducing idiosyncratic refinancing risk across the sector

fact: CoreWeave carried a '$4.2 billion refinancing wall due in 2026 on debt that predates the Meta structure' against GPUs that 'have depreciated substantially since the loans were written' (davefriedman.substack.com, Apr 19 2026); separately, banks were reported to be trying to offload AI data-centre debt as exposure mounts (resultsense.com, May 6 2026). CoreWeave addressed part of this wall via a $3.75bn high-yield bond refinancing (~9% coupon, heavily oversubscribed) and a March 2026 $8.5bn DDTL 4.0 rated A3/A(low) by Moody's/DBRS - no confirmed default or distressed exchange has been reported.
rationale: A named borrower (CoreWeave) faces a documented $4.2bn 2026 refinancing wall on GPU-collateralized debt with declining collateral values, and banks are reported offloading AI data-centre debt tranches at a discount - both qualifying signs under rubric level 1. However, CoreWeave has actively managed the wall through oversubscribed bond sales and new IG-rated facilities with no confirmed default, failed refinancing, or distressed exchange, so level 2 is not warranted.

dissent.view: US military stated 'the waterway remains open with American support' (CENTCOM, ~25 Jul 2026), implying a contested-but-not-closed framing that could imply a Level 1 reading

Straits.live (26 Jul 2026) rates the strait 'effectively closed to commercial shipping.' Brent crude ~$90-97/bbl on 27 Jul 2026, up ~30% year-on-year (TradingEconomics / Fortune, 27 Jul 2026), corroborating physical closure. Persian Gulf supplies ~44% of seaborne sulfur and ~43% of seaborne urea globally (NDSU Ag Trade Monitor, Mar 2026); those flows are halted.
rationale: The rubric's Level 2 threshold requires the strait to be CLOSED (not merely contested) AND a corroborating crude-oil price signal: both conditions are confirmed - zero tanker transits as of 25-26 Jul 2026 and Brent ~$90-97/bbl (~30% above year-ago levels). No signed ceasefire, MOU, or naval convoy operation is in force that would cap the rating at 1; Iran exited the June MOU and resumed attacks, and diplomatic talks with Oman on 26 Jul produced no change in transit conditions.

dissent.view: Military-verified data (vs. AIS-only tracking) shows ~14 vessels transiting on some days, suggesting the strait is not physically zero-traffic — more 'severely contested' than legally closed
IEA July 2026 report notes a partial flow resumption in June under the interim ceasefire, implying the situation was briefly contested (1) before re-escalating

fact: Lloyd's List Intelligence tracked only 78 Hormuz transits July 13-20 vs. 174 the prior week (USNI News, 2026-07-24); PortWatch recorded 15 transits on 2026-07-19 vs. a pre-crisis baseline of ~88/day (straits.live, 2026-07-26); Kpler data shows just 3 transits/day July 22-24 (discoveryalert.com.au, 2026-07-25). Brent crude hit ~$96-100/bbl week of July 23-26 (TradingEconomics, 2026-07-26; CNN, 2026-07-23). Red Sea: Houthis announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia and struck two Saudi oil tankers circa July 24 (CSMonitor, 2026-07-24). No functioning convoy workaround or ceasefire is in effect at Hormuz; the June 14 MOU ceasefire collapsed after fighting resumed July 7-8 (IEA July 2026 report).

fact: As of H1 2026, TSMC runs ~150,000 wafers/month at 3nm and ~50,000-60,000 wafers/month at 2nm — all in Taiwan (Tainan Fab 18, Hsinchu Fab 20, Kaohsiung Fab 22). Japan Kumamoto Phase 2 (3nm) targets 2028. Zero ≤3nm wafer starts exist outside Taiwan today. rationale: All operational ≤3nm capacity (~200,000+ combined monthly wafer starts) is located exclusively in Taiwan; overseas ≤3nm fabs are in equipment-installation or planning phases only, placing the outside-Taiwan share firmly at <10% (effectively 0%). This maps mechanically to rubric level 2 (EXTREME).

fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, up 0.6% (0.7 points) from June 2026 (130.3) and up 1.0% YoY — highest reading since January 2023. Source: FAO official press release, fao.org/newsroom, released 7 August 2026.

No corroborating funding-market stress signal (repo, SOFR-EFFR, MOVE) is required for a regulatory-status classification, and no such stress has been reported in connection with this miss.

dissent.view: CoreWeave management stated on its Q1 2026 earnings call that 'we have no debt maturities until 2029 other than self-amortizing contract-backed debt and OEM vendor financing,' suggesting near-term liquidity is more manageable than CDS implies; and the company closed a $3.1B GPU-backed facility in the same period, showing lenders still willing to extend credit at scale.

No confirmed default or distressed exchange has yet occurred. Sources: TechTimes/Bloomberg (July 29-Aug 3, 2026); Bloomberg Tax Distress Watch (July 21, 2026).
rationale: CoreWeave is a named GPU-backed borrower facing a concrete refinancing wall — its loan was actually repriced under investor pressure and now carries maintenance covenants — and its CDS prices distressed-level default odds, satisfying rubric level 1 ('a named borrower facing a refinancing wall' and 'banks offloading AI/data-center debt at a discount'). No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing has occurred, so level 2 is not yet warranted.

Brent crude peaked above $100/bbl in late July 2026, which at that point would have corroborated a rating of 2, but has since retreated to ~$83-84 as of Aug 10

No automatic reduction has been triggered (depletion has not occurred) and no legislation enacting cuts has been signed into law, ruling out band 2.

A secondary figure of 45 months (IR to signed interconnection agreement, not COD) exists but measures a different milestone and is not used as the primary value.

fact: The April 2025 MOFCOM licensing regime (Announcement No. 28/related notices) requiring non-automatic, case-by-case export licences for dysprosium, terbium, and Dy/Tb-containing NdFeB and SmCo magnets was never suspended and remains fully in force as of August 2026. MOFCOM issued a first batch of general licences in December 2025 to three named large exporters (JL MAG / Jinli, San Huan, Zhongke Sanhuan, Yunsheng) but these cover only pre-vetted named customers and are not broadly available. Statutory review target is 45 working days (~9 weeks), but in practice heavy-REE approvals routinely run 60-120+ days; a June 2025 US-China diplomatic deal produced a MOFCOM statement to 'review and approve eligible applications in accordance with law' yet Trump's August 2026 threats of 200% tariffs signal Washington remains unsatisfied with throughput. The 2026 Import-Export Licensing Catalogue added samarium, gadolinium, and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories. Source: blog.gettransport.com (July 7 2026), china-briefing.com, merics.org, arnold magnetics (Feb 2026), certivo.com (March 2026).
rationale: Licensing is case-by-case / whitelist (general licences restricted to a handful of named producers) with real-world processing times of 60-120+ days far exceeding the 30-day threshold, and new categories (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium compounds) were added to the control list in the trailing 3 months via the 2026 catalogue update — all three SLOWING triggers are met. No categorical denial to a country or announced licensing suspension exists that would support a FROZEN (2) rating, and market data show exports continuing at positive YoY growth, capping the escalation read at 1.

fact: As of mid-2026, at least three top-20 copper mines carry confirmed, active production cuts: (1) Grasberg (world\'s #2 copper mine) — Freeport delayed full restart to early 2028, targeting only ~65% capacity in H2 2026 vs. pre-incident ~1.7 billion lb/yr; copper output guided at ~700 million lb in 2026, down ~59% from plan (mining.com, May 8 2026). (2) Kamoa-Kakula (DRC, top-5 mine) — seismic/flood damage in 2025 cut 2026 guidance to 290,000–330,000 t vs. original 420,000–600,000 t target; Q2 2026 actual output was 64,328 t (Ivanhoe Q2 release, July 8 2026). (3) Codelco El Teniente (world\'s largest underground copper mine) — fatal tunnel collapse in 2025 led general manager to state production will be depressed for the next five years (CNBC, March 10 2026). Additional disruptions: Capstone Mantoverde strike (halted Jan 2026); CMOC TFM strike (June 2026); Chilean output down 9% YoY in March 2026 (Cochilco). Multiple institutions forecast a 2026 market deficit: ICSG revised from a 209,000 t surplus to a 150,000 t deficit; J.P. Morgan 330,000 t deficit; Morgan Stanley 600,000 t; ING 600,000 t (cruxinvestor.com, May 26 2026).
rationale: Three or more named top-20 mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, El Teniente) have confirmed, physically measured production cuts active in 2026, and multiple major financial institutions have revised global copper balances to a deficit — both prongs of the rubric\'s CLUSTER threshold (value=2) are satisfied.

rationale: ESMA's most recent formal assessment (Jun 2026) confirms improved liquidity buffers and no active margin crisis; absent any regulator flag of current LDI liquidity risk or a documented forced-selling episode in 2026, the evidence maps squarely to rubric band 0 (buffers adequate, no margin stress).

dissent.view: ModelDiplomat (July 2026) argues a near-term disorderly unwind is 'unlikely' given Japan's domestic investor base, long debt-maturity profile, and FY2026 primary-balance surplus, suggesting markets are stress-testing but not breaking.

fact: 10-year JGB yield touched 2.93% on Aug 17 2026 — its highest since September 1996 — driven by fiscal concerns over PM Takaichi's stimulus spending plans; yield is up ~130 bps over 12 months and ~19 bps over the past month. Funding path was specified (deficit-covering bonds, no new net issuance per May 2026 supplementary budget), but markets have continuously repriced higher. No failed auction (BTC <2) or BOJ emergency operation found; Aug 4 2026 10Y auction cleared per MOF. Sources: Euronews 2026-08-17 (https://www.euronews.com/business/2026/08/17/japans-10-year-bond-yield-hits-a-30-year-high-as-growth-data-disappoints); TradingEconomics 2026-08-14; MOF auction result page 2026-08-04 (https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/jgbs/auction/calendar/eresul/eresul20260804a.htm); CNBC 2026-06-01 (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/01/japan-pm-takaichis-budget-remarks-send-red-flag-to-bond-markets.html).
rationale: The 10Y JGB yield is up far more than 25 bps on fiscal news (rubric score 1 threshold) and the funding path, while nominally specified, has not been credibly accepted by markets — qualifying as UNCLEAR. However, without a confirmed failed/tailing auction (BTC <2) or BOJ emergency operation, the evidence does not reach the DISORDERLY threshold (score 2), per the instruction not to assign the most severe level without clear evidence.

Moody's negative outlook and S&P negative outlook would independently qualify for band 1, but the Fitch downgrade is the most severe observed action.

fact: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (issued 22 June 2026) added 10 named US entities to China's export control list, explicitly including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc. The measure bars Chinese exporters from supplying dual-use items to the named firms and prohibits any party from transferring China-origin dual-use goods to them. Multiple corroborating sources (Benchmark Minerals, SMM/Metal.com, Trivium China, StockTitan citing Reuters) confirm the listing; market reaction was muted (MP Materials roughly flat, USA Rare Earth modestly higher on the day), consistent with an entity-specific rather than sector-wide ban. The restriction is explicitly firm-specific: 'The measure is entity-specific rather than a blanket restriction on rare earth exports to the US' (Benchmark Minerals, 25 June 2026).
rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials and USA Rare Earth) appear by name on MOFCOM's export control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying the rubric's definition of score 1 (entity-specific). The listing does not extend categorically to the US rare-earth sector as a class, and multiple analysts explicitly characterise it as firm-specific, precluding score 2.

dissent.view: GERD/Nile dispute assessed as TENSE (level 1) not CRISIS: Egypt raised GERD at UNSC and signed military port agreements with Eritrea/Djibouti (strategic posturing), but no armed clash or deliberate Nile flow cut-off has occurred; analysts (pppescp.com, March 2026) assess armed conflict likelihood as 'relatively low'.

fact: India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty 'in abeyance' after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack, physically cut flows via Baglihar Dam on the Chenab (May 2025), stopped hydrological data sharing, and Pakistan reported abrupt flow drops at Marala (Chenab: 21,887 to 5,689 cusecs) in May 2026. Pakistan's Defence Minister stated 'the moment we feel our national security is under threat...we will go to war' (June 2026 CNBC). India's Home Minister vowed the treaty 'will never be restored' (June 2025, reiterated 2026). Sources: Chatham House April 2026; CNBC June 22 2026; Dawn June 2026; Britannica July 2026.
rationale: A deliberate flow cut-off was physically carried out (Baglihar Dam, May 2025 confirmed), the treaty is formally suspended/in abeyance with India rejecting arbitration awards, and Pakistan's Defence Minister issued an explicit war threat directly tied to water/dam control in June 2026 — all three crisis-level triggers in the rubric are met. The GERD/Nile dispute remains at level 1 (contested legal framework, official threats, no kinetic action or flow cut-off), but the Indus situation is the binding constraint at level 2.

BRICS Pay and the BRICS Unit gold-settlement pilot represent active non-dollar settlement launches/rhetoric but fall short of a major economy operationally moving reserve settlement off USD, placing the indicator squarely at band 1 (TALK/early-pilot).

IEA Electricity 2026 (iea.org) confirms >2,500 GW stalled in global grid queues and 'many power systems already experiencing rising congestion-related curtailment.'
rationale: Rubric Level 2 requires confirmed curtailment of data-center load, a declared grid emergency, or a power-scarcity-driven moratorium — all three conditions are simultaneously met: DOE/PJM emergency curtailment orders executed in 2026, New York statewide moratorium enacted July 14 2026, and ERCOT/PUCT curtailment authority formally affirmed July 24 2026. The IEA as primary source corroborates systemic congestion-related curtailment worldwide.
