fact: Affirm FQ2'26 Shareholder Letter (filed Feb 6, 2026, period ended Dec 31, 2025): '30+ day delinquencies excluding Peloton and Pay in X loans increased 18 basis points year over year and decreased 7 basis points quarter over quarter to 2.7%.' Allowance for credit losses 5.4% of loans held for investment. Industry BNPL charge-off rate per CFPB/Richmond Fed: 1.83% in 2023, estimated ~1.8-2% in 2024-25 (well below 3%). BTIG Research (~Aug 21, 2026) separately flagged Affirm ABS 30-59 DPD at all-time highs for newest vintages.
rationale: Affirm 30+ DPD rose +18 bps YoY to 2.7% -- up but far short of the 100 bps spike threshold for level 2; industry charge-offs remain ~1.8-2%, below the 3% containment ceiling, squarely fitting rubric level 1 (RISING, charge-offs contained). BTIG's all-time-high ABS vintage flag is a leading indicator of further deterioration but does not yet produce a reported figure breaching the level-2 thresholds.

dissent.view: Hormuz cables face only threatened (not actual) damage: Iran IRGC-linked Tasnim issued warnings in April 2026 but 'no attack has yet taken place' (Jerusalem Post, 2026-04-23)
Baltic incidents as of Jan 2026 involve anchor-drag suspicions and detentions, not confirmed active cable outages (Euronews, 2026-01-12)

fact: The PEACE submarine cable was cut in the Red Sea ~1,450km from Zafarana, Egypt, with repair expected to take 'several months' (Data Center Dynamics, ~July 2026, published ~1 month before 2026-08-24); separately, Geneva Solutions (2026-05-18) confirmed that of the four cables severed in the Sept 6 2025 Red Sea incident, 'one of which is still out of service' as of May 2026. At least two major Red Sea cables (PEACE + one from the Sept 2025 batch) are simultaneously severed and unrepaired.
rationale: Rubric level 2 requires >=1 major cable currently severed and unrepaired causing connectivity loss, or multiple simultaneous cuts; the PEACE cable (cut ~July 2026, unrepaired) plus at least one residual unrepaired cable from the Sept 2025 event meet the 'multiple simultaneous' threshold. Hormuz cables face credible Iranian threats but no confirmed cut; Baltic incidents are anchor-drag suspicions without confirmed active outage, so those alone would rate 1, but the Red Sea picture drives the score to 2.

fact: H1 2026 global insured natural catastrophe losses: Swiss Re Institute estimates $42bn (16% below 10-year trend of ~$66bn); Gallagher Re estimates $46bn (28% below 10-year average of $64bn); Aon estimates $47bn. No single event exceeded $10bn insured -- five consecutive quarters without a >$10bn event. Sources: Swiss Re Institute (swissre.com, ~Aug 20 2026), Gallagher Re H1 2026 NatCat Report (ajg.com/gallagherre, Jul 15 2026), Aon H1 2026 Global Cat Recap (artemis.bm, Jul 22 2026).
rationale: YTD insured losses of $42-47bn are materially BELOW the 10-year average (not above it, let alone >150%), and the largest single H1 2026 event was ~$5bn (U.S. SCS late-April outbreak) -- well under the $10bn threshold. Both the ELEVATED and SEVERE thresholds are unmet, mapping cleanly to NORMAL (0).

dissent.view: Fertilizer Daily (Jul 29 2026) reports China 'extended' phosphate curbs through August 2026, which could be interpreted as a new tightening action if the extension was formally enacted post-May 24 — but the underlying suspension was set in Dec 2025 and the extension appears to be a continuation, not a new restriction on additional products.

fact: The NDRC suspended orderly phosphate fertilizer exports through August 2026 (NDRC special meeting, Dec 11 2025; confirmed by S&P Global Platts, Exiger, SunSirs, Fertilizer Daily Jul 29 2026). Urea exports were partially re-opened via a ~3 million tonne quota (issued May 26 2026) with an NDRC-mandated FOB price floor of $660/t for prilled and $670/t for granular urea, covering a June-August window (Profercy, Keyuan Fertilizer, May 26-29 2026). The last NEW product broadening (NK blends + additional phosphate varieties) occurred mid-March 2026 — outside the trailing 3-month window from Aug 24 2026.
rationale: Phosphate suspension and quota-controlled urea exports are ongoing as of today, satisfying rubric level 1 (existing restrictions unchanged). The last confirmed broadening action (mid-March NK blend ban) occurred ~5 months ago, outside the 3-month window required for level 2; no new or additional product categories have been restricted in the trailing 3 months (May 24 - Aug 24 2026).

fact: NBS official press release (stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202608/t20260810_1965017.html, released 2026-08-10): 'In July 2026, China's producer price index for industrial products (PPI) increased by 3.5% year on year and decreased by 0.7% month on month.' Corroborated by Xinhua (2026-08-09) and China Daily (2026-08-09).
rationale: The signed figure is +3.5% YoY for July 2026, released by NBS on 2026-08-10; rubric scores on SIZE of move — at +3.5% this represents a notable cost-push signal that has reversed a prolonged deflation streak, flagging potential input-cost pressure spillover to trading partners.

fact: The SEC granted ONE formal one-year extension on Feb 25 2025 (Exchange Act Release No. 34-102487), moving cash clearing to Dec 31 2026 and repo clearing to Jun 30 2027. As of the SEC commissioner August 2026 update (sec.gov, ~Aug 7 2026), those dates remain unchanged and no second extension has been announced; however, SIFMA and IIB exemptive-relief requests are actively pending before the Commission (published Apr 17 2026), comment periods on combined inter-affiliate/extraterritorial relief and a 15c3-3 net-omnibus margin exemption closed Aug 31 2026, and the SEC has granted conditional exemptive relief for captive clearing subsidiaries for private funds - all consistent with multiple open exemptive-relief requests still pending.
rationale: Rubric level 1 requires 'an official extension granted OR exemptive-relief requests pending': the Feb 2025 one-year extension is an official granted extension (the first formal deadline push), and multiple SIFMA/IIB exemptive-relief requests remain pending as of Aug 2026. No second formal extension has been announced, so level 2 is not warranted.

The July 2026 data likely exceeds this given large new office delinquencies, but no confirmed figure was retrievable, warranting medium confidence on the Oct 2025 anchor. dissent.view: Maine is sometimes cited as the 'first' to pass a statewide moratorium (LD 307), but Gov. Mills vetoed it in April 2026, so it never took effect; some early sources (April 2026) incorrectly describe Maine as having enacted a statewide ban.

WilmerHale (Aug 2026) states 'legislators in six states have introduced ten similar bills' at the state level, a lower count than DLA Piper's '12 states,' reflecting different cutoff dates and counting methodologies.

fact: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an Executive Order on July 14, 2026, creating the nation's first statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centers, pausing state environmental permits for up to one year for facilities at 50 MW or more (Axios / NY Governor press release, 2026-07-14). Additionally, DLA Piper reported as of July 1, 2026 that 'more than 100 local moratoria have been adopted nationwide' and 'at least 12 states have considered moratorium legislation.' Maine's legislature passed a statewide moratorium (later vetoed). South Dakota passed SB 135 enabling local bans. Multiple counties in Georgia, Virginia (Prince William County), and Texas (Hill County) enacted local pauses.
rationale: New York has a confirmed, signed, in-force statewide moratorium via executive order (July 14, 2026), satisfying the rubric's 'statewide moratorium enacted' criterion alone for level 2; the additional 100+ local moratoria nationwide and 12+ states with bills further confirm the WIDESPREAD classification. Jurisdictions with enacted pauses/moratoria include: New York (statewide EO), Maine (passed legislature, vetoed), South Dakota (local-enabling law SB 135), Georgia (multiple counties), Virginia (Prince William County invalidation), Texas Hill County (briefly enacted then rescinded), plus 100+ other local jurisdictions per DLA Piper.

Source: Bloomberg 2026-07-30 (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-30/fitch-s-private-credit-default-rate-hit-record-in-second-quarter) and cryptobriefing.com summary of Fitch July 2026 monitor (https://cryptobriefing.com/fitch-us-corporate-default-rates-july-2026/).
rationale: The Fitch inclusive TTM private-credit default rate (counting distressed exchanges and LMEs) ticked up to 6.1% in July 2026 from the prior record of 6.0% set in Q2; this is applied directly as the rubric-anchored Fitch inclusive measure, with the July 2026 Fitch publication as the as_of period. One LinkedIn snippet from Fitch's own page cited '5.2% in July' but context suggests this references a sub-index (possibly PMR or count-based), not the headline inclusive TTM rate that Bloomberg and CryptoBriefing confirm at 6.1%.

dissent.view: Arizona short-term drought picture shows some monsoon improvement in July 2026, with D2 covering 47% of state and no D3/D4 in short-term metrics for AZ specifically — suggesting intra-region variability and partial relief

fact: According to the U.S. Drought Monitor (Drought.gov Intermountain West Status Update, August 20, 2026): 'nearly 95% of the region (Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) is experiencing some type of drought, with around 30% of the region in either Extreme Drought (D3) or Exceptional Drought (D4).' The USDA crop report (droughtmonitor.unl.edu, August 11, 2026) further notes 33% of Utah winter wheat is in poor/very poor condition vs. a 5-year average near zero, and one-half to three-quarters of rangelands in Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah are in poor/very poor condition — confirmed agricultural production impacts. No current fab water-rationing order found for Taiwan (most recent Taiwan drought impact found dates to 2021).
rationale: D3-D4 coverage across ~30% of the US Southwest (Arizona, Utah, Colorado, New Mexico, Wyoming) meets the rubric's ACUTE threshold; confirmed agricultural production curtailment (poor/very poor crop and rangeland conditions well above historical averages) provides the required physical impact corroboration. Taiwan shows no current active water-rationing order in 2026, but the US Southwest anchor alone clears the rubric for a score of 2.

dissent.view: East Asia Forum (March 2026) characterises the White House as having 'cooled' chip export controls and suspending further restrictions under Trump trade-talk priorities, suggesting the executive branch has partially softened enforcement even as Congress escalates -- this would cap the read closer to 1 if only executive action counts.

fact: US side: MATCH Act (introduced April 2, 2026) proposes blanket DUV lithography ban to China; VEU exemptions for Samsung/SK Hynix/TSMC/Micron revoked; Commerce Dept pressing ASML on EUV diversion since April 2026 (Reuters/CNBC, July 2026). China side: April 2026 Regulations on Countering Improper Extraterritorial Jurisdiction empowers Beijing to prohibit ASML-type FDP Rule compliance (Just Security, July 9, 2026); 2026 Import-Export Licensing Catalogue added rare-earth licensing controls (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium); NdPr benchmark +21.4% through July 1, 2026 as corroborating price signal (Tech-Insider, ~July 2026).
rationale: Both sides have enacted new measures within the trailing 3-month window: the US through the MATCH Act legislative push and VEU revocations (tightening), and China through counter-jurisdiction regulations and expanded rare-earth export licensing (retaliation with a corroborating commodity price spike). Rubric level 2 (RETALIATION) is met: the target country has enacted active countermeasures including legal retaliation tools and input-supply controls.

dissent.view: TrendForce (Dec 2023 projection) estimated Taiwan would hold ~60% of advanced-node capacity (16nm and below) by 2027, implying a non-trivial share outside Taiwan by that date -- but this covers all advanced nodes (not strictly <=3nm) and refers to a future projection, not current 2026 operational status.

fact: As of August 2026, all TSMC <=3nm capacity (2nm N2 at ~90,000-100,000 wpm in Fab 20/Fab 22 Taiwan; 3nm at Fab 18 Taiwan) is located in Taiwan. TSMC Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 produces N4 (4nm) only; Phase 2 (N3/3nm) has completed construction but volume production is not targeted until H2 2027. TSMC Kumamoto Fab 2 (3nm) targets 2028. Zero operational <=3nm wafer capacity exists outside Taiwan. Source: tsmc.com/static/abouttsmcaz (updated ~July 2026); TSMC Q1 2026 earnings call (April 16 2026); TrendForce/Quantumrun June 2026.
rationale: With all 2nm and 3nm production concentrated in Taiwan fabs and overseas <=3nm fabs not entering volume production until 2027-2028 at the earliest, the share of leading-edge capacity outside Taiwan is effectively 0% -- well below the rubric's 10% threshold -- and no operational overseas leading-edge fab exists, satisfying both EXTREME conditions.

fact: FAO Food Price Index averaged 131.1 points in July 2026, up 0.6% MoM from June 2026 (130.3) and 1.0% above July 2025; highest reading since January 2023. Source: FAO official press release, fao.org/newsroom, released 2026-08-07.
rationale: The composite FFPI is rising both MoM (+0.6%) and YoY (+1.0%), placing it in the ELEVATED band; the MoM gain is well below the 3% upper boundary for band 1 and far below the 5% SPIKING threshold, even though sub-components (wheat +5.8%, sugar +6%) individually spiked.

fact: The statutory deadline for federal agencies to issue final GENIUS Act implementing rules was July 18, 2026. As of August 24, 2026, every major implementing rule — OCC (NPRM Feb 25/Mar 2 2026), FDIC (NPRM Apr 7 2026), Treasury/FinCEN/OFAC (NPRMs Apr–Aug 2026) — remains at the proposed/comment stage with no final rules issued. ABA Banking Journal (Aug 2026) states: 'Congress gave federal regulators until July 18, 2026, to finalize the Genius Act\'s implementing rules. That deadline came and went without a coordinated final package.' Tech-Insider (Jul 24 2026) confirms: 'Every major GENIUS implementing rule across the OCC, FDIC, Treasury, FinCEN, and OFAC is still pending finalization.' Sources: ABA Banking Journal (https://bankingjournal.aba.com/2026/08/aba-viewpoint-the-genius-act-rules-are-almost-here-heres-what-banks-should-do/), tech-insider.org (https://tech-insider.org/genius-act-stablecoin-law/), FDIC.gov (https://www.fdic.gov/news/financial-institution-letters/2026/notice-proposed-rulemaking-establish-genius-act), OCC.gov (https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-3.html), Treasury (https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0605).
rationale: The rubric scores 2 = PROBLEMS when the statutory deadline is missed without final rules issued. The July 18, 2026 deadline has passed and all major agency implementing rules (OCC, FDIC, Treasury, FinCEN, OFAC) remain in the proposed/comment stage as of August 24, 2026, with no final rule package published. No court stay or compliance-failure event is documented, but the missed deadline without finalization is unambiguous and meets the rubric's level-2 criterion.

fact: PM Sébastien Lecornu's second minority government (formed 10 Oct 2025) remains incumbent. It survived four no-confidence votes (Oct 16 2025, Jan 14 2026, Feb 2 2026 x2), invoked Article 49.3 on Jan 20 2026 to force the 2026 budget, and the budget passed Feb 2 2026. Sources: France 24 (20 Jan 2026), Al Jazeera (2 Feb 2026), Euronews (23 Jan 2026), Wikipedia Lecornu governments.
rationale: The government is a self-described 'fragile minority' coalition in a hung parliament, surviving via Socialist abstentions and Article 49.3 — the textbook definition of rubric band 1. No confidence vote has been lost, no PM resignation since Oct 6 2025 (resolved by re-appointment), and no snap election has been called, ruling out band 2.

dissent.view: CoreWeave successfully closed a $2.6B loan facility on August 10 2026 and a prior $2B bond was heavily oversubscribed in May 2026, suggesting lenders remain willing to extend GPU-backed credit at scale, which sits in tension with a 50% implied default probability.

fact: CoreWeave's 5-year CDS spread hit ~855 bps on July 29 2026 (implying ~50% cumulative default probability); its $2.6B GPU-backed loan facility closed August 10 2026 only after spreads flexed 125 bps to clear; and the company carries a documented $4.2B refinancing wall on pre-2026 GPU-collateralized debt against sharply depreciated H100 collateral (-70-90% rental rates). PIMCO moved to sell >$14B of Oracle-linked AI data center debt in secondary markets. Sources: TechTimes 2026-07-30, TechTimes 2026-08-03, CoreWeave IR 2026-08-10, Global Data Center Hub 2026-07-08.
rationale: CoreWeave is a named borrower explicitly facing a 2026 refinancing wall with CDS at distressed-borrower levels (855 bps/50% default odds), and AI data center debt is being offloaded at a discount in secondary markets (PIMCO/Oracle-linked paper) — both are rubric-1 triggers. No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or outright failed refinancing has been documented as of 2026-08-24, so rubric-2 is not met.

WTO Trade Tracker (late June 2026) confirms fertilizer-related outbound AIS flows 'remained absent or effectively at zero' even after the mid-June MoU, and CarraGlobe (July 2026) reports the MoU broke down in early July after fresh attacks. ITC/UN News (Aug 2026) records urea exports -83% and ammonia -75% YoY through April.
rationale: The strait is physically rated CLOSED by real-time PortWatch/AIS data (1 transit/day vs 73 baseline), fertilizer/sulfur/ammonia outbound flows are at or near zero per WTO AXSMarine tracking, and Brent at ~$94 provides the required market corroboration - all three rubric conditions for a rating of 2 are met.

dissent.view: straits.live (Aug 23, 2026) characterises the Strait as 'effectively closed to commercial shipping' citing 1 transit on Aug 16 vs ~73/day normal — a rating-2 framing; however this conflicts with Lloyd's List JMIC data showing 73 transits in the full week of Aug 10-16 and U.S. military convoy operations, so rubric caps at 1.

fact: Lloyd's List Intelligence (Aug 19, 2026): 73 transits through Strait of Hormuz in week of Aug 10-16 vs ~138/day pre-conflict; the June 17 MoU expired Aug 17 without agreement, Iran resumed attacks on commercial vessels, U.S. blockade of Iranian ports active, yet non-Iranian traffic continues in both directions under U.S. naval escort. Brent crude ~$94-95/bbl (Trading Economics, Aug 21, 2026), elevated ~39% YoY but well below the April 30 closure-panic peak of $120.88. Red Sea: Houthi naval blockade of Saudi shipping declared July 20; Bab el-Mandeb transits down ~40% with lethal attacks ongoing (CNBC/CFR, Aug 12, 2026).
rationale: Hormuz traffic is severely suppressed (~7% of pre-crisis daily rate) with active attacks and a blockade — well under 25% — but U.S. naval-escorted convoys continue moving non-Iranian cargo and Brent at ~$95 is elevated but not at the April closure-panic peak of $121, which the rubric requires to confirm a '2'. Both corridors are therefore CONTESTED (1): physically threatened, partially disrupted, moving under naval escort, with no functioning ceasefire or MoU in force.

rationale: Multiple corroborating price-signal sources (Argus/Reuters, Benchmark, RareEarthExchanges, S&P Global Platts) place the heavy rare earth ex-China premium in the 4–5x range for the primary magnet HREEs (dysprosium, terbium) as of mid-to-late 2026, anchored by actual transaction data and export volume declines (~50% shipping drop per Chinese customs); best single estimate is ~4.5x as the central tendency across sources, consistent with the volume signal confirming genuine supply bifurcation rather than a paper premium.

dissent.view: insurance.com May 2026 survey finds only 7% of homeowners experienced cancellation/non-renewal and only 2-3% cited insurer market exit as the cause, suggesting the consumer-level impact remains modest and contained

fact: NAIC July 31 2026 report (MCAS 2018-2024, 715 carriers) finds company-initiated non-renewal rates up 96%-216% across all four US regions; Climate Cosmos (June 2026) names 13 states with active non-renewal waves (CA, FL, TX, LA, CO, GA, OK, and others); NAIC simultaneously characterises the market as 'operationally strong overall' with improved 2024 underwriting results. Florida Citizens fell to ~385k policies by Jan 2026 (lowest since 2012), signalling partial stabilisation. No top-10 insurer confirmed fully exiting a major state in 2026. Source: NAIC CIPR report Aug 5 2026 (content.naic.org); CNBC Aug 6 2026; Climate Cosmos June 18 2026.
rationale: Thirteen states with documented non-renewal waves places the indicator firmly in the 5-15 state band of the rubric; the NAIC confirms multi-regional acceleration, but improved 2024 underwriting and Citizens depopulation signal partial stabilisation, and no top-10 insurer has fully exited a major state, so the level-2 triggers are not met.

dissent.view: 45 months: median time from interconnection request to signed interconnection agreement (not full COD) in 2025, per LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition - a partial-process metric

fact: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition (emp.lbl.gov/queues, June 2026): 'the median duration from IR to COD was over 5 years for projects built in 2025' - separately quantified as 61 months by the same dataset (Axis Intelligence citing LBNL 2026 Edition). A separate sub-metric of 45 months covers only the IR-to-signed-IA step.
rationale: The rubric asks for the latest LBNL median queue wait in months; the headline IR-to-COD median of 61 months for projects reaching commercial operation in 2025 is the primary published figure from LBNL's Queued Up 2026 Edition, mapping directly to the indicator. The 45-month figure is a partial measure (IR to interconnection agreement only) and understates the full queue duration.

dissent.view: MERICS (undated 2025/2026) notes a MOFCOM 'green channel' and EU whitelist have allowed magnet exports to the EU to pick up since May 2025, suggesting some easing for civilian buyers; this could be read as partial normalisation toward level 0 for EU-bound civilian flows.
Rare Earth Exchanges (Apr 2026) cites licensing approval rates below 25% for European firms, which some analysts characterise as functionally approaching level 2 for certain end-users or sectors.

fact: The April 2025 rare-earth magnet licensing regime (covering dysprosium, terbium and magnets containing them) is fully in force and was never suspended. MOFCOM's statutory target is 45 working days (~9 weeks), but industry reporting (GetTransport/Duramag, July 2026) shows heavy-REE magnet approvals routinely run 60-120+ days. General licences exist but are limited to a small whitelist of pre-cleared Chinese exporters (first batch: JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng, Dec 2025); the scheme 'is not broadly available yet.' In June 2026 China added 10 US firms to its export control list (Morgan Lewis, July 1 2026), and Trump threatened 200% tariffs in August 2026 over continued supply delays (China Briefing, Aug 2026). The 2026 licensing catalogue added samarium, gadolinium and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories (Certivo, Mar 2026). No categorical denial or suspension of licensing has been announced.
rationale: The regime is case-by-case for most shippers (general licences confined to a narrow whitelist), processing times structurally exceed 30 days (60-120 days in practice), and new categories were added to the control list within the trailing 3 months — all squarely within rubric level 1 (SLOWING). No announced categorical denial or licensing suspension exists to justify level 2. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]

rationale: Both rubric-1 triggers are met: (a) fewer than 90 days remain to the Nov 10, 2026 nominal expiry with no announced renewal, and (b) China's June 22, 2026 entity-list additions of MP Materials and USA Rare Earth constitute a partial breach. Score 2 is not warranted because the broad suspension is still formally operative and market signals (muted equity reaction, analysts calling the listings 'largely symbolic') do not corroborate full collapse.

dissent.view: India cannot fully block Indus flows to Pakistan due to infrastructure limits; actual diversion is temporary and partial, not a permanent cut-off — CSIS argues the treaty suspension is legally contested but physical interdiction capacity is limited
On the Nile/GERD front, diplomacy is 'frozen' but no armed clash has occurred; GERD dispute rates TENSE (1) in isolation — New Arab, March 2026

fact: India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty in April 2025 and physically cut Chenab flows via the Baglihar Dam (May 2025). On Aug 31 2026, a Permanent Court of Arbitration panel ruled the treaty 'remains fully in force' and India's abeyance 'not permissible'; India rejected the ruling on Sept 1 2026 (Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, CNBC, Sept 1-3 2026). Pakistan's defence minister warned in June 2026 that water security could trigger war. Pakistan has logged 'abnormal, abrupt flow variations on the Chenab' (CNBC, June 22 2026).
rationale: A deliberate flow cut-off was physically carried out (Baglihar Dam, May 2025), the 65-year treaty remains formally suspended/rejected despite an international tribunal ruling it still binding, and a cabinet-level war threat tied directly to dam/river management was issued in June 2026 — all three rubric-2 triggers are met for the Indus dispute.

dissent.view: Some secondary sources (watcher.guru, informedclearly.com) claim BRICS Pay has 'gone live' and reduced USD intra-bloc trade by two-thirds, implying closer to operational action; but higher-authority sourcing (economy.com.pk, RBI statements) characterises this as technical integration still targeting the summit for full deployment, not a completed operational switch by a major economy.

BRICS Pay operational deployment and 'The Unit' sandbox constitute new non-dollar settlement system launches/agreements with official backing, placing the indicator firmly at score 1 (TALK/early launch).

dissent.view: Some secondary sources cite 2,600 GW in total U.S. queues as of early 2026, likely combining generation, storage, and large-load requests across all queue types, versus LBNL's more conservative 1,312 GW generation + 749 GW storage figure based on ISO/RTO filings through end-2025.

fact: As of end-2025/early-2026, U.S. interconnection queues held ~1,312 GW of generation + ~749 GW of storage across ~8,200 active projects (LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition, emp.lbl.gov, data through end-2025); ERCOT alone received 198 GW of large-load applications in Q1 2026, with data centers comprising ~87% of ERCOT's 410 GW large-load queue; interconnection wait times in the busiest U.S. markets run 4-7 years. FERC on 18 June 2026 issued emergency orders to all six regional grid operators to accelerate large-load interconnection, explicitly citing unprecedented data-center-driven demand backlogs. No confirmed forced curtailment of data-center load or declared grid emergency has been reported.
rationale: Queues are massive, lengthening, and causing multi-year project delays for power - squarely matching rubric band 1 (TIGHT). FERC's June 2026 emergency action confirms the severity, but the absence of any confirmed curtailment of data-center load or a declared grid emergency prevents escalation to band 2 (ACUTE).

dissent.view: Google Cloud alone grew 82% YoY in Q2 2026, which exceeds the ~77% aggregate capex growth rate, suggesting the gap may be CLOSING for Alphabet specifically; Alphabet also raised capex ceiling to $205B at Q2 earnings, partially offsetting this.

Pre-Q2 analysis (July 20 2026) flagged that 'the buildout is accelerating faster than the monetisation curve' and cited Moody's May 2026 credit-risk warning if AI profit growth fails to materialise, a more bearish framing closer to level 2.

fact: Q2 2026 actuals: Google Cloud +82% YoY to $24.8B (accelerating from +63% in Q1), AWS +37% YoY to $42.2B (accelerating from +28% in Q1), Azure +43% YoY. Sources: company Q2 2026 earnings releases; Synergy Research Q2 2026; uncoveralpha.com (Aug 3 2026); fourweekmba.com (Jul 31 2026).
rationale: Capex growth (~77% YoY aggregate) exceeds AI-cloud revenue growth for AWS (+37%) and Azure (+43%), keeping the monetization gap WIDE. However, all three hyperscalers show QoQ acceleration in AI-revenue (Google Cloud 63%->82%, AWS 28%->37%), ruling out level 2 (WIDENING FAST), which requires deceleration or an outlook cut.

Sources: Swiss Re Institute (Aug 2026), Munich Re H1 nat cat report (Jul 30 2026), Aon Global Cat Recap H1 2026 (Jul 22 2026), Gallagher Re H1 2026 Nat Cat Report (Jul 2026).
rationale: H1 2026 YTD insured losses are well below the 10-year average across all three primary sources, and no single event has crossed the $10bn insured-loss threshold; both rubric conditions for ELEVATED (score=1) are unmet. Hurricane season remains subdued under El Nino and no Q3 event >$10bn has been reported, keeping the indicator at NORMAL (score=0).

dissent.view: Maine's legislature passed a moratorium in April 2026, which would have been the first statewide enactment, but Gov. Janet Mills vetoed it — so Maine does not count as enacted.

fact: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed Executive Order 62 on July 14, 2026, creating the nation's first statewide data center moratorium — pausing state environmental permits for data centers ≥50 MW for up to one year (governor.ny.gov, July 14, 2026). Additionally, Texas Governor Abbott ordered a statewide grid audit in August 2026 effectively pausing new projects (multistate.us, Aug 19, 2026). DLA Piper (July 1, 2026) counts 56 public actions across 25 states and 100+ local moratoria enacted nationwide.
rationale: The rubric's Level 2 threshold requires 'a statewide moratorium enacted OR >10 jurisdictions with enacted pauses/cancellations.' New York's signed executive order alone clears the statewide bar; the 100+ local moratoria across 25 states independently clears the >10-jurisdiction bar. Both conditions are met simultaneously with confirmed physical permit blockages.

dissent.view: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index (count-based, senior secured/unitranche only) reported 2.51% for Q2 2026 across 716 loans representing $195.6B — roughly 3.8 points below Fitch's inclusive rate
Moody's estimated 2025 private credit headline default rates of 1.6%–4.7% excluding distressed exchanges, with distressed restructurings accounting for ~65% of all 2025 private credit defaults
IMF April 2026 Global Financial Stability Report described private credit default rates in the 2–3% range as 'manageable in magnitude'

Source: https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-14/us-private-credit-default-rate-hits-a-record-of-6-3-fitch-says
rationale: Fitch's inclusive TTM measure (counting distressed exchanges and maturity extensions) printed 6.3% for August 2026, eclipsing the prior record of 6.1% in July and the April 2026 record of 6.0%; this is the mandated anchor per the rubric and no anchor switch is required as a fresh Fitch print is available. The rate trajectory (5.6% Dec-2025 → 5.8% Jan → 6.0% Apr → 6.1% Jul → 6.3% Aug) signals sustained and accelerating credit deterioration in private direct lending, consistent with elevated PIK income at BDCs and maturity-extension-dominated default events.

rationale: D3 (Extreme Drought) covering ~30% of New Mexico meets the rubric's ACUTE threshold of 'extreme/exceptional (D3-D4)' for a named chip/agri hub in the US Southwest; the Taiwan signal is warning-level only (TSMC CEO comments, no confirmed curtailment) so the US Southwest D3 reading is the load-bearing trigger.

dissent.view: MATCH Act is still a bill, not a final BIS rule — no new Federal Register export control measure was issued specifically in June-Sept 2026, which could support rating of 1 (TIGHTENING) rather than 2 if China's April 2026 supply-chain regulations are deemed pre-period or non-semiconductor-specific
ASML CFO downplayed rare-earth control impact and China revenue remained ~20% of 2026 sales, suggesting market signals do not fully corroborate a severe disruption at level 2

rationale: Both sides have enacted or sustained formal measures in the trailing window: the US legislative MATCH Act escalation targeting ASML DUV/servicing plus executive-branch pressure on ASML (TIGHTENING), and China's April 2026 supply-chain security regulations plus rare-earth export controls constitute documented formal countermeasures (RETALIATION), satisfying rubric level 2. Confidence is medium rather than high because the MATCH Act has not yet been enacted into law and no new BIS Federal Register rule issued in the strict trailing 3-month window was found.

dissent.view: TSMC CEO CC Wei stated in July 2025 Q2 earnings that TSMC aims to produce '30% of high-end chips in the US' via Arizona build-out — interpreted by some as near-term diversification underway; however this is a multi-year target (~2030) for planned capacity, not current operational output.

fact: As of Q3 2026, TSMC's entire <=3nm capacity (~260,000+ wpm combined 2nm+3nm) is in Taiwan. Arizona Fab 21 Phase 1 runs 4nm; Phase 2 (3nm) began equipment installation July-Sept 2026 targeting 2H 2027 volume production. Japan Kumamoto Phase 2 (3nm) targets 2028. TSMC 2025 Annual Report (investor.tsmc.com) confirms 2nm ramping 'at both Hsinchu and Kaohsiung sites in Taiwan'; TrendForce/TechTimes (Aug 8 2026) puts combined 2nm+3nm at ~260,000 wpm in Q4 2026, all Taiwan. ~0% of operational <=3nm capacity is outside Taiwan.
rationale: Zero operational overseas <=3nm fab exists today and offshore share is effectively 0%, well below the <10% threshold; this maps unambiguously to rubric level 2 (EXTREME). The only overseas <=3nm fabs (Arizona Phase 2, Kumamoto Phase 2) are in equipment-install or construction phase with volume production 1-2 years away.

fact: FAO FFPI averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, up 1.9% MoM from revised July level of 130.8 and +2.5% YoY, reaching its highest level since late 2022. Source: FAO newsroom (fao.org), released 4 September 2026.
rationale: Index is rising and at a multi-year high, but the MoM gain (+1.9%) is below the 3% upper bound for Band 1; the 3-month rise (~May 130.7 to Aug 133.3, ~+2%) is far below the 10% SPIKING threshold. Rubric maps squarely to ELEVATED (1).

dissent.view: Equable Institute 'State of Pensions 2026' projects the national funded ratio at 85.0% for FY2026 (actuarial basis, 253 plans, best level since 2009)
NASRA median funded ratio approximately 73-75% for 2024-2025 (median across all public plans, broader universe, actuarial basis)

Equable's FY2026 actuarial projection of 85.0% and NASRA median of ~73-75% are alternative measures on different methodological bases but are less current.

dissent.view: Paradigm and Chapman & Cutler note agencies face 'no formal penalties' for missing the rulemaking deadline and the GENIUS Act still takes effect January 18, 2027 via the 18-month backstop, suggesting operational continuity rather than a crisis scenario.
Astraea Counsel characterizes the missed deadline as a rulemaking slip, not an Act-effectiveness failure, since the January 18, 2027 statutory backstop remains intact.

fact: The GENIUS Act Section 13 statutory rulemaking deadline was July 18, 2026. rationale: The regime is case-by-case per shipment for most exporters, general licences are whitelisted to named producers only (not broadly available), processing times routinely exceed 30 days (60–120 days observed), and new categories (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium compounds) were added to the control list within the trailing 3 months of the Jan 2026 catalogue update — all three rubric triggers for Score 1 (SLOWING) are met. dissent.view: Some sources (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) characterise BRICS Pay as already 'operational' and claim intra-bloc local-currency trade has surpassed 67%, suggesting a more advanced de-dollarisation that could edge toward ACTION; however these are non-primary, speculative outlets and the New Delhi Declaration language and RBI/EBC reporting confirm BRICS Pay remains a payment messaging layer, not a reserve settlement system replacement.

fact: At the 18th BRICS Summit (New Delhi, 12-13 Sep 2026), leaders adopted the New Delhi Declaration formally endorsing BRICS Pay - 'a decentralized payment messaging ecosystem designed to route cross-border transactions through national systems rather than the dollar-denominated SWIFT network' - and addressed the gold-backed BRICS Unit token pilot; crucially, 'BRICS Pay is not a currency and does not replace the dollar as a reserve asset' (Eastern Herald, 12 Sep 2026). No new sovereign reserve seizure occurred: Russian assets remain frozen under the pre-existing 2022 G7/EU freeze, with EU permanent-seizure proposals still debated but not enacted as of Sep 2026 (Brookings, Jun 2025; CFR, Nov 2025).
rationale: The formal adoption of BRICS Pay at the New Delhi Declaration (Sep 12, 2026) and the BRICS Unit pilot constitute new non-dollar settlement agreements and launches, squarely mapping to rubric level 1 (TALK/agreements). No new sovereign reserve freeze or operationally transformative reserve settlement shift by a major economy has been confirmed, so the evidence does not reach level 2.

dissent.view: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition reports a 10% decrease in total active U.S. queue volume year-over-year (end-2025: ~2,061 GW generation+storage), suggesting some queue relief relative to peak; FERC June 2026 orders are explicitly aimed at 'significantly shortening the multi-year interconnection queue backlog', implying easing is a policy goal, not yet a measured outcome.

fact: The DOE invoked Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act three times in 2026 within PJM — in January (cold snap), May 18 (heat/maintenance squeeze), and a third time by early July — each time authorising PJM to curtail data-center and large-load facilities that have backup generation as a last resort before rolling blackouts. Source: Utility Dive (May 19, 2026, https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-doe-emergency-order-curtail-data-centers/820571/) and TechTimes (July 4, 2026, https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319678/20260704/ai-data-centers-trigger-third-federal-grid-emergency-sending-bills-up-air-quality-down.htm).
rationale: Three confirmed Section 202(c) emergency orders authorising curtailment of data-center load within PJM in 2026 meet the rubric's top band — 'confirmed curtailment of data-center load' and 'declared grid emergency'. ERCOT (474 GW queue, Governor-ordered audit/pause) and global IEA data (2,500+ GW stalled in queues, rising congestion-related curtailment) corroborate structural tightness, but the PJM curtailment orders are the dispositive physical event that pushes the rating to 2 rather than 1. dissent.view: Sequoia (David Cahn, 2025 estimate still cited as of mid-2026) estimated a ~$600B annual gap between AI infrastructure spend and AI ecosystem revenue — broader than just hyperscaler cloud, suggesting the macro monetisation gap is larger than cloud revenue growth alone implies

Moody's May 2026 forecast revision flagged credit risk if 'strong profit growth from AI investments fails to materialise,' a more cautious read implying potential Score 2 trajectory if depreciation lands 2027-28

fact: Q2 CY2026 earnings (SEC 8-K Alphabet July 22 2026; Amazon/FourWeekMBA July 31 2026): Google Cloud +82% YoY to $24.8B, AWS +37% to $42.2B, Azure +43% constant-currency — aggregate hyperscaler cloud/AI revenue growth ~48% YoY, accelerating from ~39% in Q1. Simultaneously, combined 2026 capex guidance was raised again post-Q2 to ~$775–800B (up ~77–84% YoY from ~$413B in 2025); Amazon Q2 quarterly capex alone was $54.2B, Alphabet $44.9B. Capex growth (~77-84%) materially exceeds AI-revenue growth (~48%).
rationale: Capex growth (~77-84% YoY) clearly outpaces AI-attributable cloud revenue growth (~48% YoY), ruling out Score 0. However, AI-revenue growth accelerated QoQ (39% in Q1 to 48% in Q2) and all hyperscalers describe themselves as supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained, ruling out Score 2; this is the canonical Score 1 configuration.

dissent.view: BTIG Research (Aug 21, 2026) flagged Affirm ABS 2025-X2 vintage 30-59 DPD at all-time highs at 9 and 16 months of age, suggesting deterioration in newer cohorts that may not yet be fully reflected in reported portfolio-level delinquency

fact: Affirm 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans (ex-Peloton, ex-Pay-in-X) was 2.5% in Q4 FY2026 (ended June 30, 2026), improving from 2.7%-2.8% over the prior three quarters; Q2 FY2026 filing reported 30+ DPD up +18 bps YoY at 2.7%. FY2026 delinquency curve tracked slightly above FY2025. Industry BNPL charge-off rate ~1.83% per CFPB Dec-2025 report (latest official figure). Source: Affirm Q4 FY2026 IR release (investors.affirm.com, Aug 27 2026); Affirm Q2 FY2026 shareholder letter (Feb 2026); Richmond Fed EB-26-05 (Feb 2026).
rationale: 30+ DPD is modestly up YoY (+18 bps per Q2 FY2026 filing) and the FY2026 curve sits slightly above FY2025, satisfying 'late-payment/delinquency up YoY'; however charge-offs remain ~1.8%-2%, well below the 3% ceiling for rating=1 and far below the 5% spike threshold for rating=2. The +18 bps YoY rise is also well short of the >100 bps needed for rating=2.

dissent.view: No source explicitly confirms PEACE cable remains unrepaired as of Sept 22, 2026; the July 27 DCD article is the last authoritative update and the repair window could have accelerated
Hormuz cable threats (Iran, Sept 2026) are credible but no physical cut has been confirmed in that strait, supporting a possible read of level 1 for Hormuz specifically

fact: The PEACE subsea cable was cut in the Red Sea (~1,450 km from Zafarnaat, Egypt); Data Center Dynamics (July 27, 2026) reported the repair 'expected to take several months' with no subsequent restoration confirmed. Iran issued regulatory/severance threats against Hormuz cables (May-Sept 2026, Asia Times Sept 16 2026) and two suspicious cable faults occurred off Perth, Australia (Aug 8-9, 2026, specialeurasia.com).
rationale: The PEACE cable in the Red Sea appears severed and unrepaired as of late September 2026 — a 'several months' repair timeline from a late-July 2026 cut has not elapsed — satisfying rubric level 2 (>=1 major cable currently severed and unrepaired causing connectivity loss). The Hormuz threat signals and Perth faults add corroboration that the environment is elevated, but the load-bearing fact is the unrepaired PEACE cable cut.

fact: Global insured catastrophe losses reached ~$42-47bn in H1 2026 (Swiss Re: $42bn, 16% below 10-year average; Munich Re: $44bn, below 10-year H1 average of $50bn; Aon: $47bn), with no single event exceeding $10bn. The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is 'extremely inactive' as of September 2026 with no hurricane formed through Sept 11 (the latest first-hurricane date in the satellite era), driven by a strong El Nino. Sources: Swiss Re Institute H1 2026 sigma (Aug 2026), Munich Re H1 2026 nat cat report (Jul 30 2026), Aon H1 2026 Global Cat Recap (Jul 22 2026), Wikipedia 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.
rationale: YTD global insured losses of ~$42-47bn are below - not above - the 10-year H1 average of ~$50bn, and no single event has crossed the $10bn threshold; the hurricane season is historically quiet under El Nino suppression with zero hurricane formations through mid-September. Both rubric triggers for score 1 (YTD above average OR single event >$10bn) are absent, placing the indicator firmly at 0 (NORMAL).

fact: As of early September 2026, China expanded its 2026 urea export allowance to roughly 5-5.5 million tonnes (up from an initial 3.3Mt cap) and July shipments surged to ~403,000t from just 7,000t in June; phosphate export curbs (DAP, MAP, certain NPK) imposed since mid-March 2026 were extended at least through August 2026 per NDRC guidance reported by S&P Global/Platts (Dec 2025) and confirmed by FertilizerDaily (July 29, 2026). A quota-and-suspension regime on urea and phosphate thus remains active, with no confirmed full lift as of the assessment date. Sources: FertilizerDaily 2026-09-09 (urea $443/t, China shipments surge); FertilizerDaily 2026-07-29 (phosphate curbs through Aug 2026); S&P Global/Platts 2026-03-04 (NDRC phosphate suspension).
rationale: Existing urea quotas and phosphate suspensions remain operative structures (rubric band 1); the March 2026 expansion to NK blends/phosphates was a tightening but falls outside the trailing 3-month window (pre-June 22), and within that window China actually loosened the urea component (expanded allowance, surging July shipments), precluding band 2.

fact: China PPI year-on-year for August 2026 = +3.8%, as published by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on 9 September 2026. CNBC: 'The producer price index increased 3.8%, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday, exceeding economists forecast for a 3.6% gain.' People's Daily / NBS confirmed the same figure; NBS statistician Dong Lijuan cited imported commodity price pressures and high-tech demand as drivers.
rationale: The rubric requires the signed NBS figure: +3.8% for August 2026, released 2026-09-09. This is a meaningfully positive reading—well above zero—signalling cost-push input-price pressure that can export inflationary spillovers to China's trading partners; the engine scores on magnitude, not sign.

fact: SEC Final Rule 34-102487 (Feb 25, 2025) granted a one-year extension of compliance dates to Dec 31, 2026 (cash) and Jun 30, 2027 (repo); additionally, on Apr 17, 2026, the SEC published SIFMA's exemptive-relief request for an expanded inter-affiliate exemption (SEC Release 34-105262). No second extension has been announced as of Sep 2026. Source: sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-43; sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/uyeda-update-sec-work-toward-treasury-clearing-implementation-042026; Treasury TBAC Charge Q2 2026 (May 2026).
rationale: The rubric scores 1 when 'an official extension [has been] granted OR exemptive-relief requests [are] pending.' Both conditions are satisfied: the SEC formally extended deadlines one year in Feb 2025, and SIFMA's inter-affiliate exemptive-relief request was pending as of Apr 2026. A second extension (score=2) has not been announced, and a DTCC July 2026 survey shows 79% of firms have required account structures—above the <60% readiness threshold—so the most severe rubric level is not warranted.

fact: Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate hit an all-time high of 11.76% in October 2025, per CommercialSearch/Trepp tracker (commercialsearch.com, 'the office sector soared 63 basis points in October to set a new all-time high of 11.76 percent'). KBRA data for Jan-Feb 2026 shows office delinquency rising further to 12.8–13.9%, suggesting the Trepp figure has likely also climbed, but absent a confirmed 2026 Trepp office print, 11.76% is the anchor with medium confidence. Jurisdictions with enacted actions include: New York (statewide EO), Woodford County KY, Manatee County FL, Statesville NC, Clarendon County SC, Lima OH, McDonald Village OH, Foley AL, Woodburn OR, Marysville KS, North Little Rock AR, multiple Georgia counties, Fort Worth TX, Nashville-Davidson TN, and others.

The sequential rise from 6.0% (Apr/May) → 6.1% (Jul) → 6.3% (Aug) confirms the stress signal is intensifying, corroborated by rising PIK income at BDCs and elevated liability-management-exercise activity dominating default events.

dissent.view: East Asia Forum (Mar 2026) argued the Trump White House was 'downplaying chip controls' and approving higher-tier chip exports to China, suggesting a de-escalation rather than escalation dynamic through Q1 2026 — though subsequent June BIS guidance and MATCH Act momentum reversed that reading by Q3 2026.

fact: Within the trailing 3 months: (1) US-side: BIS issued June 1 2026 guidance affirming chip export restrictions extend to Chinese firms' overseas subsidiaries (Al Jazeera, 1 Jun 2026); MATCH Act (introduced Apr 2 2026) advancing in Congress with Senate version in parallel, targeting DUV immersion lithography and servicing bans. China also escalated rare-earth export controls in June-July 2026 targeting EU/US chip-supply chains (Tech-Insider, Sep 2026).
rationale: Both sides have enacted new measures in the trailing 3 months: the US tightened via BIS guidance (June 2026) and the MATCH Act legislative push, while China enacted two formal counter-control regulations (Order 834 and Extraterritorial Jurisdiction rules) plus rare-earth escalation, satisfying rubric level 2 (RETALIATION). US-side measures: BIS June 2026 subsidiary guidance, MATCH Act advancing. China-side measures: Order 834 (Apr 2026), Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Regulation (Apr 2026), rare-earth export control escalation (Jun-Jul 2026).

dissent.view: TrendForce (Mar 2026) projects sub-2nm capacity mix reaching ~70% Taiwan / 30% US by 2030, which would push the indicator toward '1-HIGH' on a forward-looking basis, but this is a multi-year projection, not a current operational fact.

Arizona Fab 21 Phase 2 (3nm) has completed construction and begun equipment installation in Q3 2026 but volume production is not until 2H 2027; Japan JASM Fab 2 (3nm) is not until 2028. The operational Kumamoto Fab 1 runs 12-28nm only. Source: TSMC Q1 2026 earnings call (CC Wei, April 16 2026) via TrendForce/mlq.ai; tsmc.com Arizona page (July 2026); TechTimes Aug 8 2026; TrendForce Sept 14 2026.
rationale: Zero percent of TSMC's operational <=3nm capacity is outside Taiwan today, satisfying the rubric's EXTREME threshold of '<10% outside Taiwan AND no operational overseas leading-edge fab.' The Arizona 4nm fab (Phase 1) does not qualify as <=3nm, and both overseas 3nm fabs remain pre-production.

fact: FAO FFPI averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, up 1.9% MoM from revised July level of ~130.8 and up 2.5% YoY; highest since late 2022. Source: FAO newsroom, fao.org, released 4 September 2026.

A dissenting lower median (~73-75%) from NASRA/actuarial valuations reflects older measurement-date liability snapshots and plan-reported actuarial assumptions rather than current market values.

dissent.view: Some analysts characterise the miss as operationally inconsequential because the GENIUS Act still takes effect January 18, 2027 regardless, and agencies continue rulemaking—implying a 'gaps' rather than 'problems' framing.

fact: The GENIUS Act statutory deadline for final implementing rules was July 18, 2026. As of that date—and confirmed through at least September 2026—zero final rules had been issued by any of the six mandated agencies (OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, NCUA, Treasury/FinCEN/OFAC). All ten rule packages published during the first year remained in proposed/comment form. The OCC targets finalization by November 2026. Source: OCC Bulletin 2026-3 (occ.gov, Feb 25 2026); Federal Register FDIC NPRM (Apr 10 2026); Federal Register Treasury NPRM (Aug 18 2026, comments due Oct 19 2026); Crowdfund Insider (Jul 19 2026); crypto.news (Aug 2026).
rationale: The rubric's level-2 condition is met without ambiguity: the statutory July 18, 2026 deadline passed with zero final rules in place across all required agencies, matching 'deadline missed without final rules.' No court stay or compliance-failure event is needed; the missed deadline alone satisfies the criterion.

fact: The Second Lecornu government (formed 10 Oct 2025) is the incumbent minority coalition government of France. On 23 Jan 2026, PM Lecornu invoked Article 49.3 to pass the revenue section of the 2026 budget without a vote; two subsequent no-confidence motions (LFI: 269 votes, RN: fewer) both failed to reach the 288-vote threshold, saved by Socialist and conservative abstentions. The budget was formally adopted ~2 Feb 2026. Government remains in office as a minority. Sources: Wikipedia/Second Lecornu government; Euronews 23 Jan 2026; Al Jazeera 2 Feb 2026; Stratfor/RANE 23 Jan 2026.
rationale: France has a minority/hung parliament (no party holds an absolute majority since the 2024 snap election); the government explicitly relied on Article 49.3 and survived multiple no-confidence votes in Jan-Feb 2026, the textbook definition of Rubric 1 (FRAGILE). No dissolution or government collapse has occurred since Oct 2025.

dissent.view: CoreWeave completed its $8.5B DDTL-4.0 facility (March 2026) and a $3.1B deal in Q3, suggesting lenders are still extending GPU-backed credit at scale despite CDS distress signals - some analysts read this as functioning, not stressed, refinancing.

fact: As of July-August 2026: (1) JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and SMBC spent 6+ months attempting to distribute ~$38B in Oracle-linked data-center construction debt, with some banks selling portions at a discount (TechNewsday/ResultSense, May 6 2026); (2) CoreWeave (Nasdaq: CRWV) CDS hit ~855 bps on July 29 2026, implying ~50% five-year default probability, while its $2.6B leveraged loan required improved terms to clear (metirai.com/TechTimes, July 29-Aug 2 2026). No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing has been reported.
rationale: Banks are actively offloading AI/data-center-backed debt at a discount and CoreWeave - a named GPU-backed borrower with $35B debt as of Q2 2026 - is facing a documented refinancing wall with CDS pricing at deeply distressed levels; these are textbook Level 1 SIGNS. However, no deal has actually failed or defaulted, so Level 2 is not warranted.

dissent.view: Some oil-product shipments are occurring at ~1 million b/d (vs ~4 million b/d pre-war), suggesting the strait is 'contested' rather than fully sealed for all cargoes; naval escort convoys move sporadically

fact: Strait of Hormuz effectively closed to commercial shipping as of 21 Sep 2026; IMF PortWatch recorded 8 transits on 2026-09-13 vs. ~85/day pre-crisis baseline (straits.live); WTO-AXSMarine data show fertilizer shipments (sulfur, ammonia, urea) through the strait 'near zero' in early Sep 2026 (ukragroconsult.com, ~2026-09-15); Gulf elemental sulfur exports collapsed to 147,000 MT in June vs. 11-year floor of 730,000 MT (IFPRI, ~2026-09-18); Brent crude at ~$99-104/bbl mid-to-late Sep 2026, well above pre-war levels (straits.live, 2026-09-17/19).
rationale: The strait is independently confirmed CLOSED at ~9% of baseline vessel traffic with active ship attacks, no ceasefire, and Brent crude elevated above $99/bbl - satisfying both the physical closure test and the required corroborating price-signal condition. Fertilizer/sulfur/ammonia input flows are confirmed near zero, consistent with the CLOSED rubric rating of 2.

dissent.view: Strait 'effectively closed to commercial shipping as of 21 September 2026' with only 8 transits vs 85/day — a rating-2 characterisation
Strait 'effectively closed to routine commercial shipping as of 30 July 2026' with major carriers suspended

fact: IMF PortWatch recorded 8 transits on 2026-09-13 vs. ~85/day pre-crisis baseline (~9.4% of normal); Brent crude ~$95-107/bbl; US CENTCOM naval escort convoys moving Saudi crude at 2.9 mb/d via Hormuz; Trump signalled openness to Iran diplomacy at UNGA on 2026-09-22 — no new ceasefire in force but active de-escalation talks underway. Sources: straits.live (IMF PortWatch data, 2026-09-21); Al Jazeera/TradingEconomics (2026-09-14/21); OilPrice.com/JP Morgan (2026-09-21).
rationale: Transit is at ~9% of normal with Brent well above $95, confirming severe disruption consistent with a rating-2 read on volumes alone; however, US-led naval escort convoys are physically moving Saudi barrels through Hormuz and active US-Iran diplomacy is underway at UNGA, both of which the rubric explicitly uses to cap the score at 1 (CONTESTED) rather than 2 (CLOSED).

dissent.view: Terbium oxide Rotterdam-to-FOB-China multiple is ~3.8x per same Fastmarkets Aug 27 2026 assessment, lower than dysprosium's 4.9x due to terbium's higher Chinese domestic price base

Rare Earth Exchanges (Sep 21 2026) cites dysprosium up to $3,250/kg in North America vs. $212–218/kg China domestic, implying up to ~15x for North America spot; terbium up to $7,500/kg vs. ~$997/kg, ~7.5x — but flags these as thin OTC references, not liquid benchmarks

Argus data cited by Reuters/Oregon Group (Jun 2026) puts dysprosium and terbium outside China at x4 to x5 vs. China domestic

fact: Fastmarkets weekly assessed dysprosium oxide 99.5% ex-whs Rotterdam: $1,250–1,675/kg on Aug 27 2026, vs. $270–330/kg fob China — a ratio of ~4.9x; terbium oxide ex-whs Rotterdam $4,200–5,000/kg vs. $1,180–1,270/kg fob China — ~3.8x. Source: https://www.fastmarkets.com/insights/chinas-looming-november-export-controls-test-rare-earth-refining-recycling-ambitions/ (published ~Sep 8 2026).
rationale: Rubric asks for the ex-China HREE price premium as a multiple of China price; Fastmarkets' Aug 27 2026 assessed spread yields 4.9x for dysprosium (the primary volume HREE benchmark), which is the most authoritative primary-source reading available and sits within the corroborating 4–5x range from Argus/Reuters and Benchmark Minerals.
