dissent.view: NAIC Aug 2026 report says market 'remains operationally strong overall, with broad insurer participation and improved underwriting results in 2024,' suggesting stress is elevated but not systemic/accelerating.

Climate Cosmos (June 2026) counted 13 named states with active insurer non-renewal waves, which approaches the upper end of the RISING band and could support a score of 2 if additional state-level exits materialize in H2 2026.

fact: NAIC's Aug 5, 2026 first-of-its-kind national report ('Examining Homeowner Property Insurance Market Dynamics: An Assessment of Countrywide State-Level Data From 2018 to 2024') found insurer-initiated nonrenewal rates surged 96%-216% across all four US regions (Southeast, Northeast, Midwest, West) since 2018; Florida non-renewed 3.35% of policies in 2024 (highest in nation), California 3.18%; non-renewal/market-exit stress documented across CA, FL, LA, CO, TX, GA, OK, MN and others — a third-party tally (Climate Cosmos, June 2026) cited 13 named states with active non-renewal waves. NAIC, content.naic.org, Aug 5, 2026.
rationale: The NAIC data and corroborating sources confirm elevated non-renewal waves spanning well more than 5 states (credibly 10-15+ named states) across all four US regions, but the NAIC simultaneously characterizes the market as 'operationally strong overall with broad insurer participation and improved underwriting results in 2024,' and no single top-10 insurer has executed a full state-market exit in 2026 — placing the indicator squarely in the RISING band (5-15 states, some markets stabilizing).

dissent.view: Median IR-to-signed-interconnection-agreement (a sub-phase metric) was 45 months in 2025 per the same LBNL 2026 report — a lower figure that could be cited if the rubric is interpreted as queue-study phase only, not full IR-to-COD.

fact: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition (emp.lbl.gov/queues, published June 2026, data through end-2025): 'the median duration from IR to COD was over 5 years for projects built in 2025' — independently quantified as 61 months by the same source (up from 36 months in 2015 and 22 months in 2008).
rationale: The LBNL 2026 Edition is the authoritative primary source; the headline median IR-to-COD figure of 61 months for projects achieving commercial operations in 2025 maps directly to the rubric's requested metric. This is a confirmed physical/process outcome (measured on completed projects), not a forecast.

dissent.view: MOFCOM and Global Times (June 2025) characterise the system as open and compliant, stating China 'will approve applications that meet requirements'; Trump administration claimed a June 2026 bilateral deal substantially eased approvals, though MOFCOM's confirmation was partial and China Briefing notes no substantive procedural change is confirmed.

China-briefing (updated Nov 2025) notes that MOFCOM stated it would 'review and approve eligible export applications' under the US-China trade truce, implying a more permissive posture than the market-restriction narrative; but acknowledges it 'remains unclear' whether this changed actual processing.

fact: As of September 2026, China's MOFCOM operates a mandatory case-by-case export licensing regime for seven heavy/medium REE categories and associated magnets (April 2025 Wave 1, fully enforced). General licences were issued in December 2025 to only three named major Chinese magnet makers (JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng) and are not broadly available. Real processing times run 60-120 days for heavy-REE approvals, well above the 45-working-day statutory target. August 2026 magnet shipments fell 21% month-on-month to ~512 metric tons, corroborating selective/slow approvals. The 2026 licensing catalogue added samarium, gadolinium, and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories (effective January 2026). Sources: discoveryalert.com (Sept 22 2026 customs data); duramag.com (2025-2026 market update); certivo.com (March 2026); mining.com (Dec 2025 Reuters-cited general licence report); china-briefing.com (updated Nov 2025).
rationale: The rubric scores 1 (SLOWING) when licensing is case-by-case or whitelist-only AND/OR typical processing exceeds 30 days AND/OR a new category was added in the trailing 3 months. All three conditions are met: licensing is case-by-case except for three whitelisted exporters; real approval times are 60-120 days; and new catalogue additions (samarium/gadolinium/lutetium compounds) took effect January 2026. A score of 2 is not warranted because licences continue to be issued for civilian/commercial end-users and no categorical country-level denial or formal suspension of licensing has been announced.

dissent.view: Goldman Sachs maintained a 2026 copper surplus forecast as recently as mid-2026, contrasting with Benchmark and JP Morgan deficit calls
July 2026 Chilean storm disruptions described as 'temporary, not catastrophic' with BHP northern Chile mines running normally

fact: At least three top-20 copper mines have confirmed, currently-active production cuts: (1) Grasberg (world #2 by output, Indonesia) - Freeport's May 2026 earnings revised full restart to end-2027/early 2028, targeting only ~65% capacity in H2 2026 vs normal 1.7 billion lb/yr, with actual 2026 output expected ~700 million lb - a ~58% reduction vs pre-incident levels (mining.com, 2026-05-08); (2) Kamoa-Kakula (DRC, top-5 global) - 2026 guidance cut to 290,000-330,000 t vs prior 420,000 t target after seismic damage, smelter at 60% capacity in H2 2026 (Ivanhoe Q2 2026 release, 2026-07-08; metalnomist.com, 2026-05-30); (3) Los Pelambres (Antofagasta, Chile, top-20) - 2026 guidance cut from 650,000-700,000 t to 625,000-655,000 t after July 2026 storm halted mining and processing (industrialinfo.com, 2026-08-20). Lundin Caserones also cut guidance. ICSG cut 2026 mine supply growth forecast to 1.6% from 2.3%. Goldman Sachs and Benchmark both forecast a 2026 copper market deficit driven by disruptions (oregongroup.com, 2026-07-16).
rationale: Three or more named top-20 mines (Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula, Los Pelambres) have confirmed production cuts currently active as of September 2026, and multiple institutions (Goldman Sachs, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, ICSG) have formally forecast a 2026 refined copper market deficit - this satisfies both legs of the rubric's CLUSTER threshold (>=3 major mines disrupted AND institutional deficit forecasts corroborated by price moves to multi-year highs).

dissent.view: IMF/World Bank (Sept 21 2026) note ~14% of LICs are 'in debt distress' and ~23% of EM countries 'at high risk of overall sovereign stress' -- elevated risk rhetoric, but no specific new program or missed coupon is named; risk ≠ executed distress event under the rubric.

fact: No new EM sovereign missed coupon, standstill, or new IMF distress-driven program was identified in authoritative sources for the March–September 2026 window. IMF MD Georgieva at Spring Meetings 2026 (April 15, 2026, imf.org) characterised EM balance sheets as broadly resilient with 'independent central banks, fiscal councils, built very strong reserves.' The IMF/World Bank joint statement of September 21, 2026 (Reuters/WHBL) cited structural LIC debt-distress metrics but announced no new EM sovereign program or missed coupon. Congo's March 2026 IMF assessment was a post-financing review of a legacy program, not a new distress arrangement.
rationale: Zero confirmed new IMF distress-driven programs or missed coupons among EM sovereigns in the trailing 6 months maps mechanically to CALM (0) under the rubric. The IMF's own public characterisation of EM resilience at its Spring 2026 meetings reinforces the absence of a cluster or single-event trigger.

fact: TPR Market Oversight report (thepensionsregulator.gov.uk, data to March 2025) confirms LDI market shrank from ~£1.5tn to ~£0.7tn, rate buffers rebuilt to ~300 bps, and 'LDI arrangements remained resilient in January 2025 when gilt yields increased.' ESMA June 2026 paper reviews post-2022 regulatory framework with no new stress episode flagged.
rationale: TPR and ESMA confirm LDI buffers are adequate (≥250-300 bps, well above the ~140 bps trigger seen in 2022) and no regulator has flagged a new margin-call episode or forced gilt selling in 2025-2026; this maps to Rubric 0 (buffers adequate, no margin stress). Confidence is medium rather than high because the most recent TPR data runs only to March 2025 and no real-time Q3 2026 regulatory statement was found.

dissent.view: Universal Asset Owners Probability Desk (1 Sep 2026) argues the 3% yield breach is a 'term-premium event, not a fiscal crisis,' citing robust 10y auction demand on the same day yields hit 3%

Oxford Economics raised end-2026 10y JGB forecast to 2.8%, viewing risks as 'more balanced' after June supplementary budget came in smaller than feared—implying less stress than headline yields suggest

fact: Japan 10-year JGB yield reached 3.000% on 1 September 2026 (30-year high, up ~90bps from ~2.1% in March 2026) driven by Takaichi fiscal expansion fears and a record ¥143 trillion FY2027 budget request. As of 18 September 2026 the yield eased to 2.99% (TradingEconomics). The 30-year auction on 3 September 2026 cleared with a bid-to-cover of 3.79 vs. 12-month average of 3.52 (Bloomberg, 3 Sep 2026). No failed auction or emergency BOJ operation reported; HSBC noted 'limited clarity on funding channels' with 'additional debt issuance a plausible outcome' (CNBC, 4 Aug 2026).
rationale: The 10y yield has surged well above 25bps from its early-2026 level on explicit fiscal concern (rubric threshold for score 1), but auctions are still clearing with bid-to-cover above 3 and no emergency BOJ operation has been reported, ruling out score 2 (disorderly). The funding path for the ¥143 trillion FY2027 budget request remains unspecified, satisfying the secondary score-1 condition.

dissent.view: S&P confirmed A+ with stable outlook in May 2026 and Fitch upheld A+ stable in Mar 2026, so on a forward-looking basis both are stable—could argue level 1 (Moody's negative outlook) if one counts only current outlooks rather than trailing cuts.

fact: Fitch downgraded France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) on 12 Sep 2025; S&P downgraded France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) on 18 Oct 2025; Moody's downgraded France from Aa2 to Aa3 in Dec 2024 and on 11 Apr 2026 maintained Aa3 with a NEGATIVE outlook. All three actions are within or overlap the trailing 12 months to 22 Sep 2026. Sources: Bloomberg (10 Sep 2025), France24 (18 Oct 2025), Xinhua/Moody's (11 Apr 2026).
rationale: Two Big Three agencies (Fitch, S&P) executed actual one-notch rating cuts within the trailing 12 months (Sep-Oct 2025), satisfying rubric level 2 unambiguously. Moody's additionally holds a negative outlook as of Apr 2026, reinforcing the most-severe classification.

fact: China MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (issued 22 June 2026) added 10 named US entities to its export-control list under the Export Control Law and Regulations on Dual-Use Items, including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc., prohibiting Chinese suppliers from exporting dual-use items to those specific firms. Multiple corroborating sources (Benchmark Minerals, Al Jazeera, Reuters/Bloomberg via StockTitan, SMM) confirm the listing is entity-specific and not a categorical ban on the US rare-earth sector. Share-price reaction on listing day was muted (MP roughly flat, USA Rare Earth modestly higher), consistent with an entity-specific rather than sector-wide action.
rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) are explicitly on China's MOFCOM export-control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying Rubric 1 exactly; every primary source characterises the measure as entity-specific, not a sector-wide or categorical ban, ruling out Rubric 2.

fact: Fitch Ratings data (cited Aug 2026 by Angel Investors Network/CoinDesk): 10 of 16 tracked non-traded BDCs breached their 5% quarterly redemption caps in Q2 2026; named funds include Blackstone BCRED (~$79-82B AUM), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC (~$25B), Ares Strategic Income Fund (~$10.7B), Blue Owl OTIC, Blue Owl OBDC II (fully halted Feb 2026), Oaktree Strategic Credit, Cliffwater CCLFX (~$31B), HPS HLEND, BlackRock BDEBT, and Variant Investments. Robert A. Stanger & Co. (Aug 17 2026) puts Q2 repurchase requests at 12.4% of NAV - highest ever recorded - with only 38% fulfilled and ~$9.6B in requests unfilled.
rationale: 10 of 16 Fitch-tracked BDCs gated in the same quarter (Q2 2026) is far above the rubric threshold of >=3 largest funds; combined AUM of BCRED + CCLFX + Apollo alone exceeds $135B, well above the $100B threshold for level 2. No corroborating signal is required for a structural cap-breach (these are contractual mechanisms, not discretionary gates), though equity prices of Blue Owl (-67%), Blackstone (-46%), Apollo (-41%) and KKR/Ares (-48%) confirm market-wide stress corroborating the redemption pressure.

fact: Five US banks failed in 2026 YTD (Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust $261M Jan 30; Community Bank and Trust-West Georgia May 1; Kentland Federal Savings Jul 10; Small Business Bank of Lenexa ~Jul 17; Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank $68M Aug 21); all were sub-$100M except Metropolitan Capital. Bisnow (Feb 2, 2026) identified a CRE/skilled-nursing-facility loan as a contributing factor at Metropolitan Capital via court records, though FDIC did not publicly cite CRE as cause. FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile (Aug 25, 2026) characterizes the industry as broadly sound; D&O Diary (Sep 2026) citing Law.com concludes 2026 failures are idiosyncratic. FDIC 2026 Risk Review (Apr 2026) flags ongoing CRE credit risk monitoring for regional banks. No coordinated interagency CRE emergency facility issued. Sources: fdic.gov/bank-failures/failed-bank-list (Aug 21, 2026 last update); americanbanker.com (Aug 21, 2026); dandodiary.com (Sep 2026); bisnow.com (Feb 2, 2026); fdic.gov/analysis/2026-risk-review (Apr 2026).
rationale: Within the trailing 6 months (Mar 22-Sep 22 2026), 1-2 failures occurred with at most one (Metropolitan Capital, at the edge of the window) having a credible CRE-link per Bisnow reporting, while FDIC 2026 Risk Review constitutes a public supervisory statement citing regional-bank CRE concentration; no failure exceeded $10B and no coordinated interagency action was issued, placing this squarely in ISOLATED (score=1). [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]

dissent.view: LakeLevelNow reports 24% full as of Sep 9, 2026 (slightly lower reading from same USBR feed, different calculation basis)

fact: Lake Mead elevation 1,038.44 ft, storage 6,870,680 acre-feet = 26.3% of capacity, per USBR RISE data cited by ReservoirBench.com (Sep 17, 2026); USBR Aug-31 Weekly Hydrologic Update confirms 1,038.87 ft / 26%. Minimum power pool threshold is 1,035 ft, placing the lake ~3.4 ft above that threshold.
rationale: At 26.3% of capacity, Lake Mead is below the rubric's 30% CRITICAL floor; simultaneously, at ~3.4 ft above the 1,035 ft minimum power-pool/turbine-shutdown threshold, it is well within the rubric's 15-foot proximity trigger. Both sub-criteria independently map to level 2 CRITICAL.

dissent.view: CBO (February 2026) independently estimated the 2032 depletion date but projects a steeper 28% automatic cut vs. the trustees' 22%, reflecting different economic assumptions.

fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026; primary source: ssa.gov/oact/TR/2026/tr2026.pdf) projects the OASI trust fund will be depleted in Q4 2032 -- one quarter earlier than the prior year's estimate -- at which point only 78% of scheduled benefits would be payable (a ~22% automatic cut). The combined OASDI depletion date remains 2034 (83% payable). The 75-year actuarial deficit widened to 4.42% of taxable payroll. Multiple reform bills (Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act H.R. 9187; PROMISE Act, introduced July 14, 2026) are in debate but none has been enacted. No automatic benefit reduction has been triggered and no legislation cutting benefits has been signed into law.
rationale: The trustees report worsened the OASI depletion date (moved earlier to Q4 2032) and the 75-year shortfall grew materially, satisfying rubric band 1 ('trustees report worsens the depletion date or reform actively debated'). No automatic cut has been triggered and no enacted legislation reduces benefits, so band 2 is not met.

dissent.view: KBRA July 2026 Auto Loan ABS report shows non-prime 60+ day delinquency rose 19 bps from June and 26 bps year-over-year — directionally consistent but covers a slightly broader 'non-prime' universe, implying a somewhat different absolute level
ankso.blog (Sep 2026) cites Fitch subprime 60+ delinquency at 5.49% for May 2026 — consistent with the seasonal trough but one month earlier than the July reversal

fact: Fitch Auto ABS subprime 60-plus-day delinquency index: 5.80% in June 2026, then jumped 33 basis points to 6.13% in July 2026, per CUCollector citing Fitch Auto ABS indices (published ~Sep 22, 2026).
rationale: The rubric calls for the latest reported subprime auto 60+ day delinquency rate as a percent; the July 2026 Fitch ABS index reading of 6.13% is the most recent hard figure from an authoritative ABS-tracker source, mechanically mapping to 6.13. The seasonal pattern (H2 deterioration after H1 tax-refund relief) corroborates the direction of the print.

dissent.view: ISW/AEI (Sep 1 2026) characterises the surge in coast-guard and civilian vessels as 'short-of-war' grey-zone coercion rather than military exercises, noting that formal ADIZ sorties have actually declined to pre-Lai norms since early 2026 — a framing that might imply a level closer to elevated-routine than classic drill-escalation.

fact: Taiwan's MND (globalsecurity.org mirror, dated ~20 Sep 2026) reported 5 PLA aircraft sorties and 11 PLAN ships plus 6 official ships operating around Taiwan, with all 5 sorties crossing the Taiwan Strait median line. Separately, AEI/ISW China-Taiwan Update (Sep 1 2026) documented a record 244 PRC vessels in Taiwan's waters in July 2026 and 1,247 PRC vessels near Taiwan since May 2026 when permanent PRC patrols east of Taiwan began; ADIZ median-line crossing sorties have nonetheless declined to pre-Lai baseline levels since early 2026. The most significant discrete drill in the current cycle was the PLA two-day live-fire exercise in the Taiwan Strait on 23-24 Jul 2026 (South China Morning Post), triggered by Taiwanese leader Lai Ching-te's speech. No kinetic clash or actual blockade has been reported.
rationale: Persistent PLAN/coast-guard vessel presence at record levels plus recent live-fire drills and continued daily median-line crossings constitute large-scale assertive activity well above routine, matching rubric level 1; no kinetic clash, no enforced blockade, and no full mobilization has been documented, precluding level 2.

dissent.view: Some analysts frame the overall US-China posture as a 'managed truce' under the Nov 2026 suspension framework (gallium/germanium export controls suspended, bilateral summit in May 2026), suggesting the new tariffs are incremental rather than representing a truce breakdown.

fact: USTR announced a new 12.5% Section 301 tariff on Chinese goods (forced-labor basis), effective 24 July 2026 — a broad cross-sector tariff increment >=10%. Additionally: China imposed provisional anti-dumping deposits up to 54.3% on US/Mexican pecans (MOFCOM, effective 11 Aug 2026); China imposed new export controls on drone technologies targeting the US (Aug 5, 2026); Canada made preliminary anti-dumping/subsidy determinations on Chinese forged grinding media (CBSA, 25 May 2026) and final dumping determinations on Chinese thermoformed tableware (CBSA, 28 May 2026). Total: >=4 new measures in trailing 3 months. Sources: china-briefing.com (28 Jul 2026), globaltimes.cn (10 Aug 2026), catts.eu (Jun 2026), usahousinginformation.com (5 Aug 2026).
rationale: The USTR 12.5% Section 301 tariff alone triggers the 'broad tariff round >=10% across a sector' threshold; combined with >=3 additional measures from China and Canada, the count exceeds 4, mechanically mapping to ESCALATING (value=2). No truce or market-dampening signal offsets the new measure count.

dissent.view: SEC Chair Atkins confirmed in March 2026 the December 2026 cash deadline remains intact and is 'important to achieve for market integrity,' suggesting no imminent extension — potentially a more sanguine read than level 1.
TBAC May 2026 notes 'the cash market is relatively better positioned vs repo' due to narrower scope and more developed done-away structure, implying cash friction is moderate rather than severe.

fact: TBAC's May 2026 charge paper states 'the largest challenge from an implementation standpoint continues to be the amount of legal work and documentation associated with bilateral agreements between participants,' and the SEC's August 7 2026 statement still urges firms to 'continue their efforts to prepare for a smooth and successful transition by the current deadline.' SIFMA's exemptive relief request for inter-affiliate and extraterritorial scope remained pending in comment as of August 2026, with the SEC's Rule 15c3-3 net omnibus margin notice also open. The Nov 2025 SIFMA/DTCC/Broadridge pulse survey (330 firms) found only 54% of firms 'very confident' of cash-deadline readiness and 40% for repo. (Sources: TBAC Charge Q2 2026 PDF, SEC.gov August 2026 statement, SIFMA/Broadridge Pulse Survey Nov 2025)
rationale: Pending exemptive relief on inter-affiliate and extraterritorial scope, a documented legal/documentation backlog per TBAC, and a readiness confidence level of 54% (cash) — below the rubric's 60% threshold — all map squarely to rubric level 1 (FRICTION). No deadline extension or operational failure has been confirmed, precluding level 2.

dissent.view: Some sources (z2data.com) cite a slightly different expiry date of Nov 27, 2026 for the gallium/germanium/antimony dual-use ban suspension, which would push that sub-element marginally outside the 90-day window on Sept 22; core rare-earth-element controls still expire Nov 10.

fact: China's Oct-2025 rare earth export controls remain suspended until Nov 10, 2026 (White House fact sheet, Nov 5 2025; China-Briefing, Nov 7 2025), but as of Sept 22, 2026 no renewal has been announced (<49 days to expiry), USTR Greer said parties 'remain divided' on extension terms (Bloomberg, Sept 21 2026), and China added 10 US rare-earth firms (incl. MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) to new entity restrictions in June 2026 (Reuters, cited by Modern Diplomacy, Aug 21 2026).
rationale: Two independent rubric-1 triggers are satisfied: the truce is inside the <90-day-to-expiry window with no confirmed renewal, and China's June 2026 entity-list additions against US rare-earth miners constitute a partial breach. The truce has not formally lapsed (ruling out Score 2), but fraying is well-documented.

dissent.view: GERD/Nile dispute also sits at level 1: diplomacy frozen since 2020, Ethiopia announced three new Blue Nile dams (March 2026), Egypt expanding military posture in Horn of Africa, but no flow cut-off or armed clash confirmed.

fact: On 31 Aug 2026, The Hague Court of Arbitration ruled the Indus Waters Treaty 'remains fully in force' and India's April 2025 unilateral suspension ('abeyance') was impermissible; India rejected the ruling. India had also restricted flows through Baglihar and Kishanganga dams after the suspension, and the Permanent Indus Commission has not met since May 2022 nor has India shared river-flow data since 2023. Sources: Al Jazeera 2026-09-01; Bloomberg 2026-09-01; Chatham House 2026-04-17; Britannica updated 2026-09.
rationale: The Indus Waters Treaty is formally suspended/contested by India and India rejected a binding international arbitration ruling, with a documented short-term physical flow restriction through dam controls — meeting rubric level 1 (treaty suspended/contested, official threats exchanged). No confirmed sustained deliberate flow cut-off or armed kinetic action tied directly to the dam/river was found, precluding level 2.

dissent.view: Some secondary sources (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) characterise BRICS Pay as having 'gone live' or 'operationally launched' in 2026, which could imply Level 2; however, authoritative summit outcome documents and EBC/Irish Times reporting confirm the system remains in pilot/expansion phase with no common currency and no major economy formally moving reserve settlement off USD.

fact: The 18th BRICS Summit New Delhi Declaration (12-13 Sep 2026) formally endorsed expansion of the BRICS Payment Task Force mandate for local-currency cross-border settlements and BRICS Pay, but adopted no common currency and launched no operationally live reserve-settlement system displacing USD; no new sovereign reserve freeze or seizure beyond the pre-existing 2022 Russian asset freeze was executed (sources: Wikipedia 18th BRICS Summit; entrepreneurloop.com BRICS 2026 takeaways; deepmentor.co New Delhi Declaration summary, Sep 2026).
rationale: The New Delhi Declaration constitutes new multilateral official endorsement of non-dollar settlement architecture (BRICS Pay mandate, local-currency settlement), meeting the rubric definition of Level 1 TALK. No new sovereign reserve freeze or seizure of a new target occurred in 2026, and BRICS Pay remains in pilot/expansion phase rather than operationally displacing USD settlement for a major economy, precluding Level 2.

dissent.view: FERC's June 18, 2026 tailored orders to all six U.S. grid operators are designed to 'significantly shorten the multi-year interconnection queue backlog,' suggesting policy-driven easing is underway -- but this is prospective intent, not an observed physical shortening.

LBNL Queued Up 2026 shows a 10% decrease in total active U.S. queue volume vs. prior year, driven by high project withdrawal rates rather than accelerated completions -- a signal of attrition, not relief.

fact: New York Governor Hochul issued Executive Order 62 on July 14, 2026 imposing a statewide moratorium on data center permitting citing grid cost burdens; Texas Governor Abbott on August 3, 2026 ordered PUCT and ERCOT to pause all new data-center grid connections pending a comprehensive audit -- two confirmed power-scarcity-driven moratoria. The IEA Electricity 2026 report (August 2026) simultaneously confirms >2,500 GW stalled in global grid connection queues and 'rising congestion-related curtailment' across many power systems. Sources: sheppard.com (July 29 2026), texaspowercost.com (Aug 3 2026), iea.org/reports/electricity-2026/executive-summary (Aug 2026).
rationale: The rubric's level-2 threshold is 'a power-scarcity-driven moratorium.' Both New York (statewide executive order) and Texas (PUCT/ERCOT connection pause) have enacted exactly that within the past 60 days, with grid capacity strain explicitly cited. The IEA corroborates with evidence of rising curtailment globally.

dissent.view: Sequoia/Allianz Research estimated a ~$600B annual gap between AI infrastructure spend and AI ecosystem revenue in 2025, with a ~46% capex-to-revenue divergence exceeding the 2001 telecom overbuild peak of 32% -- suggesting the gap may be worse than headline cloud growth rates imply when total ecosystem (not just hyperscaler cloud) revenue is the denominator.

fact: Q2 2026 earnings (Amazon 30 Jul, Alphabet 29 Jul, Microsoft 29 Jul): combined 2026 hyperscaler capex guidance raised to ~$730B, up ~78% YoY from ~$410B in 2025 (valueaddvc.com/ai-spending, Aug 2026). AI-attributable cloud revenue growth: Google Cloud +82% YoY to $24.8B (accelerating from +63% in Q1), AWS +37% YoY to $42.2B (fastest in 18 quarters), Azure +43% YoY; Microsoft AI business +123% YoY at $37B annualized run rate (fourweekmba.com, kucoin.com, Jul-Aug 2026). Capex growth (~78% YoY) exceeds blended AI-revenue growth for the group, but all three cloud units are accelerating YoY and no company cut its AI-revenue outlook.
rationale: Capex growth (~78% YoY) materially exceeds blended AI-revenue growth (AWS 37%, Azure 43%, Google Cloud 82%), keeping the gap wide; however, AI revenue is accelerating YoY across all three platforms (Google Cloud QoQ acceleration from 63% to 82% is particularly strong) and no hyperscaler has raised capex while cutting its AI-revenue outlook, ruling out rubric level 2.

fact: Affirm FQ3'26 Shareholder Letter (SEC 8-K, filed ~May 2026): '30+ day delinquencies excluding Peloton and Pay in X loans increased 29 basis points year over year and increased 7 basis points quarter over quarter to 2.8%.' Allowance for credit losses 6.0% of loans HFI; monthly installment loan cohorts tracking ~3.5% ultimate net charge-offs as % of GMV.
rationale: Delinquency is up 29 bps YoY (well below the 100 bps spike threshold) and charge-offs are tracking ~3.5% ultimate NCO (below the 5% spike threshold), squarely matching Level 1: RISING with contained charge-offs. Level 2 is not warranted without a >100 bps YoY move or >5% charge-off rate.

dissent.view: TeleGeography/submarinecablemap.com (updated Sept 22, 2026) lists many cables as 'in-service' and does not flag an active multi-system outage at Red Sea level comparable to Sept 2025 severity; the Sept 2025 cuts (SMW-4, IMEWE, FALCON) may have been substantially repaired by mid-2026, leaving only PEACE as confirmed unrepaired.
AGBI (March 2026) and TeleGeography (April 2026) frame Hormuz cable risk as elevated threat, not an actual cut — no confirmed severance at Hormuz.

fact: The PEACE submarine cable was cut in the Red Sea (~1,450 km from Zafarana, Egypt), reported July 27, 2026 by Data Center Dynamics/Submarine Cable Networks; repair expected to take 'several months' due to cable-ship capacity crunch — status unrepaired as of late September 2026. Separately, Iran issued explicit threats in mid-September 2026 to cut Hormuz undersea cables (Asia Times, Sept 16, 2026), and the September 6, 2025 multi-cut event (SMW-4, IMEWE, FALCON/GCX) near Jeddah had extended repair timelines. The Australia-Singapore Cable also broke on Sept 4, 2026 (Indonesia-Singapore segment, partial reroute only as of Sept 18).
rationale: At least one named major cable (PEACE, Red Sea) is confirmed severed and unrepaired months after the cut, satisfying rubric level 2 ('>=1 major cable currently severed and unrepaired causing connectivity loss'). Iran threats to Hormuz cables add a simultaneous threatened-vector, but the PEACE cut alone meets the level-2 threshold.

fact: Global insured natural catastrophe losses for H1 2026 totaled USD 42B (Swiss Re Institute, Aug 20 2026) to USD 47B (Aon, Jul 22 2026), vs. a 10-year H1 average of ~USD 50B (Munich Re) to USD 64B (Gallagher Re) — 28% below the decadal average per Gallagher Re. No single event exceeded USD 10B in insured losses through H1; five consecutive quarters without a >$10B event. Q3 2026 full recap not yet published. Atlantic hurricane season suppressed by El Niño.
rationale: H1 2026 YTD insured losses are 28-36% BELOW the 10-year average across all primary sources, and no single event has crossed the $10B threshold; this squarely maps to Rubric Score 0 (NORMAL). Absent a major Q3 hurricane or wildfire event exceeding $10B insured — of which no such event has been publicly reported by any primary source as of 2026-09-28 — the indicator remains NORMAL.

dissent.view: China reportedly lifted fertilizer export curbs specifically to India in August 2025 per a diplomatic assurance from FM Wang Yi, suggesting a partial bilateral carve-out rather than a general restriction
Philippines reported China indicated fertilizer exports would not be restricted broadly, though Chinese authorities did not publicly confirm this

rationale: Active urea quotas with binding FOB price floors plus phosphate export suspension (NDRC-directed, December 2025, extended through August 2026) confirm restrictions remain in place. The only broadening event - the March 2026 ban on NK blends and additional phosphate varieties - occurred ~6 months ago, outside the trailing 3-month window required for a rating of 2, so the rubric maps to 1 (IN PLACE, unchanged in the last 3 months).

dissent.view: Trading Economics page cached at Feb 2026 data showing -0.9% YoY; this reflects an outdated snapshot, not a competing current reading

dissent.view: KBRA office CMBS delinquency rate was 12.8% in February 2026, down from 13.9% in January 2026, using KBRA-rated private label universe only

Mills vetoed it; some sources (Multistate, April 2026) briefly characterized Maine as 'poised to become the first state' before the veto, which would conflict with the NY-first characterization, but post-veto sources confirm NY is first.

dissent.view: Arizona long-term drought remains D3-D4 in every county per AZWATER.gov (as of mid-2026 review), which would argue for rubric level 2 on a long-term structural basis

dissent.view: Once Arizona buildout is complete (~2028-2030), Wei projects ~30% of 2nm-and-below capacity in US — used by some analysts as evidence of imminent diversification — but this is a forward projection, not a current operational fact.

dissent.view: Equable Institute projects the average national funded ratio at 85.0% for FY2026 (actuarial basis, broader plan universe), up from 81.2% in FY2025, with unfunded liabilities of ~$1.13 trillion.

dissent.view: Agencies are making 'significant progress' and the overall GENIUS Act enforcement effective date (Jan 18, 2027) has not yet passed, suggesting the framework is still on track for operation — CoinDesk frames missed rulemaking deadline as procedural, not a system failure.

fact: As of 2026-09-28, no agency has issued final rules implementing the GENIUS Act. The statutory one-year rulemaking deadline of July 18, 2026 has been missed. All major regulators remain in proposed-rulemaking (NPRM) stage: the Federal Reserve only published two NPRMs on September 24, 2026 (60-day comment window pending); Treasury published its Section 3 NPRM on August 17-18, 2026 with comments due October 19, 2026; the OCC's NPRM (published February 25, 2026) is targeting a final rule by November 2026; the FDIC approved its NPRM on April 7, 2026. CoinDesk (2026-09-24) stated: 'the agencies are all well past the legal deadline.' The GENIUS Act effective date falls back to the 18-month backstop of January 18, 2027 unless final rules are issued first. Sources: federalreserve.gov (Sept 24 2026), federalregister.gov (Aug 18 2026 / Apr 10 2026), coindesk.com/policy (Sept 24 2026), occ.gov bulletin-2026-3, fdic.gov press release Apr 7 2026, treasury.gov sb0605 (Aug 17 2026).
rationale: The rubric assigns 2 (PROBLEMS) when the deadline is missed without final rules. The July 18, 2026 statutory one-year rulemaking deadline has been missed by all primary federal regulators, none of whom have issued final rules; all remain in public-comment NPRMs well past that date, mapping directly to the rubric's 'deadline missed without final rules' criterion.

fact: PM Sebastien Lecornu's Second Lecornu government (minority coalition, incumbent since 10 Oct 2025) survived two no-confidence motions on 23 Jan 2026 after invoking Article 49.3 to pass the 2026 budget revenue section (269 votes in favour vs 288 needed, per Euronews/Reuters/Al Jazeera); as of 17 Sep 2026, Lecornu is still PM and proposing a 2027 budget amid ongoing minority-government fragility (Bloomberg, 2026-09-17). No dissolution or collapse has been executed.
rationale: France's government is governing as an explicit minority relying on Article 49.3 and surviving (not falling to) no-confidence votes — the definition of FRAGILE (band 1). No snap election has been called nor has the government fallen, ruling out band 2.

dissent.view: Some commentary (tech-insider.org, metirai.com) frames CoreWeave's structure as near-crisis given $35bn debt vs ~$6.2bn TTM revenue, implying rubric 2 risk is imminent; however no actual default or failed deal has been confirmed as of late September 2026.

rationale: A named borrower (CoreWeave) faced a refinancing wall with CDS at distressed levels and was forced to offer improved terms to complete a GPU-backed debt transaction, satisfying rubric 1 criteria exactly. No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or truly failed refinancing has been reported, so rubric 2 is not met.

dissent.view: Lloyd's List Intelligence (9 Sept 2026) counted 346 non-Iranian-linked transits in August and an 82-transit week ending 30 Aug, suggesting some partial recovery/volatility rather than a total halt, though still far below the pre-war 3,000/month baseline.

No signed truce or operating convoy system is in place as of today - Trump rejected Iran's reopening proposal on 28 Sept - so the rubric cap at 1 does not apply.

dissent.view: CargoLinked (25 Sep 2026) notes some Iran-approved vessels (mostly petroleum bound for China/India) are still transiting with military escort, and CENTCOM says non-Iranian commercial traffic 'may continue' — implying partial rather than total closure, which could support a rating of 1 (contested).

fact: IMF PortWatch recorded 1 vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz on 20 September vs a pre-crisis baseline of ~85/day; Reuters-cited data showed 10 commodity vessel crossings on 23 September vs a 10-day average of ~17. Iran's IRGC declared the strait closed to 'unfriendly nations' from 2 March 2026 onward; US-Iran reopening talks are ongoing but unresolved as of 28 September. Brent crude is trading at ~$104-108/bbl on 28 September 2026, up ~59% year-on-year — a market signal fully consistent with a near-closure. (Sources: cargolinked.com 25-Sep-2026; straits.live 27-Sep-2026; tradingeconomics.com 28-Sep-2026; fortune.com 28-Sep-2026)
rationale: Transit volume at ~1-10% of the pre-crisis baseline (well under the 25% threshold) with Brent ~$105-108/bbl — ~59% above year-ago levels — satisfies the rubric's dual condition for a rating of 2: physical near-closure corroborated by an oil price signal consistent with severe supply disruption. Active but deadlocked US-Iran talks do not constitute a 'functioning convoy workaround' or a signed truce, so the 1-cap rule does not apply.

fact: Benchmark Minerals Intelligence Q3 2026 Rare Earths Price Review (published ~24 Sep 2026): 'By September, dysprosium oxide CIF Europe gained 56% to reach an average of $3,500/kg... while Chinese domestic dysprosium and terbium prices continued to retreat.' China domestic DyO reference per Rare Earth Exchanges (17 Sep 2026): ~$212-218/kg. Implied multiple: $3,500/$215 ≈ 16.3x. Terbium oxide CIF Europe $6,745/kg vs China domestic ~$996/kg ≈ 6.8x.
rationale: The rubric asks for the ex-China HREE price premium as a multiple of the China price; applying BMI's September 2026 CIF Europe dysprosium oxide average ($3,500/kg) against the contemporaneous China domestic reference (~$215/kg) yields ~16.3x, reflecting the extreme bifurcation driven by China export licensing controls post-April 2025. CIF North America references and lower-tier ex-China spot values yield a lower ~4.6-5.2x multiple for dysprosium, indicating geography and transaction type drive a wide spread within the 'ex-China' category.

dissent.view: AM Best (Sep 28 2026) reports markedly improved homeowners underwriting results in 2025 ($16.5B gain) and a calmer H1 2026, suggesting the market is stabilizing rather than still accelerating — consistent with a low-end '1' or even trend toward '0' in some states.

rationale: ~13 states are cited as active non-renewal/market-pressure zones, squarely in the 5-15 state range of rubric level 1; no confirmed full exit of a top-10 insurer from a major state market in 2026 (State Farm paused new business in CA but did not fully exit), and AM Best signals improving underwriting results, ruling out level 2.

fact: LBNL Queued Up 2026 Edition (data through end of 2025, published June 2026, emp.lbl.gov/queues): 'the median duration from IR to COD was over 5 years for projects built in 2025' — corroborated by Axis Intelligence citing the same LBNL report as 61 months (up from 36 months in 2015 and 22 months in 2008).
rationale: The rubric requests the latest LBNL median queue wait in months; the 2026 Edition reports 61 months (IR to COD) for 2025 vintage projects, the most current annual datapoint available. This is a confirmed measured outcome from actual built projects, not a forecast, satisfying the top-band physical-data anchor requirement.

dissent.view: Some sources (e.g. TechTimes, May 2026) note that general licences issued to three large Chinese magnet makers partially ease throughput for pre-vetted civilian customers, which could push toward a softer reading of Rubric 1; however, these general licences are explicitly not broadly available and do not constitute blanket coverage, so the overall classification remains 1.

fact: China's April 2025 MOFCOM licensing regime (Announcement No. 18) on seven heavy/medium rare earth elements and derived magnet products remains fully in force; approvals are issued case-by-case (per-shipment) with actual processing times of 60-120 days against a statutory 45-working-day target; a first batch of general licences was issued in December 2025 to only three major Chinese magnet makers (JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng) but is not broadly available; and the January 2026 Export Licensing Catalogue added samarium, gadolinium and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories. Trump threats of 200% tariffs in August 2026 and a ~21% year-on-year drop in magnet export volumes confirm ongoing throughput friction. Sources: China Briefing (Jul 27 2026), gettransport.com (Jul 7 2026), discoveryalert.com (Sep 2026), rare-earth-mining.com (Apr 2026).
rationale: The regime fits Rubric 1 on all three triggers simultaneously: licensing is case-by-case (not blanket), typical processing exceeds 30 days (routinely 60-120 days in practice), and new categories (samarium, gadolinium, lutetium compounds) were added to the control list within the trailing three months relative to January 2026. Rubric 2 is not warranted because new licences continue to be issued and no categorical suspension has been announced.

dissent.view: Goldman Sachs as of April 2026 still maintained a 2026 copper surplus forecast, diverging from Benchmark and JPMorgan deficit calls

Benchmark Minerals and ICSG both forecast a 2026 global refined copper deficit as a result.
rationale: Three named top-20 mines have confirmed, physically measurable output cuts currently active, and multiple institutions (Benchmark, ICSG) have issued deficit forecasts - this satisfies the CLUSTER threshold of >=3 mines disrupted OR lost output large enough for institutional deficit forecasts, awarding a score of 2.

dissent.view: Ethiopia's Eurobond exchange (from Dec 2023 default) was staged for completion in 2026 and if a new exchange/restructuring step occurred in the window it could constitute a continuing distress event, though no new missed payment was found; Deluair Consultancy (Apr 2026) notes 21 Sub-Saharan countries in active IMF programs and ~USD 100bn in external debt service due in 2026, suggesting elevated but not newly triggered distress.

fact: IMF FY2026 Annual Report (imf.org/annual-report/2026) states only 2 new nonprecautionary lending arrangements were approved in May 2025-April 2026; no new sovereign missed coupons or standstills found in the April-September 2026 trailing 6-month window across IMF.org news, S&P, or secondary sources. rationale: The rubric requires new IMF program initiations or missed coupons within the trailing 6 months; all distress-adjacent activity found (Argentina, El Salvador, Ghana) reflects ongoing pre-2026 arrangements under review, not new program approvals or sovereign payment failures, mapping to CALM (0). No fresh missed coupon or standstill event was identified in the window from any authoritative source.

dissent.view: TPR's November 2025 report (via Isio summary) notes trustees should go further in stress-testing and diversifying collateral, implying residual pockets of concern, but stops well short of flagging systemic stress or a margin-call episode.

fact: TPR's Market Oversight report (thepensionsregulator.gov.uk, data through May 2025) states: 'LDI arrangements remained resilient in January 2025 when gilt yields increased during a period of higher volatility' and that 'LDI managers have maintained higher buffer thresholds, reducing leverage and improved collateral management.' ESMA mandated a 300 bps yield buffer for GBP LDI funds from April 2024 (esma.europa.eu). No forced selling or central-bank intervention has been reported in 2026; the January 2025 gilt sell-off episode resolved in an orderly manner per TPR and industry participants.
rationale: All primary regulatory sources (TPR, ESMA, BoE FPC) confirm buffers are adequate and the system withstood recent yield spikes without forced selling or intervention; this maps directly to rubric band 0 (NONE). No evidence of any 2026 margin-call episode or regulatory stress-flag was found.

dissent.view: Sep 24 yield spike to 3.055% driven primarily by US PMI data and weak US 5y Treasury auction (global contagion), not fresh Japan fiscal news — implying the fiscal-specific signal may be overstated

fact: 10y JGB yield hit 3.055%-3.08% on Sep 24-25 2026 (30-year high since Aug 1996), up ~18bps over the prior month and cumulatively ~130bps since Takaichi fiscal stimulus plans emerged in late 2025. Most recent 10y auction (Sep 1) cleared with average bid-to-cover and the Sep 3 30y auction posted BTC of 3.79 (Bloomberg, 2026-09-03). The May 2026 supplementary budget (~3 trillion yen) pledged flat total bond issuance, but analysts flagged the financing path as not fully credible (CNBC, 2026-06-01). Sep 24 yield spike attributed partly to US Treasury global contagion (UOB/CNBC).
rationale: Yield is well above the 25bps threshold on fiscal concern (cumulative ~130bps since Takaichi stimulus), and the funding path credibility is contested; however, no auction has failed (BTC <2) or tailed severely, and no emergency BOJ operation has occurred, ruling out a score of 2 and placing this firmly in the UNCLEAR band.

fact: S&P downgraded France from AA-/A-1+ to A+/A-1 (stable outlook) on 17-18 Oct 2025 (S&P Global Ratings press release via France24/Bloomberg/Euronews); Fitch cut France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) in Sep 2025 (Bloomberg/FXStreet); Moody's kept Aa3 but moved outlook to negative on 25 Oct 2025 (France24). S&P reaffirmed A+ in May 2026 (Bloomberg) and Fitch upheld A+ in Mar 2026 (Euronews). Two of three Big-3 agencies executed actual one-notch downgrades within the trailing 12 months ending 2026-09-28.
rationale: Rubric level 2 requires an actual rating cut in the trailing 12 months; both S&P (Oct 2025) and Fitch (Sep 2025) delivered one-notch cuts from AA- to A+, squarely within the window. Moody's negative outlook would independently satisfy level 1, but the executed cuts by two agencies override it to level 2.

fact: MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (June 22, 2026) added 10 named US entities to China's export control list, explicitly including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc., barring Chinese exports of dual-use items to those firms with immediate effect. Source: MOFCOM via GlobalSecurity.org/Benchmark Minerals/Arnold & Porter, June 22-25 2026.
rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) are listed by firm — satisfying rubric level 1 (entity-specific). The restriction covers only the 10 named entities, not the US rare-earth sector as a class, and market signals (Bloomberg: 'curbs are mostly symbolic') do not support escalation to level 2.

fact: Fitch Ratings tracked 10 of 16 non-traded BDCs breaching their 5% quarterly repurchase caps in Q2 2026 (requests averaged 10.3% of NAV); named funds gated in the same quarter include Blackstone BCRED (~$79B AUM), Cliffwater Corporate Lending Fund (~$31B), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC, BlackRock Private Credit Fund, Ares Strategic Income Fund, HPS Corporate Lending Fund, Blue Owl OCIC/OTIC, and Morgan Stanley North Haven. Robert A. Stanger & Co. reported Q2 repurchase requests at 12.4% of NAV industry-wide, the highest on record, with sponsors fulfilling only 38% (~$5.9B of ~$15.6B requested). Source: Angel Investors Network citing Fitch Ratings data, August 20 2026; Trading Market Signals Private Credit Redemption Monitor, August 17 2026; CRE Daily/AltsWire/ABF Journal/White Law Group, June-August 2026.
rationale: Named funds with active gates in Q2 2026 number well above 3 and their combined AUM vastly exceeds $100B (BCRED alone is ~$79B; Cliffwater ~$31B), satisfying the WIDESPREAD threshold of >=3 largest funds or gated AUM >$100B. Corroborating signals include a 23% YTD decline in VanEck BDC ETF (BIZD), manager equity selloffs (Blackstone -46%, Blue Owl -67% from peak), Fitch recording a 6.1% private credit default rate in July 2026, and Cox Capital mini-tender offers at 14-25% NAV discounts -- all consistent with genuine liquidity stress rather than routine gate mechanics.

fact: Five US bank failures YTD in 2026 per Forbes Advisor (Aug 24, 2026); within the trailing 6 months (Apr-Sep 2026): Community Bank & Trust-West Georgia ($288M assets) closed May 1, 2026 (FDIC.gov), preceded by a Federal Reserve enforcement action in April 2026 against its holding company citing capital and board deficiencies; separately, FDIC OIG issued a Failed Bank Review for Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust on May 29, 2026 (fdicoig.gov), with Bisnow (Feb 2, 2026) credibly reporting CRE-linked real estate loan exposure. No coordinated interagency CRE-specific emergency action found.
rationale: At least one enforcement action (Fed, April 2026) and one FDIC OIG review within the 6-month window overlap with CRE-adjacent exposure per credible reporting, and no failure exceeded $10bn or triggered a coordinated supervisory response — fitting ISOLATED (1) rather than CALM (0) or CLUSTER (2). The Fed enforcement action did not explicitly cite CRE concentration as a primary cause, holding confidence to medium. [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]

dissent.view: reservoirs.earth (using NID design capacity of 28.26 maf rather than USBR operational capacity of 26.12 maf) reported 24.4% as of Sep 5, 2026 — a lower percentage due to different capacity denominator, but directionally consistent with CRITICAL classification

fact: Lake Mead elevation 1,037.79 ft, 26.13% of capacity (191.21 ft below full pool of 1,229 ft), per USBR gauge data via water-data.com/lakemead and corroborated by Colorado River Monitor (26.1%, Sep 27) and USBR Weekly Hydrologic Update Aug 31 (26%, 1,038.22 ft). Hoover Dam minimum power pool is 1,050 ft — lake is currently ~12 ft BELOW that threshold.
rationale: At 26.13% of capacity, Mead falls below the rubric's 30% CRITICAL floor; it is also operating approximately 12 feet below Hoover Dam's 1,050-ft minimum power pool threshold, confirming confirmed physical impact to hydropower generation — satisfying both CRITICAL triggers simultaneously.

dissent.view: AARP/Brookings cite the combined OASDI depletion date as 2034 (unchanged from 2025 report), which could imply no deterioration — but the action-forcing OASI-only date did move earlier (2033→2032), and the 75-year shortfall grew 16%.
CBO (February 2026) estimated a steeper automatic cut of 28% vs. the trustees' 22%, reflecting different economic assumptions, though both confirm the 2032 OASI depletion date.

fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026, SSA.gov/oact/trsum/) projects the OASI trust fund depleted in Q4 2032 — one quarter earlier than the 2025 report — with the 75-year actuarial deficit rising to 4.42% of taxable payroll. No benefit cut has been enacted or automatically triggered; multiple reform bills (e.g., Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act H.R. 9187; PROMISE Act, July 14 2026) are in active debate but none has been signed into law.
rationale: The trustees report materially worsened the OASI depletion date (2033→2032) and widened the long-term deficit, satisfying the rubric's Band 1 condition of a worsened depletion outlook. No automatic reduction has been triggered (trust fund still solvent) and no legislation enacting cuts has been enacted, so Band 2 is not met.

dissent.view: ankso.blog (updated ~August 2026) cites May 2026 Fitch subprime 60+ DPD at 5.49% as the low point and projects mid-to-high 5% to low 6% range for remainder of 2026, implying current rate may be tracking toward or above 6%.
S&P Global reported full-year 2025 subprime auto ABS 60+ DPD at a record 6.18% average (vs. 5.78% in 2024), a distinct annual-average metric vs. Fitch's monthly index.

fact: Fitch Auto ABS subprime 60-plus-day delinquency index rose 33 basis points in July 2026 to 6.13%, up from 5.80% in June 2026, per CUCollector citing Fitch (published ~September 2026). The series peaked at 6.90% in January 2026 (all-time record) and seasonally retreated to 5.80% in June before reversing. KBRA's July 2026 Auto Loan ABS report independently corroborated non-prime 60-plus-day delinquency rising 19 bps month-over-month and 26 bps year-over-year.
rationale: The rubric asks for the latest subprime auto 60+ day delinquency rate as a percent; the most recent monthly Fitch ABS index figure publicly reported is July 2026 at 6.13%, which is the load-bearing fact. August/September 2026 Fitch data have not yet been publicly disseminated in the sources found, making July 2026 the latest hard figure.

dissent.view: ISW-AEI (Sep. 1 2026) notes monthly PLA ADIZ incursion totals are less than half August 2024/2025 levels and have reverted to pre-Lai baselines since start of 2026, suggesting strategic de-escalation rather than escalation—a lower-intensity read within level 1.

fact: Taiwan's MND official press release (Sep. 5, 2026) confirmed 20 PLA aircraft sorties—including J-11, Su-30, H-6 bombers, Y-8EW and KJ-500—of which 12 crossed the median line entering northern, central and southeastern ADIZ sectors in a 'joint combat readiness patrol'; a follow-on patrol on Sep. 9 extended coverage to Taiwan's northern, central and eastern airspace. China Coast Guard 'law enforcement' patrols east of Taiwan have been ongoing since July 2026. No kinetic clash or blockade was reported. (Sources: ROC MND press release mnd.gov.tw Sep. 5 2026; ISW-AEI China & Taiwan Update Sep. 11 2026; The Diplomat Sep. 22 2026)
rationale: Persistent median-line crossings, multi-type aircraft joint readiness patrols, and regularized CCG patrols east of Taiwan fit rubric level 1 (elevated: large-scale assertive patrols/blockade rehearsals, no kinetic clash). Overall sortie volumes remain below the 2024-2025 peak, precluding a level-2 read absent any blockade or kinetic event.

fact: In the trailing 3 months (Jul-Sep 2026) at least 6 confirmed new major-economy trade measures against Chinese goods were imposed or opened: (1) US 12.5% Section 301 forced-labor tariff on all Chinese goods, effective 24 Jul 2026 (USTR/Federal Register, 23 Jul 2026); (2) EU definitive AD duties on Chinese car/lorry tyres 4.3-45.3%, EU Reg 2026/1540, 8 Jul 2026 (EC trade policy site); (3) EU definitive AD on ferrosilicon from China, EU Reg 2026/1794, 27 Jul 2026; (4) EU definitive AD on synthetic polyamide yarns from China, EU Reg 2026/1823, 27 Jul 2026; (5) EU provisional AD on sodium benzoate from China, EU Reg 2026/1854, ~Aug 2026; (6) South Africa new 52.34% safeguard on Chinese flat-rolled steel, Jun 2026 + 5 AD amendment notices 18 Sep 2026 (ITAC Report 778/768). The US-China economic truce was extended 2 months to 10 Jan 2027 on 23 Sep 2026, and a bilateral tariff-cut list (77 US categories, 1,619 Chinese categories) was published 28 Sep 2026 but with no rates or dates set.
rationale: Six or more distinct new tariff/AD measures by major economies against China in the trailing 3-month window far exceeds the rubric threshold of >=4 measures for ESCALATING=2; the US broad 12.5% Section 301 rate across all Chinese goods also qualifies as a broad tariff round >=10% across a sector. The truce extension and tariff-cut list publication introduce some de-escalation signal but do not reverse any of the measures already imposed, so the rubric cap-at-evidence rule does not reduce the rating.

dissent.view: NY Fed President Williams (cited in Cryptobriefing ~Sep 2026) characterised the transition as 'ahead of schedule,' and a DTCC GSD member survey showed most respondents 'already prepared or actively completing final readiness activities' for the Dec 31 cash deadline, suggesting the cash leg alone might score 0 (SMOOTH).

fact: SIFMA/BNY/Broadridge/DTCC June 2026 Pulse Survey (340 experts, released 22 Sep 2026): 'The survey suggests the industry is positioned well for the cash implementation but there remains considerable work to do as the industry prepares for the repo deadline.' 86% are at least somewhat confident of meeting the overall mandate; 88% of deferred programs cite legal/contract-negotiation as driving delays; 72% say they need more regulatory clarity; 51% have no formal backup plan; pending exemptive-relief requests (SIFMA inter-affiliate, IIB cross-border) were still open for public comment as of Aug 2026 per SEC Commissioner Uyeda statement (sec.gov, Aug 7 2026); TBAC Q2 2026 charge (May 2026) flags documentation backlog for done-away bilateral agreements as 'the largest challenge from an implementation standpoint.' Cash deadline Dec 31 2026 appears on track; repo deadline Jun 30 2027 has 'considerable work' remaining. (Sources: dtcc.com press release 22 Sep 2026; sec.gov Uyeda statement 7 Aug 2026; home.treasury.gov TBAC Q2 2026 charge May 2026)
rationale: The rubric scores 1 (FRICTION) for documentation backlog or pending exemptive relief or readiness surveys <60% 'very confident.' The June 2026 survey confirms an active documentation/legal backlog (88% of delayed firms cite contract negotiation) and unresolved exemptive-relief petitions still in SEC comment as of Aug 2026; while the cash deadline looks achievable, the repo leg shows material execution gaps — matching the FRICTION definition precisely. No deadline extension or major operational failure (score 2) has occurred.

dissent.view: US officials (USTR Greer, Sep 2026) state China's rare-earth deliveries 'have not been up to par' and China added MP Materials and USA Rare Earth to its export-control entity list in June 2026 - signalling partial breach of spirit of truce.

fact: On 23 Sep 2026, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US and China agreed to extend their trade truce - including China's suspension of rare-earth export controls - by two months to 10 January 2027, pushing back the original 10 Nov 2026 expiry. Source: ms.now / Reuters reporting, 23 Sep 2026.
rationale: The truce is formally extended and in force through 10 Jan 2027, well beyond the Nov-2026 nominal expiry, satisfying rubric level 0 (EXTENDED/holding). Partial compliance fraying (delayed rare-earth deliveries, June 2026 entity-list additions to MP Materials/USA Rare Earth) is noted by officials but did not prevent extension and is not sufficient to shift the reading to level 1.

dissent.view: Some analysts (Atalayar, Aug 2026; African Arguments, Sep 2026) characterize Egypt's documented military strike planning and proxy encirclement of Ethiopia as crossing into de facto conflict-level behavior that could merit a '2' classification.
Other analysts (FPRI, Oct 2025; pppescp.com, Mar 2026) assess armed conflict likelihood as 'relatively low' given the structural and logistical constraints on Egypt projecting force against GERD.

fact: Two active disputes: (1) GERD/Nile — Egypt reaffirmed at UNGA on 26 Sep 2026 that Nile water is a 'non-negotiable existential priority'; Ethiopia's army chief accused Egypt of backing Tigray rebels as of 27 Sep 2026 (Euronews/AP); Egypt's MoD has active operational strike plans vs. GERD (Atalayar, Aug 2026); diplomacy frozen, no binding treaty, no direct kinetic action or deliberate flow cut-off confirmed. (2) Indus — India kept treaty in 'abeyance' since Apr 2025, rejected Hague Court of Arbitration ruling of 31 Aug 2026 that treaty 'remains fully in force' (Al Jazeera/Bloomberg, 1 Sep 2026); Permanent Indus Commission has not met since May 2022; Pakistan's Defense Minister made conditional war statement in June 2026 (CNBC, 22 Jun 2026).
rationale: Both disputes are at rubric level 1: the Indus Waters Treaty is formally suspended/contested by India despite an international ruling, and the GERD dispute features official war threats and proxy-conflict accusations exchanged at the UN level — but no confirmed armed clash between riparian states over the dams/rivers, nor any deliberate flow cut-off, has been documented, keeping both below the level-2 threshold.

dissent.view: Some media (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) characterise BRICS Pay as already 'live' or 'operational' in 2026 with 67% intra-bloc local-currency trade; this overstates execution — SGT Report and EBC confirm the New Delhi summit leaders only 'took note' and no fully unified live system was launched.

Modern Diplomacy (Dec 2025) and kohenavocats.com (Sept 2026) describe an EU 'push' toward permanent seizure of Russian assets in September 2026; however this remains a political proposal, not an executed confiscation, so Band 2 is not met.

fact: The 18th BRICS Summit (New Delhi, 12-13 Sept 2026) unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration, which formally endorsed BRICS Pay as a decentralized cross-border local-currency settlement platform and expanded the BRICS Payment Task Force mandate; however, BRICS Pay was NOT operationally launched — leaders 'took note' and the declaration called for continued work, with no common currency created and no sovereign reserve seizure executed. On the reserve-freeze front, Russian CBR assets (~€260-300bn) remain frozen/immobilised in Western jurisdictions but have NOT been seized/confiscated; as of late September 2026 the debate remains political/legal, with the CBR filing an annulment action before the EU General Court on 3 March 2026. Sources: Irish Times (10 Sept 2026), SGT Report (Sept 2026), Forbes India BRICS 2026 takeaways, kohenavocats.com (Sept 2026), Brookings.
rationale: The New Delhi Declaration constitutes official rhetoric plus a formal mandate endorsement for non-dollar settlement (BRICS Pay), placing the event squarely in Band 1 (TALK/agreement without operational execution). No new sovereign reserve seizure was executed in 2026; Russian assets remain frozen under existing 2022 measures, not newly confiscated, so Band 2 is not triggered.

dissent.view: Some sources frame 2026 conditions as severe queue congestion and project delays (Level 1 territory) without referencing the emergency curtailment orders, focusing on the 2,600 GW national interconnection backlog and 5-12 year wait times as the primary story.

IEA Electricity 2026 report characterises the situation as projects 'stalled in connection queues worldwide' and a need to raise grid investment by 50% by 2030 -- framing that implies structural tightness rather than active curtailment events.

fact: The U.S. DOE invoked Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act at least three times in 2026 to curtail data-center loads on PJM and ERCOT: (1) ERCOT emergency order 202-26-01 issued Jan 24 2026 (DOE.gov); (2) PJM emergency order issued May 18 2026 (Utility Dive, May 19 2026); (3) two PJM emergency orders in effect July 1-3 2026 during a record 168,158 MW peak, forcing data centers >=50 MW onto diesel backup within 15 minutes (electricchoice.com / techtimes.com, July 4 2026). In parallel, New York passed a statewide data-center moratorium (July 2026) and Texas halted new data-center permits pending an energy audit (Sept 2026), per environmentamerica.org.
rationale: Confirmed curtailment of data-center load under declared federal grid emergencies satisfies the rubric's Level 2 threshold exactly; multiple separate DOE 202(c) orders on both PJM and ERCOT constitute confirmed forced curtailment and declared grid emergencies, not merely warnings or forecasts. State-level power-scarcity-driven moratoria (NY, TX) add further corroboration.

dissent.view: Some analysts argue the gap is effectively 'closing' for AWS specifically, citing AI at a $25B+ run rate growing triple digits and AWS margin expansion to above pre-AI-cycle levels, suggesting returns are arriving faster than feared.
Meta's FCF collapsed (only $12B against $145B capex plan) and markets punished Meta ~6% for raising capex without proportional revenue proof, suggesting for Meta the dynamic may be closer to score 2.

fact: Combined hyperscaler 2026 capex guided ~$725B, up ~77% YoY (vs ~$410B in 2025); Microsoft FY26Q3 capex $30.9B–$34.9B up ~85% YoY with AI revenue run rate $37B +123% YoY; Google Cloud Q2 2026 +82% YoY; AWS Q2 2026 +37% YoY (fastest in 18 quarters); Amazon raised 2026 capex to ~$220B; Alphabet to $195–205B; Microsoft to ~$190B. Sources: Microsoft FY26 Q3 press release (Apr 29 2026, microsoft.com/investor), tech-insider.org Oct 11 2026, earningsshot.com Jul 2026.
rationale: Capex growth (~77–100% YoY aggregate) materially exceeds AI-attributable cloud revenue growth (~37–82% YoY), placing the gap firmly 'WIDE'; however, AI revenue is still strongly accelerating YoY across all four hyperscalers with no guidance cuts, so rubric score 1 applies rather than 2.

fact: Affirm Q4 FY2026 Earnings Supplement (Aug 27, 2026): 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans ex-Peloton/Pay-in-X = 2.5%, down from 2.7-2.8% in prior three quarters but up ~29 bps YoY in FQ3'26 per shareholder letter; cohort net charge-offs track ~3.5% of GMV (lifetime vintage). CFPB Dec-2025 report: aggregate BNPL pay-in-four charge-off rate 1.83% in 2023 (latest official figure). Richmond Fed Feb-2026: 'no direct evidence of rising aggregate BNPL charge-off rates to date.'
rationale: 30+ DPD rose ~18-29 bps YoY through mid-FY2026 before improving in Q4, placing it squarely in the RISING band; the <100 bps YoY move precludes Score 2, and charge-offs remain below 3% on the regulator's pay-in-four series and below 5% on Affirm's own vintage metric, consistent with Score 1.

dissent.view: September 2025 Red Sea cuts to SMW4/IMEWE/FALCON/EIG may still be unrepaired given repair-ship scarcity and geopolitical permitting delays in Red Sea conflict zone
Iran threat to cut Hormuz cables assessed as operationally feasible and affecting project planning, implying elevated risk beyond mere threat

fact: On 6 September 2025, at least four Red Sea cables (SMW4, IMEWE, FALCON GCX, Europe India Gateway) were severed near Jeddah by likely commercial anchor drag, causing internet degradation across India, Pakistan, Gulf states and Africa (Capacity Global / Gulf News, Sept 2025). PEACE and AAE-1 cuts from early 2025 were repaired by April 2025. No confirmed new Red Sea, Baltic, or Hormuz cut is reported in 2026; Iran issued credible Hormuz cable-cut threats (Asia Times, Sept 2026) and Baltic incidents remain under hybrid-warfare investigation but no unrepaired severance confirmed.
rationale: The Sept 2025 Red Sea multi-cable cut is the most recent confirmed severing event but ~13 months elapsed and prior cuts of similar scale were repaired within weeks-to-months, so current severed status is unconfirmed; Iran Hormuz threats and ongoing Baltic hybrid-warfare pattern constitute credible ongoing threats, mapping to rubric level 1 (THREATENED) rather than 2 (CUT), as no market-corroborated unrepaired outage is confirmed for October 2026.

dissent.view: Aon H1 2026 estimate of $47bn is slightly above the 21st-century H1 average per Aon's own framing ('slightly above the 21st-century average'), though still below Munich Re's 10-year H1 average of $50bn and Swiss Re's trend of $66bn

fact: H1 2026 global insured nat-cat losses: USD 42bn (Swiss Re Institute, Aug 11 2026), 16% below the 10-year average of ~USD 50bn for H1; Munich Re confirms USD 44bn vs 10-yr avg of USD 50bn (Jul 30 2026); Aon estimates USD 47bn (H1 2026 recap). Hurricane Isaias (first hurricane of season, Cat 3 at peak) made landfall ~Oct 9-10 with pre-landfall insured loss estimates of USD 4-6bn (BMS/Gallagher Re, Oct 9 2026, theinsurer.com), explicitly below USD 10bn. No single 2026 event has exceeded USD 10bn insured. YTD total remains below the 10-year average.
rationale: YTD insured losses are below the 10-year average through H1 and the only hurricane of the season (Isaias) is tracking to sub-$10bn insured losses; both conditions required for NORMAL (0) are met - YTD <= 10y average and no single event >$10bn.

dissent.view: Bloomberg (reported via agbull.com, Aug 27 2026) indicates China's 2026 urea export allowance was expanded to ~5.0-5.5 Mt, near 2025 levels, suggesting partial normalization on nitrogen -- though phosphate restrictions remain firm.

fact: China's NDRC-linked phosphate export suspension (announced Dec 2025, extended March 2026 to cover additional phosphate varieties and NK blends) continues through at least end-2026; the 2026 urea export quota is set at 3.3 million tonnes with FOB price floors of $430-440/t -- a 34% cut vs 2025 actuals -- though Bloomberg (Aug 2026) reports the allowance was later revised up to ~5 Mt. Food Security Portal August 2026 update: 'phosphate stayed tight on constrained Sulphur supply and China's continuing export suspension.' (Sources: foodsecurityportal.org Aug 2026; S&P Global/Platts Dec 11 2025; fertilizerdaily.com Jul 29 2026; procurementinstitute.io; discoveryalert.com Sep 2026)
rationale: Active phosphate export suspension and urea volume quota with price floors are both confirmed in effect as of August-September 2026, squarely matching rubric level 1 (restrictions in place, unchanged). The last confirmed broadening occurred in March 2026, outside the trailing 3-month window from Oct 12 2026, so level 2 is not warranted.

fact: China PPI rose +3.8% year-on-year in August 2026, per NBS release dated 9 September 2026 (landedmath.com citing NBS; corroborated by admiralmarkets.com preview table and investing.com calendar). September 2026 data is not yet published; NBS release scheduled 14 October 2026.
rationale: The rubric requires the signed YoY percent as published by NBS; +3.8% is the latest confirmed official figure. The engine scores on magnitude: +3.8% is a moderately elevated positive reading, signalling cost-push pressure at factory gates that could export input-cost inflation to trading partners.

dissent.view: ICI submitted a letter to Acting Chair Uyeda in Feb 2025 requesting a further extension of at least 24 months (to at least Jun 30 2028) for Treasury repo clearing; if granted this would push to score 2, but SEC has publicly refused further extension as of Sep 2026.

TBAC (May 2026) noted 'it is possible that clearing will not be available to all participants in all regions by the deadline,' signaling readiness risk but stopping short of characterizing a second delay.

fact: On Feb 25, 2025 the SEC formally extended compliance dates by one year (90 FR 11134, eff. Mar 4 2025): cash from Dec 31 2025 to Dec 31 2026; repo from Jun 30 2026 to Jun 30 2027. As of Sep 22 2026, Acting Chair Uyeda stated at the 2026 U.S. Treasury Market Conference that 'the SEC does not currently intend to extend these deadlines' (sec.gov, Sept 22 2026). No second extension has been announced; the Dec 31 2026 cash deadline has not yet passed.
rationale: One official 12-month extension was formally granted (Feb 2025), satisfying the rubric's score-1 criterion of 'an official extension granted.' No second extension has been announced and the first deadline has not yet passed, so rubric score 2 is not triggered.

dissent.view: KBRA reports a higher office CMBS delinquency rate of ~12.8% (Feb-Mar 2026) due to inclusion of a broader KBRA-rated universe and different loan classification methodology

fact: Trepp September 2026 CMBS office delinquency rate: 12.16%, up 16 bps from August's 12.00%; per vaquerowealth.com (Oct 6 2026) and curatedcommercial.substack.com (Oct 12 2026), both citing Trepp September 2026 data.
rationale: The Trepp September 2026 office CMBS delinquency rate of 12.16% is the most recent published figure and maps directly to the rubric, which calls for the latest percent reading from Trepp; this sits near cycle highs and reflects persistent maturity-default stress in the office sector.

dissent.view: ICSG preliminary monthly data showed a 51,000-tonne refined copper deficit for July 2026, suggesting the actual year-to-date trajectory may be tightening relative to the April full-year surplus forecast.

ICSG Jan-May 2026 preliminary data showed a 221,000-tonne apparent surplus (189,000t adjusted), well above the April full-year forecast of 96,000t surplus, pointing to a wider surplus than the annual projection.

fact: ICSG April 2026 Copper Market Forecast revised the 2026 refined copper balance to a surplus of approximately 96,000 tonnes, reversing its October 2025 projection of a 150,000-tonne deficit; source: ICSG via MarketScreener/IndexBox/MiningWeekly, dated 23 April 2026.
rationale: A forecast surplus of +96,000t sits just outside the +/-100kt balanced band on the surplus side, mapping to rubric band 0 (SURPLUS). Confidence is medium because the margin is narrow — only ~4kt beyond the balanced threshold — and ICSG's own July 2026 monthly data showed a 51,000-tonne deficit, suggesting the full-year balance remains highly uncertain.

dissent.view: electricchoice.com (Oct 2026) claims '482 moratoria currently in force across 44 states' — a figure far higher than other trackers and likely includes proposed/pending actions or very minor local ordinances, not just enacted construction pauses

fact: New York Governor Hochul signed Executive Order No. 62 on July 14, 2026, imposing the first enacted statewide data center moratorium in the U.S. (pausing DEC permits for facilities ≥50 MW). Additionally, DLA Piper (July 2026) reported 'more than 100 local moratoria have been adopted nationwide,' with confirmed enacted pauses in Baltimore MD (June 16), Snohomish County WA (June 24), St. Charles MO (May 19 permanent ban), Lysander NY (May 7), Austin County TX, and multiple Indiana counties, among others. Sources: davispolk.com (July 23, 2026); dlapiper.com (July 1, 2026); dcmap.us (Oct 2026).
rationale: Rubric level 2 requires a statewide moratorium enacted OR >10 jurisdictions with enacted pauses: New York's EO 62 (July 14, 2026) is a confirmed enacted statewide moratorium, and corroborating sources document well over 10 additional local enacted pauses across multiple states, satisfying both prongs of the top band.

dissent.view: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index: 2.51% for Q2 2026 (counts payment and financial-covenant defaults only, excludes maturity extensions)
KBRA Middle Market Default Monitor by count: 3.3% for twelve months to 30 June 2026 (adds imminent defaults and interventions)
KBRA Middle Market Default Monitor by debt: 2.4% for twelve months to 30 June 2026 (dollar-weighted)
Moody's private credit estimate: 1.6%-4.7% range for full-year 2025 (range depends on whether distressed exchanges are counted)

fact: Fitch Ratings reported the trailing 12-month US private credit default rate (across ~1,300 borrowers, inclusive of distressed exchanges and liability-management exercises) rose to a record 6.3% at end-August 2026, up from 6.1% in July; Fitch also recorded the highest monthly default event total in the prior 12 months (14 events in August). rationale: The 6.3% Fitch TTM print (August 2026) is the load-bearing fact under the rubric: it uses Fitch's broad definition inclusive of distressed exchanges and maturity extensions, is a fresh record above the April 2026 prior record of 6.0%, and no newer Fitch monthly print is publicly available as of 2026-10-12. The escalating trajectory — 5.7% Q1 → 6.0% Q2/April-May → 6.1% July → 6.3% August — corroborates sustained and worsening funding stress in private credit, consistent with elevated PIK-loan reliance and dealer-balance-sheet sensitivity to middle-market credit deterioration.

dissent.view: By ~August 2026, recent rainfall improved southern Taiwan reservoir levels, reducing immediate pressure on industrial water supplies — suggesting conditions may have retreated from acute to emerging by Q4 2026.

The US Southwest concurrently improved to D0-D1 after tropical moisture (USDM Oct 8, 2026), so Taiwan is the binding region driving the score.

fact: Within the trailing 3 months (July–October 2026): (US/allied side) BIS June 1 2026 notice extended AI-chip licensing requirements to Chinese-company subsidiaries outside China; South Korea joined the Netherlands and Japan in licensing advanced chipmaking-equipment exports effective September 1 2026 (AsiaAI Chip Export Controls Tracker, updated ~Oct 1 2026); the MATCH Act (DUV blanket ban on ASML sales to China) remains before Congress. rationale: Both sides have enacted new export-control measures in the trailing 3 months: the US/allied bloc tightened semiconductor-equipment licensing (South Korea join, June BIS guidance) and China enacted retaliatory entity-list additions targeting US and EU firms plus a new legal retaliation framework — satisfying rubric level 2 (target country countermeasures active). dissent.view: A Phoenix city government release (July 2026) cited by tech-insider.org projects ~30% of 2nm-and-beyond capacity in Arizona 'once expanded fabs are complete' — a forward-looking estimate, not current operational capacity.

dissent.view: Paradigm GENIUS Act Rulemaking Tracker shows '0/25 Final Rule completed' as of ~Oct 2026, consistent with a deadline miss but frames agency misses as common and without formal penalty, implying limited systemic consequence.

fact: The GENIUS Act Section 13 rulemaking deadline of July 18, 2026 passed with zero final rules published by any primary federal regulator (OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, NCUA, Treasury/FinCEN/OFAC). As of October 2, 2026, 13+ NPRMs and one interim final rule had been issued but none finalized; the Federal Reserve only issued its NPRM on September 24, 2026 with comments open until November 30, 2026; the OCC is targeting a final rule by November 2026. There is no court stay or compliance-failure event, but the plain deadline miss with zero finalized rules is sufficient for a 2 rating.

fact: The Second Lecornu government (formed 10 Oct 2025) is the incumbent minority government of France. It has survived multiple no-confidence votes (most recently 2 Feb 2026, when two motions fell short of the 289-vote threshold), invoked Article 49.3 repeatedly to pass the 2026 budget, and PM Lecornu remains in office as of 9-10 Oct 2026. Sources: Wikipedia 'Second Lecornu government'; Euronews 02 Feb 2026; Al Jazeera 02 Feb 2026; JPost 09 Oct 2026.
rationale: France operates under a hung parliament with an explicit minority-coalition status; the government has governed only by deploying Art. 49.3 and surviving successive no-confidence votes without ever holding a working majority — the textbook definition of rubric band 1 (FRAGILE). No collapse, resignation, or dissolution has occurred.

dissent.view: Moody's awarded its first-ever Aaa to a data center securitization (Compass Datacenters, $830M, Feb 2026), and CoreWeave closed an $8.5B investment-grade GPU-backed facility in Q2 2026, suggesting the rated/hyperscaler tier is still accessing markets normally.
